WEARY.

I would that you had folded my tired hands, So weary grown with reaching forth in vain. I would that you had put me by to sleep Beneath the tender grass and splashing rain, And that with softened voice at eventide, With gathering tears you spoke of me and said That I was gone to that dim, distant land Where peace and rest are to the quiet dead. But no, it may not be, for I must tread With faltering, tired steps, the path of life • No, I must bear the scorching armour's weight, And wield my heavy sword amidst the strife. Tify head is dizzy, and my eyes are dim; Oh God, who are my foes, and who my friends ?! I struggle madly in the bitter fight, But cannot see which way the battle tends. Oh, shall I ever reach the pearly gate, And tread the golden streets within the wall? Shall I look back o'er all the way I trod, Paved thick with tombs, and shadowed by the pall? I would that you had folded my tired hands, And put me in the quiet grave to rest; Or care, or grief could ever reach me there, Like child soft sleeping on its mother's breast. PATTY HONEYWOOD.

Practice flews from principle; for as a man thinks so will he act. The slowest man ever heard of was one who could not get out of his own way. That circumference cannot be small of which God is the oentre.—Hannah More. The youth who would have a will of his own has been struck out of that of his father. In a game of cards, a good deal depends on good playing, and good playing depends on a good deal. People say that blackberries are good for the complexion; but who wants a blackberry complexion? The foundation of all happiness, temporal and spiritual, is faith in the goodness, the righteousness, and the lot e of God.—F. W. Robertson. So that they may not make beasts of themselves, the 716 persons who travel with Barnum's beast show are pledged to total abstinence from all intoxicants during the existence of their engagement. Some one jocularly observed to the Marquis Wellesley, that in his arrangements of the Ministry, his brother, the Duke, had thrown him overboard. "Yes," said the Marquis, "but I trust I have strength enough to swim to the other side." Louisa had the toothache, and cried. Her mother tried to pacify her. "I'm ashamed of you. I wouldn't be such a baby before everybody," said she. "Oh, yes, mamma. it's all very well for you; when your teeth ache you can take them out." Kind words produce their own image in men's souls, and a beautiful image it is. They soothe and comfort the hearer. They shame him out of his unkind feelings. We have not yet begun to use them in such abundance as they ought to be used.—Pascal. A four-year-old, visiting a neighbour, was asked if she would have bread and butter. "No, thank you," she said; "mamma said I must not take bread and butter when from home ;" but suddenly brightening up, she added, "but she said nothing about cookies." Life is a leaf of paper, white, Whereon each one of us may write His word or two, and then comes night; Though thou have time But for a line, be that sublime; Not failure, but low aim, is crime.—J. R. Lowell:

• A FIRM-HOUSE LEGEND.—There is an immense fund of romance and tradition associated with our old farm-houses. This is particularly so in Essex, a county which it is the fashien to consider uninteresting, although, as a matter of fact, it is among the most romantic of the forty. In the parish of Tolleshunt Knights, near Kelvedon, there is to be let Barn Hall Farm, the property of Sir Thomas Ardy, Bart., a farm which rejoices in a very eerie legend indeed. The legend is that Barn Hall was intended, originally, to be built upon another and less picturesque site. The materials were brought to the spot, and the moat was actually made. When matters had proceeded as far, a great potentate, who shall be nameless, interfered. For some unexplained reason his Majesty had a strong objection to the site, and, taking up one of the wooden beams prepared for the new house, he threw it a full mile away, exclaiming— Where this beam fall Shall stand Sam Ball. The builder waa not disposed to try conclusions with his royal visitor, and so did as he was bid. His Majesty's no- tions of the picturesque were very correct, for the house commands some beautiful views across an undulating coun- try to the German Ocean.—Land.

CONCEALING His ADVANTAGES.—OId Ned's son returned from college the other day. The old man had looked for- ward to the event, and had arranged a dinner, to which he invited a number of acquaintances. The young man was modest, and to the great humiliation of his father made no attempt to clisplay his learning. The old man waited seve- ral days, and when at last he saw no evidence of his son's education, he approached him and said—" Jim, it do seem ter me dat ye's puffin' yer edycation ter a mighty po' use. I ain't heard a big word from yer yet. I can un'erstan' yer gis as well as I did for yer went ter dat school. Ef a man's edycated I wants him ter talk 20 as I can't nnderstan' him. Me an' yer madder had been talking 'bout this matter, an' we'se grieved way down in de flesh. Jim, what's de big word fur.grasshopper ?" " Orthopterous insect of the genus Gryllus, according to Webster,' replied the young man. "But de tuther day, when dem folks was heah, ye spoke of a grasshopper just de same as de ignorest nigger in de coun- try, an' brought shame down on de heads ob madder an' myself. What's de big word fur goat ?" "Mammiferous quadruped of the genus Capra," answered the young man. "But why didn't yer say so 'stead ob saying goat like a niggar, an' bringin' de tingle ob embarrassment to yer fader's face? What did I gin yer dal schoolin' fur; ter talk like an unedycated son ob a po' white man? Think dat I'se gwine ter keep yer heah in idleness 'lessen yer ken refleck credic on de family? Jim, what is de big word for blamed fool ?" "I don't know, sir." " Yer doan ? Den yer ain't acquainted wid yerself. Yer doan recognise whar yer stands. Go out dar in de field wid a mule an' identify yerself." CARDINAL MANNING'S CAREKR.—Cardinal Manning is in his seventy-fourth year. He is the son of the late William Manning, M.P. and Governor of the Bank of England, and was educated at Harrow and Baliol, migrating thence after, taking the highest honours, to become a Fellow of Merton. i He is a typical public school man, and could scarcely have been at any but a fashionable public school. Men who have not had such a training may have courtly manners, may be thorough men of the world; those educated at home may have equal, sometimes more, erudition; but the combina- tion of learning worn lightly like a flower, great frankness of manner with power of reticence when needed, aptness for oeing at home in any society, from the rough to the cour- tier, and simple unconscious ease, are generally to be found among Englishmen only in those educated at our first-class public schools. These were the qualities which, joined with his birth and his father's position, gave him, even as a young man, a commanding influence in Oxford society, which raised him to be Archdeacon of Chichester at the early age of thirty-two, and which have made him so great a power in his own communion since he joined it. They have also given him influence among very various classes of society, especially among the great, so that his brother-in-law, the late Bishop of Winchester, smarting under the desertion of his friend, and unable to deny himself the use of epigram, called him the "apostle of the genteels." He became Rec- tor of Lavington and Graffham, in Sussex, in 1834, and married the youngest Miss Serjeant, one of the co-heiresses of the Lavington property, two other sisters having mar- ried Samuel Wilberforce, afterwards Bishop, and Henry Wilberforce, his brother. Mrs. Manning survived her mar- riage but a few months. . . . . When the spiritual grace of baptism was denied by Mr. Gorham, and his view pronounced to be tenable within the Church of Eng- land, Archdeacon Manning, with many others felt the very ground on which they stood cat from under them. If the Church of England denied sacramental 'grace, which to them involved the very essence of religion, there was indeed nowhere to turn but to the Church of Rome, however impossible it had once seemed that they should do so. Immediately after the Gorham judgment was pronounced, Archdeacon Manning shook from his feet the dust of an heretical Church, to join that towards which his steps had so long unconsciously been advancing; when no doubt he found that the boundaries were by no means so difficult to overstep as they had seemed to him on that November day. After the short retirement, inevitable on his change, preparatory to taking orders in the Church of his adoption, his rise was rapid and signal. He, too, like his brother cardinal, founded a congregation, that of the Oblates of St. Charles Borromeo, filling in the interim the dignified office of Provost of Westminster. In 1865, Mon- signor Manning was consecrated Archbishop of Westminster. In 1875, he was created a cardinal with the title of Saints Andrew and Gregory. Since his appointment as archbishop few men have ever been more before the world. Not only is he a constant preacher in and a frequent preacher out of his diocese; not only has he been a combatant in intellec- tual contests, especially in the Metaphysical Society, a club which met monthly, where he held his own with such dis- putants as Dr. Martineau, Mr. Frederick Harrison. and Pro- fessor Huxley,—he has also taken part in the social life of London to such an extent that there is hardly a philan- thropic work in which he could consistently co-operate wherein he has not been a sharer. Conspicuous above all has been the aid that he has given to total abstinence socie- ties both in and out of his Church. In politics he is under- stood to take a strongly democratic view, and has been heard to say that, were he not what he is, his choice would be to be a demagogue. On the Irish question, and to some extent on the extreme Irish side, he has been very outspoken; and should it hereafter prove to be possible that the Catholic Church, at least in the West, should ally herself with the cause of the people, as distinguished from the cause of the oligarchs, Cardinal Manning's name will be found on the rol- of those who have helped the fusion.—The Centur. y.

div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Lott Rayleigh has, it is stated, accepted the presidency I of the meeting of the British Association in Canada in I 18S-1. The Athenannt understands that 410 members have now declared their intention of being present at the Mon- treal meeting. Senor Bolivar has recently returned to Madrid, after an extensive exploration of Morocco. He has secured more than a thousand species of insects, reptiles, and birds, as well as a large collection of plants, many of them quite new to science. A gentleman living at Montreal recently ordered from England the works of Professor Huxley, Professor Tyndall, and Mr. Herbert Spencer. But the books were all stopped by the Collector of Customs, and confiscated as being "im- moral, irreligious, and injurious." A similar thinghas been known to happen at Oxford.—Aeade2ny. Mr. John Francis Ure, well known as engineer to the Tyne Improvement Commissioners, is dead. The improve- ments effected by Mr. Ure in the navigation of the Tyne have placed him in the first rank of his profession. Mr. Ure was the senior partner of the firm of John Elder and Co., the shipbuilders and engineers of the Clyde.—A thenaum. ' A Turin jeweller has made a tiny boat formed of a single pearl, which shape it assumes in swell and concavity. Its sail is of beaten gold, studded with diamonds, and the bin- nacle light at its prow is a perfect ruby. An emerald serves as its rudder, and its stand is a slab of ivory. It weighs less than half an ounce. Its price is £l,OOO. A niece of Burns, being the daughter of Mrs. Begg,, sister of the poet, died last week at the age of 83. For the last forty years she had lived near Alloway Kirk; and she.was ever ready to impart her family knowledge to all who paid a pilgrimage to that historic spot. Such knowledge she had derived not only from her own mother, but also from the mother of the poet, with whom she passed several years of her early life. THE NATIONAL GALLERIES.—The sum devoted to the purchase of pictures for the National Gallery is, for 1882-3, £25,600, for the National Portrait Gallery £2,727, and for the National Gallery, Ireland, £2,000; the Gallery of Edin- burgh receives nothing. This is a veritable Scottish griev- ance, and we would suggest that some of the northern re- presentatives to Parliament—Lord Bosebery or Dr. Stewart —should take the matter up, and endeavour to secure a , sum which will allow a nation with much artistic instinct ' to acquire at least one new picture every year.—Art

Journal. TIIE ELECTRIC RESISTANCE OF GLASS.—M. Foussereau has lately -measured the electric resistance of glass by charging a condenser from a known battery through a given thickness of the glass, and observing the time required to raise the potential of the condenser to a given degree. Bo- hemian glass was found to be from 5 to 20 times as good a conductor as ordinary glass, whilst flint glass was from 1,000 to 1,500 times as good an isolator. M. Foussereau found also that annealing the glass increased its resistance in some cases elevenfold.

The Athenantna says :—An unfortunate newspaper pro- prietor at Breslau has been found guilty of the terrible offence of " Majestiitsbeleidigung." He is said to have ap- plied when at the theatre an epithet, "blase," belonging to the argot of Silesia, to the Emperor William and his Court. The accused protested that he did not remember having used the word, and that, if he did, he did not intend to apply it to the Emperor or his Court ; and a specialist in Silesian slang was called who declared that the word had sno offensive meaning. However, the Court held it might have, and condemned the accused. P. Roblet, a Roman Catholic missionary stationed in Madagascar, has collected materials for a new map of the province of Imerina. He has ascended the TsiAfajavona, or cloud-capped mountain," the highest peak of Ankaratra and of the whole island, and determined its height at 8,633 feet. Another French missionary, P. Causseque, has pub- lished a French grammar in Malagasy. There were in July last 80,905 Roman Catholics in the island, with 48 priests, 20 sisters, and 538 teachers. The schools were attended by 19,103 children. A "History of the Catholic Mission," and a work on native customs, &c., are about to be printed at the French mission press at Tanarivo.—ilthenteum. In view of a possibly hot summer, the Corporation of London are taking precautions against any excessive effluvia from their abbatoirs at Deptford, where all foreign cattle and sheep are compulsorily slaughtered on landing. Ther- mometers are fixed to give daily records not only of the temperature and humidity of the air, but of the heat of the Thames at the surface and at a depth of ten and twenty feet. Hitherto these observations have been made by the Royal Observatory. The summer of 1846, when the heat of the Thames water registered 73 degrees, was noted for its abominable stinks. It was the same again in 1859. Yes- terday the heat of the Thames was 57 degrees. About 18,000 sheep and 6,000 beasts are slaughtered every week at Deptford. ARTIFICIAL LEATHER FROM LEATHER WASTE. —An artificial leather, consisting of leather waste mixed with five to ten per cent. of sinew and pressed in sheets like ordinary cardboard, has recently been made in Germany. Both materials are prepared separately; the leather pieces are washed, cut, boiled in alkaline lye, torn, neutralised with hydrochloric acid, and finally carefully washed once more to remove all traces of acid; the sinews are treated simi- larly, but steamed in an acid bath until they begin to assume the consistence of glue. The materials are then mixed, pressed into sheets, moistened on both sides with a concentrated solution of alum, and the upper surface is finally treated with a thin coat of a solution of caontchouc in carbon bisulphide to increase its resemblance to leather. Engineering. THE ULTRA-VIOLET RATS.—M. de Chardonnet has en-

deavoured to ascertain the behaviour of the ultra-violet rays ta the ocular media, and has determined that they can traverse the cornea and vitreous humour, but are absolutely intercepted by the crystalline lens, so that under normal circumstances the sensitive plate of the retina is unaffected by them. In order to determine the precise role played by the retina, recourse was had to two persons on whom the operation of extraction of the lens had been successfully performed. These individuals were placed behind a glass coated with silver, before which an electric arc burned. From descriptions of the form and movements of the arc given by the observers, of which arc they had no knowledge prior to experiment, it was proved that the ultra-violet rays did affect the retina.

CURIOUS PROPERTY OP MAGNETIC OXIDE. A paper was read at a meeting of the Society of Engineers recently by Mr. G. Bower, on the Bower-Barff process of preserving and ornamenting iron and steel surfaces, in which the pro- cesses were described, and models of the improved furnace were shown. Mr. Bower exhibited a very curious pro- perty of magnetic oxide. He applied brushes formed of wires of different metals, first of all, to a casting which was not coated, and on which no effect was produced; then to a similar one which had been coated, when the casting was immediately covered at all the parts touched by the brush with a beautiful shining coat of the metal of which the brash was formed. He attributes this result to the fact that magnetic oxide, not being metallic, and to some extent gritty and porous, had rubbed off by attrition some of the metal from the wires; and he expected that this would supersede the existing methods of bronzing and of deposit- ing metals for the commoner kinds of Birmingham goods. A NEW TRICYCLE.—Mr. W. J. Fraser, who has long studied the mechanical properties of tricycles, has intro- duced a new one, which is better suited to the natural movements of the body than the older types. It is worked both by hands and feet, and the weight of the body is uti- lised in driving it. In appearance it is like an ordinary " front-steerer," made of a steel tube frame, with two large driving wheels four feet six inches in diameter, and a front steering wheel fifteen inches in diameter. The pedals hang on a central bar supported across the frame work. The hand-levers are vertical, and also supported by the frame work. The handles are level with the elbow, and placed within easy reach. A saddle seat is provided over the pedals, allowing the legs freedom to swing and work the pedals, as if the rider were walking and at the same time sitting. On ascending a hill the tricyclist throws all his weight on the pedals. The machine is adapted to suit the movements of the body in walking, and is likely to prove a decided improvement on the ordinary tricycle.—Cassell's Family 31agaz1ne.

A PRz-HrsTogic CEMETERY.—Two miles from Mandan (Dakota), says the Pioneer, a paper published at that place, on the bluffs near the junction of the Hart and Missouri rivers, is an old cemetery of fully 100 acres in extent filled with bones of a giant race. This vast city of the dead lies

just east of the—Fort Lincoln-road. The ground aas the appearance of having been filled with trenches piled full of dead bodies, both man and beast, and covered with several feet of earth. In many places mounds from Bft. to 10ft. high, and some of them 100 ft. or more in length, have been thrown up and are filled with bones, broken pottery, vases of various bright-coloured flints, and agates. The pottery is of a dark material, beautifully decorated, delicate in finish, and as light as wood, showing the work of a people skilled in the arts and possessed of a high state of civilisa- tion. This has evidently been a grand battle-field, where thousands of men and horses have fallen. Nothing like a systematic or intelligent exploration has been made, as only little holes two or three feet in depth have been dug in some of the mounds, but many parts of the anatomy of man and beast, and beautiful specimens of broken pottery and other curiosities, have been fonad in these feeble efforts at excavation. Five miles above Mandan, on the opposite side of the Missouri, is another vast cemetery, as yet unex- plored. We asked an aged Indian what his people knew of these ancient graveyards. He answered "Me know nothing about them. They were here before the red man."

An awkward-looking countryman, who was gazing into one of our shop windows one bright afternoon lately, attracted a good deal of attention on account of his odd dress and apparent verdancy. Becoming annoyed at last, he turned upon a man who was looking at him with opened- mouthed surprised, and sneeringly remarked, "I say, yeou, ef yeon keep yeonr mouth so wide open, yeou'll sunburn yeour teeth," and walked away, leaving the other to be :aughed at by the crowd, who always laugh with the win- ning party.

REVCCTION or RENT.—The Earl of Durham returned 10 per cent, to his tenants at the rent audit held at Chester-le- Street on Monday last. SIGNS OF' IMPROVEMEN'r.—As a sign of improving times, Messrs. Denn and Soman, land agents, of Tunbridge Wells and London, state that farms are letting readily at fair rents, and the demand for agricultural holdings this season is very great. Truly the lion and the lamb do fraternise sometimes. A correspondent writes :—" In a small covert here is an old main drain, in which a vixen fox has laid up her cubs, five in number; and on the top of the said drain a hen pheasant has her nest, at present containing ten eggs, which my head keeper intends taking when she has laid her full number." Professor Tanner, Director of Educatit,n under the Insti- tute of Agriculture, South Kensington, will shortly proceed to Canada with the object of making an official inspection of various portions of the Province. He will gladly extend his assistance to any who may be desirous of personally acquainting themselves with the special advantages pos- sessed by different portions of the Dominion of Canada. Some of the American papers report the existence of a "grain bug" in California, which is said to be destroying the wheat crop to a serious extent. All insects are " bugs ' in the United States, and as this particular creature is green, it may be the green aphis. A so-called " new insect," previously mistaken for the Hessian fly, is officially re- ported to be doing mischief to the wheat crop in Illinois. The best sign of a good farmer is to make the most of manure. Anyone can grow large crops on land already rich, but the secret is in maintaining fertility whilst so doing. The man who wastes the fertility of his land is running in debt as certainly as if he were adding to the mortgage every year. Such a loss of fertility is the most helpless kind of indebtedness. VERMIN.—The Breslau Agricultural Commission have made an offer of 1,000 marks for the most successful method of destroying field mice. A writer in a contem- porary quotes Dr. Max Schmidt, of the Frankfort Zoologi- cal Gardens, as to the success which has met his use of a new German remedy for the destruction of rats, called. " Gliricine." The rata eat it greedily, and no domestic ani- mal will touch it. HEAVY FINES.—Sir Hugh Dalrymple, Bart., and his brother magistrates, at a Justice of Peace Court at Had- , dington, last week, fined Mr. Jas. Davidson Harper, farmer, Snawdon, £5O, with the alternative of three months' im- prisonment, for removing 400 sheep infected with foot and mouth disease from two fields which had been declared "in- fected places" by the County Local Authority, to the hill land on his farm. For making a false declaration in order to obtain a license for the removal of two cows from Orton, Westmorland, to Leybourn, in Yorkshire, a cattle dealer from Gaisgill was fined £2O and £3 Os. costs. Entries for the twentieth annual horse show at the Ag- ricultural Hall finally closed on Monday. The show opens to-day, and will be divided into fifteen classes. The prize list will exceed £l,OOO in money, besides various challenge cups, medals, and plate. The hunters will occupy the four first classes, the prizes being £6O for first, £3O for second, and £2O for third best horses. The riding horses, covert hacks, and roadsters will be well represented. The display of harness horses; perk cobs, and ponies will be large, and the entries of stallion roadster trotters and Arabs are more numerous than on previous occasions. The leaping prizes have been increased.

Dips containing strong alkalis are injurious to the yolk of the wool, and render the wool itself harsh, destroying its lustre. Carbolic acid is not without its drawbacks when used on the skin of an animal, but when combined, with glycerine these seem to be nullified, and the dip so formed —an emulsion of carbolic acid miscible in cold or warm water—is very effective. Carbolic acid coagulates albumen and destroys the life of ticks, maggots, lice, acari, be., by asphyxiating them; it also destroys the eggs of the acarus, or scab parasite, and the eggs of flies, by coagulating the albumen they contain. Added to this, the glycerine softens and cleanses the skin and brightens the wool, whilst the odour of carbolic acid is very deterrent to insects of all kinds. The "Glycerine Dip" has been introduced to the notice of New Zealand sheep farmers. Several trials on a large scale have been reported by the New Zealand press, in one of which 5,000 sheep were dipped, and in each case great satisfaction was expressed at the result. A Napier paper states that in one of these public trials requested by the sheep inspector of the Napier district at the Ram Fair, a sheep which had an unusual number of ticks was selected, and the dip was prepared in the quantity of forty parts of water to one of the composition. The water was taken from an artesian well on the ground, which from its hard- ness was not considered the most suitable for the experi- ment, but an excellent solution was obtained, the sheep was immersed, and one minute afterwards every parasitg was dead. The dip is likely to prove of great value to colonial sheep farmers.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

POTATOES must now have some earth drawn up to them, and the quantity should be in proportion to the depth the tubers are planted. When we have planted early, that is as soon after Christmas as the weather would permit us work- ing the soil, we have placed the sets eight inches deep; in that case there was but little earth drawn to them, and others were not done at all, and we could not perceive any difference in the produce. When planting is done 4in. or 6in, deep all the earth that can be spared is drawn to them. We say "draw," for we invariably use a draw hoe for the purpose. some, we know, prefer the spade, but it can only surpass the hoe in those cases where the land has not been properly tilled. If we are dubiousf.phout its condition we examine it as soon as the plants are sufficiently advanced to indicate the rows, and if it is at all unkind we set to to fork it as deep as we can, and we allow it to remain roughly un- til it is crumbled by rain and winds. The earthing up can then be proceeded with with ease. If all the rows are done on one side first, when the other side comes to be done foot- marks will be obliterated.

PEAS will require staking, a troublesome and expensive business. We think the cheapest support for peas and scarlet runners is Gin, mesh tarred twine netting. It is to be purchased fot 3d. per yard, and will last long, especially if it is dipped in tar every two years. For fixing it is necessary to have a few stout stakes driven into the ground. Pieces of quartering are the best, and if put opposite can be braced at the top. The stakes can be fixed any time before the seeds are sown, rather better than when they are up, for there is liability to injure them. There should be two rows a foot apart, and two or three yards distant in the row. The nets can be attached when the peas demand it. Few will be bothered with sticks when they get accustomed to this useful contrivance.

RHUBARB should have the floivering stalks cut off, as they have a tendency to weaken the plants. Celery before being planted in the trenches should have the small leaves at the base carefully moved, also any small side shoots or suckers that may be seen. The weather being so dry we found it necessary to give celery plants a good watering, and they have held their heads up very well. TURNIPS require thinning. As we sow in rows we find it a very easy matter. An Bin. draw hoe is used to cut gaps of that length, leaving intermediate patches of four or five plants which in a few days will be gone over by hand and reduced to one plant. FRONT GARDEN.—This is becoming weekly more inte- resting. There are a few lingering primroses in flower, double daisies, wallflowers, white rock, violas, or violets as some call them, polyanthus, forget-me-not, iberis, alyssum, samatile, catha palustris flore plino, the two latter bearing yellow coloured flowers, lily of the valley, and a variety of blue bells, are an excellent collection, if they were only all represented by a plant or two in each garden. But after inspecting some dozens of gardens in this neighbourhood, we only saw one solitary specimen of each of the four last named, and they were in different gardens. The violas should have their seed pods picked if the plants are to maintain their respectability for the summer. Few plants can flower continually and produce seeds too. The latter are more exhausting than flowers. The double daisies he they become shabby may be taken up and planted in the back garden or grouped closer together in the front garden if there is no other accommodation, and remain so until re- quired next autumn or spring. The various kind of bedding geraniums may be planted, or some may have the pots plunged to the rim in the ground. In this way they will not grow so rampant, but will flower more freely. Old and ill-shaped fusehias will also do well in this way. The latter prefers a shady corner, and both may be taken up in the autumn and kept over the winter in-doors. Lobelias and verbenas are beautiful plants to embellish the front garden. The verbena is also one of the best flowers for cutting pur- poses. _ _

IMPORTED CATTLE INSPECTION IN FRANCE.—Very strin- gent regulations are now in force at the ports from which the exportation of live stock is permitted. Each animal must be submitted to inspection upon the quay before em- barkation, and a strict examination of the ship and gang- ways must be made. If a case of disease is discovered the certiiieate mast be refused to all animals of the same lot and all others which may have come in contact with the diseased animals. The landing-stages must be disinfected immediately after each departure. The veterinary inspec- tors are to receive per head for each horse, ass, or mule up to six animals, 60c., and above six 90c.; for each head of cattle, 60c. up to 12, and 90c. above; for each sheep or pig, 20c. up to 30, and 30c. above that number. TtsnsuP FLY.—Something was said in these columns a week or two ago with respect to the turnip fly, since which an interesting letter has been written by a gentleman who has given thought to the subject. He says that he noticed some years ago that the fly prefers white turnips to swedes, the former being usually sown upon the headlands. This induced him to sow them in between his drills, which he was enabled to do the more easily as he uses a drill with two hoppers. A third was introduced between these, so that at one and the same time the two rows of swedes and one row of white turnip seeds are deposited. In this way he sows 21b. per acre, and when it has served him it is hoed up with a horse hoe, and done with. He has found the greatest benefit, and has had a crop in the driest of seasons. SCOUR IN CatvEs.—There are many breeders of good stock who are troubled with scour among their calves at this season of the year, consequently chiefly upon their being turned out to grass. Remedies, it is true, are plenti- ful, but very few are successful. When a calf which is old enough to turn out has this complaint for a length of time and drugs fail, cotton-cake ground very fine and scalded will be found a useful remedy, and it will also give strength. If the scour is checked, then cake can be mixed in a day or two with oileake dust, hay chaff being given all the while. Then if all goes on right, in order to prepare the animal for green food, grass may be dried in the sun and chaffed with the hay. If this answers without any bad effect, the dry or wilted grass may be gradually increased until by degrees the calf is fitted for turning out, but the cake dust mixed may still be continued with advantage. APPLES FROM AUSTRALIA.—A small consignment of apples of various kinds grown at Melbourne has recently been received in this country. They were shipped at Mel- bourne on March Ist, and were landed in London on April 20th. They were exhibited at the evening meeting of the Royal Horticultural Society, held at Burlington House on the Bth inst. The apples were sent to this country to ascer- tain if they would bear the long sea voyage. March is the time when the fruit is fit for gathering at Melbourne, and it would reach here about fifty days after despatch. Many kinds will remain good for from three to four months after gathering, so that cargoes might perhaps be expected to arrive as late as June. The point as yet unsettled is whether apples can be brought to this country at such a cost for freight as will permit of their being sold at a moderate price, and yet yield a sufficient profit to the growers to ensure a good supply being despatched. THE WlNDow.—With an increase of light and sun, plants in the window will require more air ane. water. There are not many plants grown in windows that would not do now equally well on the window sill, if properly secured. They must be examined daily so that they do not suffer from want of water. The musk plant will soon be forward enough to diffuse its fragrance, and every cottager should be pos- sessed of this redolent both in the window and the front garden, as it is apt to die indoors through being over coddled, and kept too dry probably, in the winter. Cot- tagers contemplating exhibiting at their local shows should cultivate the tuberous-rooted begonias. Moderate sized plants procured now would flower well in the autumn, and until they increase in size they should not be watered before becoming dry. They require a rough, rich compost, and a liberal admixture of sand to grow in. The drainage of the pots must be particularly attended to. They dislike stag- nant moisture round their roots. Consequently no water must be left in the pans or saucers which the plants stand in. There are only few plants that will bear to be always standing in the water without injury.

_ COLOURING WINDOW FLOWER: P-OTS.—We must protest against painting or colouring the pots, which is usually done with red. All such applications have a tendency to close the pores in the pots. Plants always thrive better in porous pots than in those hard baked, or in any kind of glazed earthenwate. Nothing can improve the appearance of a pot if washed clean. ..
"OUR OLD NOBILITY,"
[Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblelchite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission]. THE BUTLERS.

The great house of Butler has for centuries played an important part in Irish history. At the present time there are no less than five Irish Peers who bear the name, four of whom are descended from one common Norman ancestor. These are the Marquis of Ormonde, the Earl of Carriek, Viscount Mountgarret, and Baron.Dunboyne. The Marquis of Ormonde owns 31,873 acres in Kilkenny and Tipperary, with a rent-roll of £17,457; Viscount Mountgareet 14,823 acres, nearly all in Kilkenny, with a rent-roll of £9,090. The landed possessions of the other two appear to be but small.

The first of the family in Ireland was Theobald Walter, son of one of the followers of William the Conqueror, who accompanied Henry 11. in his expedition to Ireland, and, after the partial conquest made by that monarch, became possessed of the Baronies of Upper and Lower Ormond and other territories. Henry 11. also conferred upon him the office of Chief Butler of Ireland, on account of which the surname Butler was assumed by his son. The sou married the heiress of another Norman Baron, John de Marisco, who brought him considerable additions to his estates. The next heir followed his father's example by marrying a De Burg heiress. From a younger son of the next heir Lord Dun- boyne is descended. This heir, Theobald Butler, obtained from Edward I. a grant of the prizage of wines in Ireland towards the close of the thireenth century. This grant was more or less in force down to 1810, or more than 500 years. How much the Butlers obtained from it during that period it is, of course, impossible to say; but in 1810 it was re- purchased by the Crown for the sum of £216,000. This is certainly one of the most remarkable instances of the power of the dead hand on record in our history, especially as the head of the house was attainted, and his lands and dignities forfeited for treason, in 1715. But towards the close of last century it was decided by the House of Lords that no act of the English Legislature could affect Irish dignities, and this ancient grant of the " prizage " of wines was still held to stand. I suppose we must be thankful that, with such enormous powers of taxing posterity to all time, the kings of former centuries were considerate enough not to dispose of the whole of the fruits of our industry. The next heir but one of the Butlers obtained the title of Earl of Carrick. The second Earl of Carrick, who received during his lifetime valuable grants from the Crown, was created Earl of Ornionde. The third Earl of Ormonda pur- chased of the Despencers the ancient castle of Kilkenny, which has since been the chief seat of the family. The ; fourth Earl, who, like several of the others, held the office of Lord Justice of 'lreland, was one of the first Irish nobles to enrich himself from the Church, for he obtained a grant of lands of the See of Cashel for ten years after the death of the Archbishop. The next Earl, who was Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland and Lord High Treasurer of England, was beheaded by the victorious Yorkists after the Battle of Towton. His brother was attainted, but Edward IV. regranted him the title and estates. This nobleman had two daughters, one of whom was the mother of Queen Anne Boleyn. At his death without male issue, the next heir was compelled to forego the title in favour of Anne Boleyn's father, and, as a com- pensation was created Earl of Ossory, but, after his death, the rightful heir again resumed it. At the death of the tenth Earl the title passed to a grandson of the ninth, but Lord Dingwall, who had married the tenth Earl's daughter, contrived to secure the estates. The injustice was happily rectified by the marriage of Lord Dingwall's heiress with the twelfth Earl.

This nobleman, an ardent Royalist, was created Marquis of Ormonde soon after the outbreak of the Civil War in 1642, and at the Restoration he was elevated to a Duke- dom. Macaulay speaks of him as the most illustrious of all the Cavaliers, who, though an ardent supporter of Mon- archy, was no friend to Popery and arbitrary power. He was supposed to be one of the richest subjects in the king- dom, his income being £22,000 a year, at a time when the average income of noblemen was but £3,000. The eldest son of the Duke, "the gallant Ossory," died in his father's lifetime, and the grandson therefore succeeded to the Duke- dom. This young nobleman, who had fought at Sedgmoor, like Marborough and others in high command, deserted James for William. He fought at the battle of the Boyne, and in the reign of Anne commanded the force which sank the Spanish galleons in Vjgo Bay. In the latter part of the reign of Queen Anne it was proposed to bestow upon the Duke all the forfeited estates in Tipperary, but, this being objected to, another course was adopted. He happened to owe very large sums of money to persons whose estates had been forfeited, and the Crown had therefore become his creditor. The House of Commons actually made him a present of the whole of the debt, a proceeding which Macau- lay rightly denounces as indefensible. In 1715 there were not a few nobles tainted with Jacobitism besides those actually engaged in the Rebellion. Chief among them were Oxford, Bolingbroke, and ()monde. The impeachment of the latter was carried with some difficulty; but as, instead of 'standing his ground, he fled to France, there was less difficulty in following it up with an Act of Attainder. Soon after Ormonde made an unsuccessful attempt at rebellion by landing on the coast of Devon. He escaped once more, but, all his honours and estates being forfeited, he not only had to eat the exile's bitter bread, but to subsist on a pension from Spain, against whom he had formerly successfully fought. He left no heir; neither did his brother, the Earl of Arran. In 1791 Mr. John Butler, descendant from the eleventh Earl of Ormonde, was declared to be heir to the titles, except the Dukedom and Marquisate, on the grounds before mentioned. This nobleman married the heiress of the last Earl of Wandesford, who appears to have had some property in Kilkenny. His son obtained the title of Maiquis, as did also his brother, whq succeeded him. . _ . _ _ .
There is another Butler in the Peerage of Ireland beside the four above-mentioned, viz., Butler-Danvers, Earl of Lanesborough, who owns in— _
Cavan Fermanagh Leicester 1,854 „
Total 15,499 „ with a rent-roll of £15,297

He is descended from the younger son of a Huntingdonshire squire, who settled in Ulster in the reign of James I. Sir Stephen Butler was one of the " undertakers" who received from James a grant of a few thousand acres, to which he afterwards added by purchases. The chief seat of the family for a time was at Newtown Butler, afterwards at Belturbet, which town, returning two members to the Irish Parliament, gave to the Butlers a cheap, safe, and regular seat. By the way, they appear to have sold their Parliamentary influence, shortly before the Act of Union, to the Earl of Belmore, who obtained £15,000 for his bargain. The Parliamentary influ- ence of the Butlers, of course, obtaimed for them a good share of Irish offices; and the grandson of Sir Stephen Butler, in particular, held the Clerk,hip of the Pells and of the Court of Exchequer. In 1715 he was created Baron Newtown-Butler, and in 1728 his son was advanced a step in the Peerage, with the title of Viscount Lanesborough. The second Viscount was elevated to an Earldom. The second son of the second Earl, whose descendant now inherits the Lanesborough title and estates, married the daughter and heiress of Sir John Danvers, a Leicestershire baronet. Ihe Danvers family had played an active part in politics. By successive marriages, Swithland, in Leicestershire, an estate valuable for its slate-quarries (Swith is an old Northern word for slate), had passed from its Norman possessors into the hands of the Danvers family. One of this house, the Earl of Danby, was an active Cavalier; another, Sir John Panvers, an equally active Parliamentarian. Fortunately for himself, Danvers the Regicide died before the Restora- tion; but, as it stands recorded on his tomb, his infant son was despoiled of estates in Oxfordshire and elsewhere amount- ing to £lO,OOO a year, and only Swithland was left to him. Swithland being bequeathed by the last Baronet to his daughter's husband, the Earls of Lanesborough have since borne the name of Butler-Danvers.

div.head: CORONATION OF THE CZAR.
div.p: CORONATION OF THE CZAR.

The Emperor and Empress of Russia were crowned in the Kremlin on Sunday, and it would be difficult to imagine a more imposing spectacle than that which took place. The procession was brilliant in the extreme, and the enthusiasm of the people, who thronged every available spot where a view could be obtained, was unbounded. It was an occasion which will live long in the memories :of those who witnessed it. The actual ceremony took place in the Cathedral of the As- sumption, the officiating ecclesiastics being the Metropoli- tans of St. Petersburg, Novgorod, Kieff, and Moscow. The cathedral was filled with a brilliant array of Imperial and Royal personages. The Emperor and his Consort were greeted everywhere with the greatest enthusiasm. We are told that when the Imperial procession issued from the Palace the immense multitude without reverently uncovered and then burst into long and loud acclamations. The in- vestiture of the Imperial pair with the outward symbols of sovereignty was accomplished in the customary form. The Emperor himself crowned the Empress, and it is related that during the ceremony the bearing of the Czar was dignified and noble, that of the Empress sympathetic and touching. Tremendous shouts of "Long live the Emperor" filled the building, and salvoes of artillery announced to Moscow that the ceremony bad been completed. It is evident that the Czar need not have delayed his coronation so long from any fear that it would be would be utilised for the vile purposes of the Nitillists. The loyalty of the populace of Moscow would, in fact, appear to be beyond question, though no doubt they would be in- fluenced for the time being by the glare and glitter of the ceremonial.

On Monday congratulatory telegrams were received by the Czar from all the Sovereigns and heads of foreign States on the occasion of the coronation. The Emperor of Germany sent a long and extremely cordial one, to which the Emperor of Russia, in his reply, acknowledged the respon- sibility that had been imposed upon him, but hoped with the aid of Providence to carry out his mission to the end.

The illuminations of the City of Moscow, following the coronation proceedings, were of an extensive character, those of the Kremlin, the Ivan Veliki Tower, and the Cathedral of the Assumption being perfectly successful. Hundreds of electric lights were brought into use, while the interior of the church towers and the steeples were lit up by coloured fires. Every public building, the theatres, the opera house, boulevards, and principal streets contributed to the display. One telegram states that the Emperor, un- accompanied by an escort, rode through the city in order to see their eff,ct. It is computed that the influx of visitors to Moscow is equal to five or six times the usual population of the city. In a rescript addressed to M. de Giers the Czar says that t he great extension cf the Empire excludes from his mind " any idea of further conquest." The " peacealle develop-

ment of the forces of Russia, the welfare of her children in the various domaias of civil life, and promotion of every useful work" form exclusively, says the Czar, the object of the solicitude of the Government, and will always consti- tute before everything the aim of his pacific policy, which is directed towards the preservation both of friendly rela- tions with other powers on the basis of existing treaties and of the unassailable dignity of the Empire. The Czar issued a manifesto at six o'clock on Sunday evening. Its leading features are a remission of all arrears of taxes due up to the Ist January, 1883, including those of the poll tax and direct and indirect imposts; a mitigation of the penalties incurred under judgments which have not yet been enforced, a partial pardon for various crimes, and a mitigation of punishments not yet fully undergone, the re- moval of police supervision, and permission to return to their homes for persons banished by administrative proce- dure, permission to return for refugees who have left the country, a full amnesty to all classes of participants in the last Polish insurrection who have been under prohibi- tion from residing in the capital or other towns of the Polish provintes and from entering the public service. This.amnesty does not apply to persons guilty of assassina- tion, robbery, or incendiarism. Great crowds besieged the printing offices to obtain copies of the manifesto, and its perusal gave rise to great rejoicing.
CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.
MR. G. W. LATHAM ON THE AGRICULTURAL
HOLDINGS BILL.
The half-yearly meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held at Chester, on Saturday. Colonel France-Hayhurst presided, and there was a large attend- ance.

The SECRETARY (Mr. Rigby) read the report of the Coun- cil, which referred to the importation of contagious diseases, and suggested as the only remedy for the introduction of such diseases that imparts of cattle should be prohibited from all countries where foot-and-mouth and other con- tagious diseases exist. The Council also reported that they sent a memorial to the Board of Trade asking that the powers of the Railway Commissioners might be extended to enable them to deal with such questions as illegal charges and un- due preferences as a Court of Record. Concerning the Agricultural Holdings Bill, the Council express a hearty approval of the principle of the measure in making the basis of compensation " such sum as fairly represents the value of the improvements to an incoming tenant." They wish, however, to see the same principle extended to the "sitting tenant" in cases where the rent is raised on account of im- provements he has effected; and that when compensation is secured to a tenant by agreement it should be made impera- tive that such compensation should in all cases be equiva- lent to what would be awarded under the Act. The Council farther desire that twelve months' notice to quit should be made compulsory and not permissive, and suggest certain re-arrangements and alterations in the schedules to the Act. Subject to these suggested modifications the Council accepts the bill as an efficient measure for putting into force the desire of the Chambers of Agriculture generally on the subject.

Mr. -Cr. W. LATHAM (Bradwall Hall), in moving the adoption of the report, said the difficulty the farmer and landowner had to contend with in securing the slaughter of cattle at the ports of debarkation—the safest and best mode of preventing the spread of contagious diseases in this country—was the belief entertained by the great constituen- cies of England that such a course would raise the price of meat from 2d to 4d per lb. What the landlords and their tenants had to do, therefore, was to convert the towns into a belief, which he held most strongly himself, that the way to cheapen the price of butcher's meat was to lesssen by every- possible means the importation of contagious diseases into this country: (Hear, hear.) As to the Agricultural Holdings Bill, although it could not of course satisfy them all, it contained certain provisions which entirely met with his approval. For instance, it provided that the tenant was to be paid not only for the actual outlay of money in mak- ing improvements, but also for such skill and wisdom as he might show, supposing he should by a small outlay contrive to make a great improvement. Brains as well as money came in there, and he held that every, tenant farmer ought to be paid for his skill as well as for his outlay in money. (Hear, hear.) Another good point in the bill was that the question of time had nothing to do with the matter of compensation. If an improvement was unexhausted at the end of 30 or 40 years, a tenant was en- titled to be paid for that improvement, no matter what amount of time had elapsed. (Hear, hear.) It seemed the height of absurdity, when a man had made an improvement which was good for 50 years, that because 20 years had elapsed he should not get paid for it. (Hear, hear.) The great shortcoming of the bill, however, was that in order to secure its benefits a farmer would have to leave his farm. He was not prepared to say exactly hew the difficulty was to be met, but he thought that if provision was made that when a landlord wished to raise the rent of a farm he should state the increased rent he required, and that then an arbitrator should be called in, just as in the case of leaving tenants. Then, when the value of the tenant's improvements had been ascertained, if he elected to stay on, such amount should be paid down to him in cash or go towards the reduction of his rent for the next series of years. That would not be prejudicial to the land- lord, and would be perfectly fair to the tenant. (Hear, hear.) The power to contract out of *the Act ought also to be withdrawn, and the twelve ,months' notice should be made compulsory. He was also sorry that the bill did not contain a clause giving them freedom of sale and freedom of culture, and that the law of distress was not adequately dealt with. He considered the English system of land tenure very defective, and if that system was made a means of injustice the time might come when, under a lower franchise and under different circumstances to the present, that system might be swept away, and something which they were not at all prepared for substituted for it. (Hear, bear.) Mr. SLATER seconded the motion for the adoption of the report.

Mr. TOMKINSON said he viewed with great suspicion the permissive tendency of the bill, and it also appeared to him that the bill ought to be made retrospective, especially in the matter of drainage improvements. (Hear, hear.) Mr. SPEAKMAN considered that the recommendation of the Council to extend the provisions of the bill to the sit- ting tenant ought to be struck out, and also the suggestion to allow an appeal to the Enclosure Commissioners in cases where the landlord refused permission to allow certain im- provements to be made. He should move, as an amend- ment, that these recommendations be struck out of the report. Mr. WOLLEY DODD seconded the amendment.

Mr. D. DUNCAN (ene of the Liberal candidates for West Cheshire) was of opininion that if the bill passed as now drafted it would enable grasping landlords throughout the country to raise the rents of their tenants who had made improvements, or drive them out of their holdings. Now, they ought to do nothing that would drive a good tenant out his farm, or confiscate any part of his property—(ap- plause)—but they might depend upon it that would be the result unless clauses were introduced protecting the sitting tenant. Ha was quite unable to tell them what those clauses should be, but some such idea as this occurred to him, that the present rental should not be raised for five years or more. That, he thought, would to some extent meet the case, but in some way or other they must unquestionably give the good tenant an interest in what he had already done for the soil. (Hear, hear.) On being put to the vote, the amendment was lost by a very large majority, and the report was adopted. Mr. HOLLAND (a tenant farmer) proposed, and Mr. LAT• Ram seconded, a resolution condemning the landlord's pre- ferential right under the law of distress, and expressing re- gret at its retention in the bill.—This was carried by 23 votes to 3.

Mr. LATHAM next proposed that a memorial be presented to the Prime Minister and Mr. Dodson, asking them to agree to such variations in the bill as may ensure-1. Security to the sitting tenant. 2. Compensation under agreement to be made not less than the compensation under the Act. 3. That the twelve months' notice be made pos:tive,not optional. 4. That there may be an appeal against a landlord in case of refusal of matters in part lof the schedule. 5. The trans- fer of permanent pasture frcm part 1 in the schedule to part 3of the schedule. G. That the bill shall be made retrospec- tive as to drainage and such improvements non' included part lof the schedule, except buildings, as have raised the agricultural value of the holding. 7. That the law of dis- tress shall be totally abolished.
Mr. niIII secondel the motion for the adoption of the memorial, which was agreed to. The other business before the meeting was purely formal.

FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY AT ORMSKIHK. As the 9-45 express train from Exchange Station, Liverpool, to Preston was passing Ormskirk, on Tuesday morning, an old man who was walking on the line was run over, his body being shockingly multilated. The deceased, whose name has not been ascertained, is believed to have been a cattle drover. No blame attached to the driver of the express, which at the time of the occurrence was travelling at the rate of about 40 miles an hour.

A DESIRABLE RAILWAY IMPROVEMENT.—When Dr. Arthur lost his life in the burning Pullman car on the Midland Railway, at Leeds, the public learned with astonish- ment that according to the rules of the company a driver was not to stop his train on the ringing of the alarm bell with which the communication cord is connected, unless he could see on looking along the train that something was seri- ously wrong. It was clear that under this rule the grimmest ot tragedies might be in progress within one of the car- riages, but that no amount of tugging at the communica- tion cord would bring relief, and Colonel Yolland, in report- ing upon the accident, stated that if the train had been stopped immediately Dr. Arthur's life would have been saved. Under these circumstances, a reconsideration of the extraordinary rule was incvitable, and it is satisfactory to learn that it has been reformed in a manner that will give the public some sense of security. Under the new rule the driver, after looking carefully along the train, is to come to a stand with as little delay as possible, and the guard is to use his full brake power for the same purpose; but, except in cases of great emergency, the train is not to be stopped in a tunnel. It is to be hoped that the rules of other companies substantially agree with this reformed regu- lation.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, RINE 2,1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, RINE 2,1883
MISCELLANEOUS.

The Queen arrived at Balmoral on Saturday afternoon. At Ballater Her Majesty had to be carried from the railway carriage to her private carriage. The training ship Mars' stationed at Dundee, was de- stroyed on Saturday by a fire which broke out in the cap- tain's cabin. There was no loss of life, but one of the boys in the panic jumped overboard, and narrowly escaped being drowned. The Queen's birthday was celebrated on Saturday in official circles and by the naval and military services. In London the illuminations were spoiled by the incessant rain; and from the same cause the parade of the Household troops WaS postponed. A clerk in the Wolverhampton branch of the Midland Banking Company has come unexpectedly into a fortune of £50,000. To add to his good luck, a rich uncle in Australia is written to him that if he will go out there he will leave him at his death an extensive and highly productive sheep farm. Early on Sunday morning the dead body of an elderly woman named Catherine Gregory, was found lying on the floor of a house inhabited by Thomas Armstrong, at Leeds. Death had apparently rasulted from violence, there being a large wound on the weman's head, and Armstrong has been taken into custody. At a special meeting, on Monday, of the inhabitant rate- Payers of the township of Manchester, held in the Cathe- dral, authority was given for an application to be made by the churchwardens to the Ordinary for a faculty to enable them to take down the north gallery and to carry into effect the alterations and additions recommended by Mr. J. S. 'Crowther, the arcoitect, in his report. There has been issued, upon the motion of Mr. Wills, a Parliamentary return showing the number of seizures of to- bacco by the Customs in the years 1880, 1881, and 1882, from which it appears that the total seizures were 4,120, the quantity seized being 74,6761 b., the value of which was £21,330 13s 8d; 3,959 persons were convicted in connection With these seizures, and penalties were imposed to the amount of £48,252 14s. Lord Richard Grosvenor, Liberal whip, who has repre- aented Flintshire about 22 years, has addressed a letter to One of his constituents denying the rumour of his probable retirement. His lordship says :—"I should be glad if you Would give an unqualified denial to the report that I intend retiring from the represerration of Flintshire, as I certainly hope to represent the cunstituency as long as they will honour me with their confidence." MURDER OF 1. POLICEMAN.—A Kirkcaldy policeman tamed Lamond has been brutally murdered. He and a brother constable entered a disorderly house at midnight on Friday for the purpose of quelling a row, and they were set upon by several drunken melt. Lamond sent the other policeman for assistance, and locking the door and putting the key in his pocket, he pluckily fought his assailants un- aided. The odds, however, were too great, and the poor fellow was so beaten and battered about the head that when the door was opened he fell dying into the arms of a passer- by, and he expired a few hours afterwards. Four men and three women are in custody. A DUNBAR BOAT CAPSIZED: FOUR FISHERMEN DROWNED.--On Monday, a fishing yawl was returning to Dunbar when it was capsized, and the four occupants were • drowned. The accident took place about a mile and a half ' from Dunbar harbour, and was caused by a sudden squall. Assistance was immediately sent out, but was toe late; but timeons help was given to a second boat in distress. The Yawl lost was named the Peggy. The names of the four reen drowned are James Punton, aged 55, who leaves a Widow and six children and his mother, 94 years of age; James Marr, who leaves a widow and two children; Thomas Punton, who leaves a widow; and Robert Punton, who was the sole support af two younger sisters. A PROPOSAL TO TAX AMUSEMENTS.—Mr. Holyoake, of the Inland Revenue Department. who recently proposed a stamp duty on tickets of admission to theatres, music halls, and "gate money" race meetings, to be devoted to the reduction of taxes on necessaries and industries, has re- ceived the following letter :—" 30, St. James's-place.--Sir, air Stafford Northcote desires me to thank you for your in- teresting paper ('The Taxation of Public Amusements'). The taxes you propose might well commend themselve to a 'Chancellor of the Exchequer as a fruitful source of revenue; but Sir Stafford is disposed to doubt whether they would be equally satisfactory to the British public.—l remain, Your obedient s-rvant, Arthur Saurnarez." "PAYMENT BY RESULTS."—Payment by results is often either an inadequate or an excessive moda of remuneration. 'Good effort may prove futile, while bad or poor enterprise may chance to succeed. Nowhere else, however, is payment by results so pernicious as it is in relation to the enterprise Kg education. Brains are overworked and minds crippled for life because teachers "want money," or desire to make a show of results, and therefore resort to any process of forc- ing and " cram " which can be devised in order to push their pupils rapidly through a corriculum, and compel them to pass the ordeal of an examination. This is one of the radical defects of the system extant under the Educa- tion Acts. A remedy must be found, and with the least delay practicable. Instances of injury wrought in this way are becoming so numerous as to attract attention which Must mean that they are very common indeed.—Laincet. " HORSH-BEEF " IN MANCHESTER. At the Liverpool Police Court on Monday, James Smith, the son of a dealer in worn-out harses, at Burscough Bridge, was charged with truelty to a horse, at Liverpool, on the 20th ultimo. Mr. Motum, of the Itoyal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, stated that on Saturday afternoon he SAW the Prisoner leading a horse, having a saddle and bridle upon it, down St. John's Lane. The animal was very lame on two legs, and in his opinion it was an act of cruelty to make it travel. The prisoner at the time said that he was going to lead the horse to Burscough Bridge, and then to send it to Manchester for beef.—ln reply to the stipen- diary (Mr. Rafdes) Mr. Motum stated there was (mite a trade going on in Manchester in old horses which -were being purchased at prices as high as £3 and £4, to be utilised as food in the lower parts of the city. A penalty of 20a. and costs was inflicted. NARROW ESCAPE OF THE E3iPRESS EtIGENTE. The Empress Eugenie had a narrow escape from a serious acci- dent on Sunday. While returning to her residence at Farn- borough, from attending divine service at the North Camp Roman Catholic Church, Aldershot, one of the horses became restive and commenced to plunge violently. The other horse, on being kiclred, reared, and added to the danger. Finally, one of the animals got his hind leg over the carriage Pole, both the beasts, noev maddened, plunging more vio- lently than ever. Fortunately Mr. Hengist, of the Welling- ton Hotel, Aldershot, drove up with two friends and ren- dered every possible assistance in rescuing the party from their dangerous position. One of the gentlemen in attend- ance had his leg somewhat hurt, but he was speedily attended to by Dr. Cuffe, of Aldershot Camp, who was summoned by Mr. Hengist. The Empress suffered a severe shock, but re- tained her self-possession throughout, and walked home With her attendants.

AMUSING SCARE AT HAWARDEN.—An amusing scare 18 reported to have taken place at Hawarden. Recently visitors Poured into the place in order to catch a glimpse of the Premier during his excursions. Among the visitors was a mysterious individual, who put up at a village inn. With him he brought simply a portmanteau, which he left at the inn, representing that he would auly return at night after Walking through the castle grounds. He having failed to return, however, speculations arose as to the contents of the bag, and eventually it was consigned to an adjacent shed. There it remained for two or three days, the subject of a great deal of curiosity. As the owner dil not come back it began to be believed that the bag contained either an infernal machine or at least some kind of explosive. The Ostler was at last instructed to 'wen the bag, and when be did so it was found to contain a flask of whisky, some stale sandwiches, a razor and shaving brush, a railway ticket, and a " Bradsbaw's Guide." This discovery excited unbounded Mirth and no inconsiderable relief to the neighbourhood The owner has not since been heard of.—Globe. A JUMP FOR LIBERTY.—At about half-past 12 o'clock on Monday a man who was in custody of a Liverpool police- man and waiting on the Liverpool Landing Stage for the Birkenhead boat, broke loose from the officer and jumped into the river. He jumped between the Birkenhead and the Seacombe boats, where, fortunately, there was little or no tide. A lifebuov was promptly thrown to him, and with the aid of a boathook he was soon brought to the side of the stage. One of the stagemen then went down a rope ladder and succeeded in grasping the man by the collar. He seized the chains and attempted to draw himself under the Pontoons, but eventually a rope was passed round his body, and he was hauled on to the stage, and again given into the Policeman's custody. Before reaching Woodside stage he Made another attempt to escape from the officer, but this time also it was frustrated. The man, whose name is Itichard Jones, a joiner in Liverpool, was being removed from Liverpool to the custody of the Cheshire police on a 'charge of attempting to criminally assault a servant girl at Seacombe, on Sunday. THE END OF TUE EXTRAORDINARY KIDNAPPING CASE. will be recollected that a short time back, and during _the excitement occasioned by the dynamite explosion ill rarliament-street, London, a clerk employed in the tele- graph department of the Post Office, named Walter Guy, ,whe had been absent from duty without leave, made an ex- traordinary statement for the purpose of accounting for his absence, to the effect that he had been forcibly se!zed and 'carried away by several men who were supposed to be con- hected with the Fenian organisation. He further stated that these men had endeavoured to extract information from him with regard to the machinery and works used at !tie Post Office for the purpose of carrying out the electric I?l.egraph system, with the object, it was suggested, that • ts machinery should be destroyed, and thus cause an ?.!iormous amount of mischief and confusion. The Post ;tince authorities did not appear to place much reliance on 'lac statement, which Guy subsequently volunteered to sup- It3ort by making an affidavit that all which he had stated was true. He was not permitted to do this, but, in order that 4.;i7er'Y opportunity should be afforded to Guy to make out truth of what he had stated, by the direction of Mr. i;a_rfcett, the Postmaater-General, an officer attached to the Office was directed to accompany him to various Zg• ees where it was said that certain things in connection cult the alleged " kidnapping " had taken place. The re- Was so unsatisfactory that the authorities of the Post cl refused to give any effect to the statement made by 1`129'. he was allowed to resign his appointment, and he is no unirr connected with the Post OX.ce.—Dispatch. to h " necessary, during hot weather t) avoid beverages likely aurmeat or stimulate the system Cecoa, depiived of the super- au4noiti, and guaranteed ab.olutely pure, is a mr,s`, soothing, n Cedbar ,g, and refreshing beverage Be sure that you get Y 8 Cocoa Essence when you ask for it, as imitations are 14.,• 1' Pushed by shopkeepers for the sake of extra profit.
