Two youths, aged respectively 19 and 17, were drowned - on Monday es ening at Walthamstow while bathing. The English and Scotch navvies at present employed on the works at the Baton new reservoir banded together on Monday against their Irish fellow-workmen, and compelled them to quit the place. As a consequence, no Irishmen are now employed at the reservoir. A smith named Henry Cully, at Nottingham, on Tuesday, fired several shots from a revolver at a girl named Winfield, and wounded her severely. He afterwards tried to commit suicide but failed. The motive for the crime was furnished by Winfield's refusal to resume a fcrmer intimacy with her assailant. The annual meeting of the London and Counties Liberal Union was held on Tuesday, Sir John Lubbock presiding. Resolutions were adopted urging the introduction, as soon as possible, of a new Reform Bill, and requesting the com- mittee to present an address to Mr. Bright at the approaching Birmingham celebration. The leading members of the Conservative party held a consultative meeting at the Carlton Club on Tuesday, Sir Stafford Northcote presiding. It is stated that the Govern. ' ment proposals in reference to business arrangements in the House and their leading measures were discussed, and a line of policy in regard thereto was adopted. The Judges are weary of the Belt v. Lames case. On Tuesday when the reading of the summing up of Mr. Baron Hnddlestone had been resumed for some time, the Lord Chief Justice interposed to put a stop to what threatened to become a" public scandal." The reading of the learned Baron's oration was discontinued,and counsel were requested to address themselves to the grounds on which a new trial was requ,strd. A strange story of crofters' grievances was laid before the Highland Commissioners at Lochboisdale, in the South Uist, on Monday. An old man named Mackay told how in 1850 or 1851 the people were compelled to emigrate, being hunted down for tke purpose by "authorised officers," and caught and snipped "just like animals going to matket." One man, he said, who had a child dead in the house, was seized and tied and kicked on board despite the remonstrances of an aged priest. What would have occurred in Connaught or Monster in like circumstances ? RAILWAY COLLISION.—A collision occurred on Tuesday on the Midland Railway at Leicester station. A London and North-Western train from Nuneaton drew up behind a Midland engine, and the North-Western train was followed by'a Midland engine running tender first; .but instead of being switched into the centre road the engine dashed into the North-Western train, throwing it forwatd, and the train was crushed between the two engines. But for the Westing- house brake the collision would have been much more serious. The engine and three coaches were damaged, but no personal injuries were sustained. COMPLAINT AGAINST TREASURY OFFICIALS.—At the Cen- tral Criminal Court, on Tuesday, the grarvj jury intimated to the Recorder that they had concluded all other business, and asked him whether he could not charge them in the dynamite case and allow them to be discharged. The Re- corder replied that the bill had not yet been prepared by the legal advisers of the Treasury, and he consequently could not discharge them, but must request them to attend again on Thursday morning. The grand jury complained of being pat to unnecessary expense and trouble in consequence of this delay on the part of the Treasury officials in doing their duty. NEW RAILWAY IN THE LAKE DISTRICT.—The Carlisle Journal states that the London and North-Western Railway Company are taking preliminary steps for the construction of a branch railway from their main line to Ulleswater Lake. The route projected is from Yanwath, about two , miles south of Penritb, on the Lancaster and Carlisle Rail- way, to Pooley Bridge, at the north end of Ulleswater, a I distance of about four miles along the vale of Eamont. At present, the communication between Penrith and the Ulles- water steamers is by coaches, which the new line would supersede. The branch would be mainly intended for passenger traffic, and especially tourist traffic, but it will also accommodate the lead mines at the head of Ulles- water, the produce of which, is now carted 13 miles to a railway. THE RAID ON NEWCASTLE BETTING MEN.—A meeting, attended by over four thousand people, was held in the Circus, Newcastle on Tuesday night, to protest against the police raid upon betting-houses on the Derby Day and the 1 arrest of sixty-nine persona, against sixty-four of whom no charge was made by the police. A joint telegram was read from Mr. Cowen and Mr. John Morley, stating that the Home Secretary had been questioned on the matter, and that his reply was that he had no jurisdiction over the local ! police. A resolution strongly condemning the proceedings of the police was passed, and it was determined to forward a memorial to Messrs. Cowen and Morley asking for the repeal of the Act which empowered such arbitrary and despotic action. i FEMALE BRUTALITY. A shocking example of female brutality has been revealed by the depositions of Bridget Gallagher, who is at present in the Brownlow-hill Hospital, Liverpool, in a condition which has rendered it advisable that her depositions should be taken. A fortnight aga she saw three women, named Ann Mackenzie, Mary Rowan, and Mary Ann Rowan, knock her brother down and beat him while he was on the ground, Mary Rowan using a poker, Mary Ann Rowan a can, and Mackenzie a knife. The woman bravely threw her arms round her brother to protect him, and was herself so severely injured that her left arm has had to be amputated, and, as mortification has set in, her life is in danger. Her assailants were charged with the assault before Mr. Raffles, on Tuesday, and remanded. ABUSE OF THE MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT.—A case in which the Married Women's Property Act has been very questionably resorted to has been brought under the notice of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce by the Pro- vision Trade Association. A month before the Act came into , force a debtor's liabilities were about £1,900. On January Ist be transferred the whole of the retail branch of his busi- ness to his wife, who had previously had neither part nor lot in it, retaining himself the wholesale business, which, gradually collapsed. At the end of February the man's creditors were called together and presented with a statement , showing liabilities amounting to £1,550, and assets £194 ss. This abuse of a valuable Act has been brought to light in time, it is hoped, to allow precautions to be taken in the new Bankruptcy Bill against its repetition. I THE PREMIER AND THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC.—At a largely- attended meeting of brewers, licensed victuallers, and others, recently held in Sheffield, resolutions were passed condemning the legislation proposed in relation to the liquor traffic, and urging that clubs should be placed on the same footing as licensed houses. Copies of the resolutions were forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, whose private secretary has replied as follows :—" Mr. Gladstone desires me to acquaint you that he has had the honour to receive the resolutions adopted at the nveting of brewers, licensed victuallers, and others, recently held in Sheffield. In reply I am to state that Her Majesty's Governraent will take no part in relation to legislation on any of the subjects touched upon in the resolutions without a due regard to the state of public feeling, as well as to general equity. With respect to the question of clubs raised in the second resolution. Mr. Glad- stone wished me to add that he will not fail to refer the matter to the Chancellor of the Exchequer." MURDER AND SUICIDE AT PRESTON.—On Sunday night, shortly after ten o'clock. a shocking murder and suicide oc- curred in the road in front of Fnlwood Workhouse, near Preston. A solicitor's clerk named James Proctor' through jealousy, it is supposed, shot his sweetheart, adomestic servant, with a revolver, and afterwards shot himself. Both were found directly afterwards within a yard of each other, and were taken inside the workhouse. Proctor died almost immediately, but the girl survived until one o'clock on Mon- day morning. The murdered girl, who is twenty years of age and named Mary Yates, is the daughter of a labouring man, and was of a sweet disposition, industrious, and of a reliable nature. She was engaged to be married at an early date, but her friends urged ker to give Proctor, a lawyer's clerk, up as unsuitable. It is thought she was hinting her intention of breaking the engagement when he shot her. The revolver was new, British bulldog fashion, with five barrels. The murder was evidently premeditated. The couple were seen to be apparently quarrelling just before he shot her, and she moved away from him twice. The tragedy was committed within a few yards of the Fulwood Post Office. Proctor was found dead lying partly in the hedge, the bullet having passed through his head, and the girl was across the path, shot in the temple, breathing, but insensible. They had been for a walk through the fields. When she left home she was in high spirits. At the inquest on Tuesday, the jury found that Mary Yates was murdered. by James Proctor, and that the latter subsequently com- mitted suicide by shooting himself through the head-. No question of" temporary insanity" was admissible in such a case.

THE LANCASIDRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—The iron market continues very quiet. In pig iron there is, if any- thing, a tendency towards easier prices, although actual quotations are not materially lower as compared with Friday. Lancashire makers still quote 45s to 465, less 21 for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but with no business coming forward at these figures they are now open to offers. In Lincolnshire pig iron a small busi- ness is being done on the bases of 44s 6d for forge and 45s 6d for foundry, less 21 delivered here, but even at these figures buyers are not at all eager to place out orders, and in some cases underselling is reported. Some of the finished ironmakers report orders to be coming forwaad more freely. Quotatiovs are unchanged, and prices generally are steady, at £6 5s for good bars delivered inlo the Manchester district, although some buyers still hold back from this figure, and there are sellers in odd cases to be found at a trifle less. Business in the coal trade has been only quiet following the holidays. Round coal, both for house-tire and general trade purposes, is only in very moderate demand, and althongh engine classes of fuel move off fairly well, sup- plies generally are equal to requirements, and common quali- ties of slack are in many cases rather a drug. The restric- tion'of the output, caused by the recent stoppage of the pits for the holidays, has created a temporary shortness of sup- plies, which has prevented any great pressure to sell, and the month closes with, so far as prices are concerned, a generally steady tone throughout the market. In a fevr odd cases there is a little giving way in the top quotations for some classes of house-fire coal, but this does not mate- rially affect current selling prices, and in the Manchester district the list rates of the present month are being main- tained throughout. At the pit mouth the average prices are about as under :—Best coal, 9s ; seconds 7s to 7s t3d ; common round coals, 5s 6,1 to 6s ; burgy, 4s 91 to 5s ;better gnalitieS of slack, 34 9d to 4s 3d ; and common sorts 3s to Gd. per ton. Although the season is advancing, and stocks are known to be low at many of the home ports, there is still only a limited business doing far shipment. Prices at Liverpool and Garston remain without material change, ordinary Lancashire steam coal delivered being still obtain- able at from 7s to 7s 6d per ton. Coke is without change in price, and local makers report a fair demand.

• The National Miners' Conference was resumed at Man- chester, on Wednesday, and passed resolutions in favour of restricting the output of coal. Mr. John Albert Bright, eldest son of Mr. John Bright, was married at the Unitarian Chapel, Rochdale, on Nirednes- day, to Miss Edith Shawcross. Mr. John Bright was present. Conservatism in Sheffield is in a bad way. The Con- servative Club (Limited) of that town has just had its possessions brought to the auctioneer's hammer to satisfy the claims of the landlord for rent. The Court of Criminal Appeal Bill was finally disposed of by the Grand Committee on Law yesterday, but it has not been decided yet when the bill will be reported to the House, the Attorney-General being desirous of reporting it and the Criminal Code Bill at the same time. Another case of attempted murder is reported from Leicester, where a pensioner named Arrowsmith on Wednes- day tried to cut his wife's throat with a knife. The injuries he inflicted were not serious, but afterwaaels he cut his own throat, and now lies in a critical condition. With the view of avoiding further splits on the occasion of Parliamentary elections, the Preston Tories have adopted a scheme for "the popularisation of the party organisation." %h is scheme of reorganisation bears a close resemblance to what, in relation to the Liberal party, has been designated the "caucus." MR. BRADLAUGH.—Writing in reply to an invitation to attend a demonstration at Halifax in favour of Northamp- ton's electoral rights, Mr. Herbert Gladstone expresses his pleasure that the Liberals of Halifax are raising their voices against systematic persecution, injustice, and dis- loyalty to the Constitution. On Thursday morning a man named Patrick Fay, em- ployed as a labourer at the Bolton Iron and Steel Works, met with a shocking accident. He was standing in the pit as molten steel was being paured into ingots, when one of them burst, and the steel caught him. His shirt and clothes were burnt, and he was frightfully injured. He was conveyed to the infirmary, where he lies in a critical state. On Wednesday night a heavy fall of coal took place at the Rowley Hall Colliery, Rowley, which resulted in the death of one miner named Joseph Williams and shocking injuries to two others named Plant and Millward. A sudden shaking of the mine took place and before the men could effect their escape a portion of the roof fell in and a number of them were buried. Williams was dead when found, his injuries being of a terrible character. Mr. M. T. Bass, M.P. for Derby, has written to his con- stituents announcing his intention of resigning his seat in consequence of advancing age. The hon. gentleman, who was born in 1799, entered Parliament for Derby at the bye- , election in August, 1848, and had since continued to sit for the town, having, at every election except one, been returned at the head of the poll. Two of his sons remain in Parliament.

At Oldham, on Thcrsday, James Humphrey, a railway clerk in the employ of the London and North-Western Rail. way Company, was charged with embezzlement. The prisoner had collected money to the extent of £283 on account of carriage of goods, and this money he failed to account for. There were between thirty and forty charges against him. The prisoner, who was said to have indulged in betting, was committed for trial. . .

A STRANGE STORY--The Manchester police are investi- gating an extraordinary story. A girl 12 years of age states that on Tuesday night she heard a man and woman agree to drown two children whom they had with them. She followed them, and eventually saw them throw the chil- dren, aged six years and six months respectively, over a bridge into the river. The police are dragging the river, but have found nothing yet. A HEARTLESS LOVER: WATCHING A SWEETHEART DROWN. —At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thursday. William Emery, cattle drover, was charged on remand with murder- ing his sweetheart, a girl named Sarah Davis. It was stated that there was no evidence of prisoner having pushed the 1 girl into the canal, and be was therefore discharged; but I the stipendiary said it was clear that the prisoner had watched the girl struggling for help for several minutes and I then sink without making the slightest effort to save her. His conduct was disgraceful and inhuman. THE DISAPPEARANCE OF LORD COMBERMERE'S BUTLER: FINDING THE BODY.—On Wednesday afternoon the body of Keeping, Lord Combermere's butler, who mysteriously disappeared from the Abbey on the 12th of February, was I found by Coggins, one of the keepers, floating on the lake (near the Rookery, facing the Abbey. In consequence of de- composition the features were unrecognisable. The deceased ' wore a pair of trousers and drawers, two shirts, and a dres- sing gown. The police and Lord Combermere, who is in London, were at once communicated with. lEXTRAORDINARY ACCIDENT.—On Thursday afternoon an accident of a singular nature occurred at a new floor- • cloth factory in course of erection at K ircaldy. A donkey engine and boiler, with lifting apparatus attached, were at ; work on the third floor raising stones from the ground below when the whole apparatus fell to the bottom, a distance of 60 feet. Thomas Goodson the engineman in charge, fell I along with the engine, and was so badly injured that he died in a few hours. Considerable damage was dons to the building. DEATH OF GENERAL BURNABY, M.P. Major General Burnaby, M.P. for North Leicestershire, died on Thursday evening at seven o'clock. About three weeks ago be went to Brighton for the purpose of paying a visit to his aunt. At that time he was unwell, and during his stay he gradually became worse, and notwithstanding the constant , and assiduous attention of Dr. Towers be expired on Thurs- day evening. General Burnaby, who was a Conservative, was returned for North Leicestershire at the general election. I THE FENIAN PLOT TO DESTROY LONDON: IMPORTANT RsvenkrroNs.—The detective department at Scotland•yard have obtained a considerable amount of additional evidence I with reference to the Fenian conspiracy against London. It has been discovered that a large number of explosions were to have been simultaneously, caused in different parts of the ; metropolis within a week of the roceipt of full consign- ments of nitro-glycerine, and that in the midst of the de- vastation, alarm; and confusion which it was contemplated to create, a general robbery of bullion and other valuables , should be made.

THE FENIAN CONSPIRACY.—AI the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, the grand jury specially attended to deal with the dynamite conspiracy case. The Recorder, addressing them, said the indictment would charge Galla- gher, Whitehead, and other prisoners with treason-felony and with being in possession of explosives with intent to commit murder. The man Norman had been admitted Queen's evidence, and would describe the Fenian conspiracy which existed in America. The grand jury found true bills against all the prisoners. Application will to-day be made by the Attorney-General to fix a day for the trial. SIXPENNY TELEGRAMS!—We take the following from a Manchester contemporary :—" Mr. Fawcett is not unnatur- ally alarmed at the prsspect of the sixpenny telegram. It is stated that a soap manufacturer has already announced his intention of forwarding 50,000 telegrams the first day the sixpenny tariff comes into operation, and several other large advertising firms have got wind of this, and numerous inquiries are being made at the Central Office, all threaten- to rival the soap merchant's enterprise. Considering that three years are required to produce efficient telegraphists, that the present practised hands are working in many cases 40 hours per week overtime, that there is really no available reserve, male or female, to draw on, and that there is no room at the office for more instruments, the apprehension of the Postmaster-General may be well understood."

A singular domestic drain has just been enacted on the Liverpool Landing Stage. As passengers were embarking on an Atlantic liner, a policeman was called, and a woman given into custody. At the detective office it transpired that the prosecutor was Mr. Dobson, landlord of the Wild Boar, Bolton-road, Bradford, and the prisoner a woman he had married seven years ago. They had lived together amicably until Tuesday, when the woman fled, taking with her all the cash she could lay bands on. Dobson then dis- covered that the woman had already had-a husband in America of whose existence she had been aware all along, and to whom she was flying with her plunder. The woman confessed that all this was true, but her plea for forgiveness was so successful that not only did Dobson decline to pro- secute, but attended the errant fair one to the Landing Staze and took a cordial farewell of her there. THE LAND LAWS IN THIS HIGHLILNDS. A meeting of _ _ _ _

the Highland Land Law Reform Association was held. on Wednesday night in the Memorial Hall, London; Mr. Mac- farlane, M.P., presiding. Professor Blackie, who moved the first resolution, calling for the repeal of the unjust laws which were depopulating the country. said human feeling was more than political economy, and where laws existed which encouraged a moral wrong-doing, men were made selfish. Cash spending or getting should not be recognised as the only bond between man and man. He thought the Highland crofters compared favourably with any peamotry. They had suffered toe much and too long, and were alto- gether too meek towards their landlords' oppressors. He advised them to continue agitating until tbz,ir wrongs were redressed. Mr D. Peddie and other speakers followed, sup- porting the resolutions and regretting the absence of a crof- ter on the Royal Commission. No alteration of the land laws could give satisfaction which did not give the High- landers a permanent footing upon their native soil. All the resolutions were carried unanimously.

AMUSING AT:VENTURE OF PRIESTS AT CRESTER.—An incident of a remarkable character, which might have had a sad termination, occurred on the river Dee, at Chester, on Tuesday evening. A party of five or six pleasure-seekers-- who are described as Roman Catholic priests, and who said they belonged to Liverpool—hired a boat at the Groves, on Tuesday afternoon, for a row up the river as far as Eccles- ton Ferry, stowing along with them a good quantity a re- freshments. On the return journey the party made a halt near the Heron Bridge, and landed for the purpose of enjoy- ing the refreshments on the banks of the river, leaving one of their Dumber in charge of the boat. They had not been landed long before they became so thoroughly " refreshed " as to attract the observation of pedestrians en the other side of the river, some of whom go so far as to describe the party as "prancing about the field in the attitude of maniacs." Whether this description is a little overdrawn it is difficult to say, but it seems tolerably clear that the movements of the pleasure-seekers were anything but priestly. After the " prancing " had gone on for some time one of the priets became suddenly solicitous about his brother in the boat, and attempted to get to him, but fell into the river. Another came to the rescue, but be shared the same fate, and both- embraced each other in the water amid cries for help and prayers, which strikingly con.rasted with the " prancing." With the assistance of the occupant of the boat, the priests on terra firma succeeded in rescuing their unfortunate brethren from a most perilous position, and the whole party thereupon got into the boat and rowed for home, reaching the Groves at dusk. Three of the number proceeded to the general station and took train for Liverpool.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The business was of little public interest. The Municipal Corporations (Unreformed) Bill was read a secoud time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. AFFAIRS IN SOUTH AFRICA.—Sir M. HICKS-PEACH gave notice of his intention to move at the earliest possible oppor- tunity that the House should resolve itself into a Committee to take into consideration the administration of affairs in South Africa. ERRINGTON'S MISSION —Mr. COWEN asked if Lord Granville had written to Mr. Errington expressing satisfac- tion at the success of his representations to the Vatican respecting the state of Ireland.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE re- plied that no such letter had been written, and Lord Granville had requested him to state, with respect to his answer on Thursday, that when he said that he had sent no letter to Rome, he meant no letter to Mr. Errington, who was in Rome, nor to anyone else, and he regretted that the answer, being more comprehensive than the question, had given any trouble to the House. FRIDAY NIGHT'S COUNT OUT.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE drew attention to the count-out on Friday, suggesting that no effort had been made by the Government to keep a House, and he asked what business would be taken that evening.— Mr. GLADSTONE said they would go on with Supply, and afterwards take up the Irish Constabularly Bill. As to the incident of Friday night, he showed that it was not the fault of the Government that the House was counted out. THE SEIZURE OF THE KERRY SENTINEL.—There was a short discussion raised by a personal statement of Mr. Har- rington as to the suppression of his journal, the _Kerry Sentinel, by the Government, after which the House went into Committee of Supply on the civil service estimates, and several votes were agreed to. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuzsDAs. The House passed the Representative Peers (Scotland) Bill through Committee, and forwarded some provisional orders bills a stage. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. DISFRANCHISED BOROUGHS. SOUTH AFRICA.. The claims of Chester, Oxford, and the other disfranchised boroughs were brought forward by Mr. LEWIS, who was told by the PRIME MINISTER that he should not advise the House to attempt to deal with them until the House had fixed its views in the provisions of the Corrupt Practices Bill. The right hon. gentleman informed Sir M. Hicks-Beach that the Colonial Office were not yet in possession of information en- abling it to say to what extent pecuniary compensation would, in conformity with a previous declaration of the Government, be payable to chiefs in South Africa in con- nection with events in Bechuanaland. MADAGASCAR.—Lord E. FITZMATIRICE stated that the Government had not addressed any protest to the French Government against tne action of the French authorities in Madagascar, nor had any further information been received respecting the capture of Majunga. THE ORDER OF BUSINESS.—Mr. GLADSTONE made an im- portant announcement in reference to the Government pro- gramme. He said the Government had thought it right to make a survey of the condition of business in the House with a view of relieving the House from any uncertainty as to the anticipations in reference to the very important measures before them, and to state what in the view of the Government was the amount of basiness which lie trusted the House would be prepared carefully to discuss. They did not propose to introduce the bill dealing with the muni- cipal government of London. They proposed to proceed with the Tenants' Compensation Bill, the Corrupt Practices Bill, and the bills returned from the Grand Committees. So far as it was right for the Government to announce its intentions, ha had to announce that the Government would spare no effort to obtain the judgment of the House in regard to these bills. —ln reply to Sir M. H. Beach, Mr. Grans-rortx stated that as soon as the Government learnt what course the Cape Go- vernment were to take in reference to Basutoland, he would confer with the right hon. gentleman as to a day for the discussion of the subject. Replying to another member, he said that after Tuesday next it was the intention of the Government to ask for morning sittings on Tuesdays and Fridays.

M'Coan would proceed no farther in the matter, and the regular course would be, in the ab- sence of Mr. O'Kell,y, to move that the hen member should be requested to be in his place on Friday. He would accordingly make the motion.—Mr. O'BRIEN could not say whtther Mr. O'Kelly would be in the House on Friday or not, but for himself, he always tried to settle private quarrels without seeking the interposition of an Enzlish Parliament.—Mr. SIIIEL thought it was a matter that might have been better settled in a police court.—Mr. PARNELL deprecated the interruption of public business by private quarrels of this sort, and, believing that Mr. M'Coan had no claim on the protection of the House, he should op- pose the motion.—The House divided, when there voted for the motion, 250; against, 19. The House afterwards went into Committee of Supply.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

It is stated that Michael Devitt has been asked to submit his views to the Royal Commission on Technical Education, which will sit in Dublin in a few days. It is accepted in legal circles that Lord Chief Justice May is about to retire, owing to failing health. Thus there will be judicial preferment -both to the Atterney-General and Mr. Murphy, Q.C.

A farmer, named Gaffney, has been waylaid and savagely assaulted in the neighbourhood of Cootehall, near Boyle. Two men, named Moran, have been arrested, and,. having been identified by the injured, were committed for trial. The office of the Kerry Sentincl,A newspaper published in Tralee, was entered by a strong body of the Irish constabu- lary at a late hour on Friday night, and a quantity of books, papers, type, &c., was seized and removed to the poliCe station.

CARDINAL CULLEN'S VIEW OF SEDITION.—Under the title of " Ireland and the Holy See," there has been issued from the Propaganda Press at Rome a pamphlet containing copious extracts from the pastoral letters and addresses of the late Cardinal Cullen in condemnation of seditious and illegal movements in Ireland. The earliest passage selected bears the date of 1850, and the latest was written at Christ- mas, 1877. The pamphlet is printed in English. A desperate attack was made on Tuesday night upon three water bailiffs at Bally3inecot, Tipperary, near Carrick-on- Suir. Shortly after midnight the bailiffs came upon a num- ber of men poaching. A struggle ensued, and all three bailiffs were thrown into the river. On reaching the shore they were again attacked, beaten with boat oars, and left in a senseless condition. On recovering consciousness the bailiffs made their way to Carrick-on-Suir, where they re- ported the occurrence. Warrants were subsequently issued for the arrest of three young men named Connors. Vatious awards have been made by the Government to the Crown witnesses in the recent conspiracy trials. Patrick Farrell, a voluntary witness, who first gave evidence in court as to the conspiracy to murder, though he knew nothing of the murder in the park, will receive £l,OOO, and Michael Kavanagh, the carman, £250. It is understood that Farrell and Kavanagh will leave the country. The girl Alice Carroll will receive £5OO. The Careys will also receive some portion of the reward, but as they had been involved in the conspiracy, especially James Carey, they will not get a large sum. AWARDS UNDER THE CRIMES A CT.-1 he following awards are gazetted :—£3oo to Thomas Huddy, of Crevagh, for the murder of his father, Joseph Huddy, at Cloughbrack ; £2OO to Michael Huddy, of the same place, for the murder of John Huddy, at Cloughbrack ; £4OO to Mary Whelahan, of Knockane, Tipperary, for the murder of her husband, Martin Whelaban ; £6OO to Catherine Farrelly, of Mearscourt, for the murder of her son, Patrick Farrelly ; £4OO to Catherine Dono!eue, of Cionmel, for the murder of her husband, James Donohue • £1,500 to Isidore WWilliam Bourke, of Rahas- sane, for the murder of his father, Walter M. Bourke, at Castle Taylor; and £BOO to Julia Connors, of Kilariff, Gal- say, for the murder of her husband, James Connors.

EEECCTION OF MICHAEL FAGAN: - The execution of Michael Fagan for complicity in the murder of Mr. Burke , in the Phcenix Park took place on Monday at Kilmainham Gaol. The condemned man slept well and rose at a quarter before six o'clock, when he engaged in prayer until the arrival of the chaplain at 6-40. Mass was then celebrated. It was exactly eight o'clock when the flag was hoisted, showing that the laws demands had been fulfilled. There were then about five hundred persons outside the gaol. Amongst them were several women, who recited the Litany for the Dying, and immediately the flag was hoisted they knelt down and prayed, as did also several men in the crowd. Fagan's brother was present, but refused to give any information concerning his brother when he was ques- tioned. The crowd soon afterwards dispersed. Inquiries from the gaol officials show that the convict made no state- ment hatever, and walked firmly and unflinchingly to the scaffold, comporting himself exactly as did Brady and Curley. He seemed calm and unconcerned up to the moment the drop fell on the stroke of eight o'clock. The governor of the gaol, the deputy-governor, the chief warder, the sub-sheriff, the surgeon, and several warders %ere the only persons present. Fagan held a crucifix in his left hand during the execution and it was taken out of his grasp after the body was cut down. The white cap was so ill- adjusted With the rope that when the body was droping it wis carried off by the rush of air, and rose almost to the beam. When the rain began to fall Marwood carefully covered the rope with cloth. The drop was Oft. _ .

THE AGRICULTURA HOLDINGS BlLL.—Precedence hav- ing been given to the Agricultural Tenants' Compensation Bill, Mr. DOBSON formally moved its second reading.—Sir W. BARTTELOT asked for a specific declaration from the Government of the course they intended to take. He inti- mated that he should support the measure, bat he hoped that in Committee the limit of restraint would be made two years instead of one. He was willing to accept the bill, if it were not materially altered, as a fair and honest bill.— Mr. BORLASE was ready to accept the bill, because it would give scope for future legislation of a more drastic character, but the bill, he confessed, had been a great disappointment, as at tbe general election they had been led to expect a much more extensive measure.—Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE remarked that all the reports which had been made led the Government to the conclusion that to a very large extent all over the country tenant farmers were without compensation for improvements, and a compulsory measure was therefore necessary. The Government intended that their measure should be a reality and not a sham. He denied the asser- tion that no protection was given to the sitting tenant, and contended that the bill woull give him important encour- agement and support, especially at the point when the landlord migtet seek to raise the rent. The Bill would have the effect of placing the landlord and tenant in an equal position as to these important mutters. He thought the Farmer's Alliance were seeking to bring about a condi- tion of affairs similar to that which existed in Ireland, and 'tending towards judicial rents. As to the law of distress, he was convinced that the farmers generally were in favour of , a moderate law of that kind, and would certainly oppose its 'total abolition.—Mr CHAPLIN approved of the principle of the bill, which gave security to the tenant for the capital he had embarked in the soil, and he thought the measure a good one, inasmuch as it secured the certainty of compensation, and at the same time left the largest amount of freedom of contract as between landlord and tenant, but he thought there ought to be a provision by which the landlord could prefer an original claim against the tenant for waste and delapidations, and there ought to be a provision to prevent the compensation awarded to a tenant being in excess of the cost of the improvements effected.—Mr. HOWARD asserted that the bill fell very abort of what was expected by the country, and that it would en- tirely fail to accomplish the objects in view. He held that the measure would, on the whole, be injurious rather than beneficial to the farmer. He should not, however, in deference to the opinions of many friends around him, move , the amendments that stood in his name, but would wait and see the form the bill would assume in Committee.—The de- bate was continued by Mr. Bidden, Mr. A. Arnold, Mr. T. Rogers, Colonel Harcourt, and Mr. Pell, after which the bill was read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS—WEDNESDAY. A MONSTER PETITION.—Mr. STEVENSON presented a pe- tition, signed by 177,994 women in 'England, in favour of the General Sunday Closing Bill; and, in addition to that, a petition from 26,072 women in Scotland, Ireland, and Wales, praying that the benefit of Sunday closing enjoyed in these countries might be extended te England. THE DURHAM SUNDAY CLOSING BILL.—Mr. T. FRY moved the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill.—Mr. WARTON moved that the bill be read a second time that day three months. —Mr. THOMASSON moved " that the House, while willing to discuss the question of county government, declines to con- sider public bills affecting only a single county'.'—Mr. P. TAYLOR seconded the amendment.—Mr. ARNOLD could not vote for the bill on account of its being a local instead of a general measure.---Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT supported the measure. He stated that the opinion of the Government had never changed on this subject. Parliament allowed the people of Scotland, Ireland, and Wales to have their way in this matter, and he saw no reason why it should not be so in the county of Durham.—The House divided, when there voted for the rejection of the bill, 57; against, 153. The bill was then read a second time. THE LABOURERS (IRELAND) BILL —Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR moved the second reading of the Labourers (Ireland) Bill. Its object was to provide better cottages for Irish labourers, and its principle was to extend to the rural sanitary autho- rities the powers contained in the Artisans' Dwelling Act. On a representation from 12 ratepayers that the cottage accommodation was inadeqnate, the rural sanitary authority would take up a scheme for improving:it. After some discus- sion the second reading was agreed to. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Thunsatay. The royal assent was given by commission to a number of public and private measures, including the Customs and In- land evenue Bill and the Isle of Man Harbours Bill. The Ribble Navigation (Preston Docks and Borough Extension) Bill was read a second time, as were also the Bill promoted by the London and North-Western Railway Company to en- large the Eustou Square station by appropriating a portion of the burial ground of St. James's, and the Tithe Rent Charge Bill.—Lord ROSEBERY introduced a Bill for the bet- ter protection of young girls, which was read a first time. THE ATTE'MPT TO INTIMIDATE IRISH JURORS.—At the Liverpool Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. Raffles, stipendiary, Patrick O'Brien Michael Hynes, and Patrick Slater were again charged with conspiring to pervert and de- feat the cause of justice by publishing documents alleging that recent juries in Ireland had been packed. The principal document was, it will be remembered, an analysis of 18 juries, and this was printed at the office of Mr. Hynes, the order being taken by Patrick Slater. When the pamphlet was sent through the post it was accompanied by another document, declaring woe against all persons who mtght have any of the goods of the jurors named in their houses; "for vu," it said, "as well as they, will have the blood and sufferings of the innocent people on your head." Where this second paper was printed is apparently not known, and it is not even suggested that it was produced at Hynes's office.—Mr. Superintendent Williams detailed the circumstances in which he first called upon Hynes, who, he ' explained, made no attempt to conceal the fact that he bad printed the jury list, and showed his books and file of proofs ,• without hesitation. Mr. James Why, who for eighteen ; months has been foreman to Mr. Hynes, but who had been ill for some time:before the printing of the jury analysis, happened to be in the office on the day when Mr. O'Brien called with the' job, and his description of the manner in which the printing was undertaken showed that it was ap- parently an ordinary trade transaction. Evidence was then given as to the postage of the pamphlets through the Man- chester Post Office to addresses in Ireland, and a number of witnesses were called from Dublin and other parts of Ireland to show the distribution of the documents in that country. The prisoners were then committed for trial, but were ad- mitted to bail.

div.head: CHESHIRE QUIRTER SESSIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE QUIRTER SESSIONS.

The May adjourned Quarter Sessions of the peace for the county of Cheshire commenced on Monday at the Court- house, Nether, Knutsford, Mr. Theophilus Bailey Waters, manufacturer, of Timperley, being foreman of the grand jury.--Mr. Horatio Lloyd, the chairman, in charging the grand jury, commented on the fact that there was rather a less number of prisoners than is usual at this timrn of the year.—Colonel Hamersley, chief constable of the county, submitted the following report on cattle disease :—" Since the last Quarter Sessions on the 2nd ult., foot-and-mouth disease has appeared in twelve places, 332 cattle and 22 swine having been affected with the disease. There remained under treatment 146 cattle, 28 sheep, and 19 swine on the 2nd of April last, making a total of 547 animals to be ac- counted for. Of this number, 439 cattle, 28 sheep, and 39 swine have recovered, one cow has been killed, and 23 cattle and two swine died, leaving 15 cattle under treatment on two farms at Lower Bebington and Pott Shrigley. Since the last sessions swine fever has appeared upon six places, seven animals have been attacked, four killed, and three died. Sheep scab exists upon two farms, three animals remaining under treatment." SENTENCES AND ACQUITTALS.

George Bailey, aged 27, betting man, indicted for steal- ing a saddling ring ticket at Tarporley races, was found not guilty and discharged. John Thomas Darlington, labourer, aged 25, indicted for stealing a quantity of furniture, the property of his step- father, Henry Marshall, at Wistaston, near Nantwicb, one menth's hard labour.

George Miles, aged 47, labourer, for stealinga shirt, quilt, &e., the property of Thomas Taylor, at Kingsley, near Froth sham, two month's hard labour. John Dearne, aged 20, labourer, for stealing ten hens and four ducks, the property of William Dawson, at Dunham Massey, three months' hard labour. John Thomac Carless, aged 20, labourer, for breaking in the house of William Jones, at Smallwood, near Sandbach, and stealing £7, a silver watch, suit of clothes, &c., twelve months' hard labour.

div.head: _FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: _FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
TERiIBLE DISASTER IN NEW YOBK.
PANIC ON A SITSPENION BRIDGE: 3:5 PERSONS 'KILLED AND 26 INJUREI

_ . The new suspension bridge connecting New York and Brooklyn, opened on Thursday week. was on Wednesday afternoon, at four o'clock, the scene of a fearful accident. About 5,000 holiday makers were on the bridge, when a block occurred just where the New York approach joins the bridge. A woman fainted, and on a man fighting to protect her, universal fighting commenced. Immense crowds rushed from bath sides towards the struggling mob, and men, women, and children were hurled over fourteen very steep steps which are constructed near the New York approach. Women were trodden to shapeless masses. Twelve persons were killed and 26 seriously injured. A Central News telegram from New York on Thursday , morning says:—The block was first caused by some persons stopping to jeer at a man whose hat was blown off. .A wo- man fainted, a man fought to protect her, and umversal fighting at once ensued. Crowds passed to the scene of com- motion from both ends of the great bridge, and the over- whelming pressure hurled men, women, and children down fourteen very steep stone steps, by which passengers from the New York side get on to the bridge. The steps cud surroundings were jambed with a seething mass four deep. free and unrestricted admittance was continued at the end of tha bridge ; and the noise at the steps acted like a deadly charm drawing on the multitude. For a quarter of a mile the bridge was packed with a vast struggling crowd, yelling and shrieking and grasping vainly for anything to catch at. Some scares altogether were swept over the steps, ,and 12 were trodden to death, among this number being seven wo- men, whose bodies were crushed to shapeless forms. A full quarter of an hour bad elapsed after the disaster first occurred before any help could be rendered. Then the railings on the side footpath were torn down, and the dead and dying removed to the hospital on waggons. Scores who left the bridge alive did so with scarcely a ves- tige of clothing, so desperate had been their struggles. The one policeman on the spot, by desperate efforts, saved the life of the first woman who fell, almost losing his own in so doing. One man jumped over the bridge and was killed. The panic was in no way due to a fear that the bridge would give way. No one dreamt of that, but what made the dias- ter possible was the action of the authorities in permitting such crowds upon the bridge at one time, and also the very great steepness of the stone steps. Undoubtedly, when the block once commenced the immediate confusion intensified the horror and disaster of the scene. A warning that what has now happened might some day occur was several times given to the proper authorities. The latest reports from New York state that thirty-five persons were killed through the panic on Brooklyn bridge. It appears that a number of women fell down a flight of stairs connected with the bridge, and it is alleged tbat the panic was produced by some pickpockets raising a cry of "Danger."

div.head: TERRIBLE BOAT ACCIDENT. LOSS OF TWENTY-TWO LIVES.
div.p: TERRIBLE BOAT ACCIDENT. LOSS OF TWENTY-TWO LIVES.

News has arrived at Milan from Aleggio, a town about fifty miles from Milan, of a terrible accident which has just occurred in its vicinity. A number of workmen, who had just finished their day's work on the Villoresi Canal, had to cross the river Tessin, which supplies it. On their return home, instead of making two journeys across, the boatman, whether from indolence or indifference, took the whole twenty-eight labourers at once in his boat. When they had reached the middle of the river the boat, which was greatly overladen, capsized, the boatman, apprehending a catastrophe, haying already flung himself into the water; and of the twenty-eight passengers twenty-two were drowned. Their bodies not having been recovered, it is believed they were carried by the current into the river Po, into which the Tessin flows near Pavia. The Po is greatly swollen by the heavy rains and by the melting of the snows. The melancholy news spread desolation through Aleggio, where mcst of the men lived. Several of them were married, and leave sorrowing families.

div.head: FIGHTING IN TONQUIN.
div.p: FIGHTING IN TONQUIN.

Fighting has begun in Tonquin sooner than was ex- pected. The French garrison, who were beleaguered in Fort Hanoi by the Annamites, have made an unsuccessful sortie, in which the commander, Capt. Riviere, and twenty- six men were killed and fifty-seven wounded. This repulse has caused a great sensation in France, where the news has come as a complete surprise, as the Government had con- cealed the fact that the French forces had been reduced to straits so desperate as to necessitate a premature com- mencement of hostilities. Reinforcements have been or- dered to bo sent from Cochin-China, and the expedition, which has been preparinc, for some time, is to sail at once from Toulon, with General Bonet in the chief command. The vote of credit which has been under discussiom in the Chamber of Deputies was hastily and unanimously voted on Saturday, the Extreme Left having given way because, as M.Perrin declared, "it was now necessary to avenge the death of Commandant Riviere, and save the honour of the French flag." Much uneasiness is felt in Paris as to the attitude of China, and it is conceded on all sides that the Tonquin expedition will be very far from a military promenade. According to a private telegram from Paris, it is reported that the French Government has given assurances to the British Cabinet that it has no intention of annexing Ton- quin, and that it merely desires to uphold its treaty rights. At the same time, after the recent defeat, the French Minis- try feels bound to exact full and complete satisfaction at the hands of the Emperor of Annam. Several of the Paris journals ridicule the suggestion that the Tonquin expedi- tion iq the prelude to a French protectorate of Siam. They declare that the French Government has no such in- tention.

The people of Zurich have voted the repeal of the com- pulsory vaccination law, and sanctioned the re-introduction of the penalty of death. • It is proposed to hold a national exhibition in Paris in 1885, principally for the smaller industries. This will be preparatory to the Grand International Exhibition to take place in 1889. There has been a remarkable display on the part of bicy- clists in New York. On Monday the members of a conven- tion of bicyclists, some of whom came from Montreal and scme even from San Francisco, numbering one thousand riders, paraded the fashionable thoroughfares in the Central Park.

A pitched battle has been fought in Hayti between the Government troops and the rebel forces under Balzelais, who is reported to have gained the victory over his oppo- nents, inflicting heavy loss. He also sank by artillery fire two Government war vessels which were assisting President Soloman. The insurrection is described as spreading, several important towns having declared for the rebels. A telegram from Damascus announces the death of the famous Abd-el-Kader, the Arab Chief who for many years gallantly withstood the French in Algeria. The funeral was celebrated with unparalleled pomp, amidst an innumerable concourse of sorrowing spectators. The procession included Christians, Moms, Dervishes, the civil and military digni- taries, foreign consuls and notables, Freemasons, and the representatives of every guild in the community. The body was placed in the Mosque of Sanahieh, where, by the special favour of the Sultan, it was laid alongside the sacred tomb of Muhieddim. THIRTY THOUSAND PERSONS ON THE BROOKLYN BRIDGE.-A New York correspondent says the scenes at the Brooklyn Bridge still continue to be very remarkable. On Sunday two hundred and fifty thousand passengers crossed it, entirely filling the roadways and footwalks. At one time, when thirty thousand people were upon it, a deflection of several inches was caused ; but as the engineers have allowed for a much great deflection, this caused no alarm. The heaviest vehicles are permitted to drive at any speed. A regiment has crossed without breaking step, and the vibration was only just perceptible. The engineers them- selves are astonished at the solidity of the structure. It becomes clearer every day that the effect upon the two cities will be beyond what was expected.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
THE WARMNGTON OPPOSITION CONCILIATED.

At the Ship Canal inquiry, yesterday week, Mr. Daniell Adamson was further cross-examined. He stated that the promoters of the bill had in a great measure settled with the Corporation of Warrington, and one of the counsel for the • bill added that the traders of Warrington had arranged with the promoters that morning. Mr. Stevens, of the firm of Marshall, Stevens, and Co , steamship agents, Liverpool, Garston, and Rouen, and a member of the Ship Canal Pro- visional Committee, testified to the grievous charges to which ships and cargoes arriving at the port of Liverpool were liable. He laid stress on the burdensomeness of " the master porter," wh.i, he said, was only known in the case of I Liverpool. The "master porter" was authorised to charge for certain services whether he performsd the whole of them or not, and the post being a very lucrative one, most shipping agents and many merchants and brokers were " master porters." The Bill was again before the Committee on Monday, evidence in its favour being continued. Mr. Marshall Stevens, a Liverpool shipowner and the Cunard agent, gave figures concerning dock dues and charges, and said those impoets had had the effect of driving from Liverpool trade in certain goods the direct market for which was not in that city. lie particularly condemned the system of porterage charges, which often were paid for services not rendered. Should the canal be formed, those inequalities would be avoided at Mancheeter by the institution of a uniform system under one head, whereby private competition and profits would be abolished. Mr. Reuben Spencer, a director in the firnl of Ryl aids and Sons, Limited, deposed to their dealings with foreign countries, and the effect the canal would have on their export trades. He estimated their annual saving under the new dock dues and charges at £2,000 upon the cotton alone they new received through Liverpool. Before the Committee rose for the day Mr. Pope said: We were told last week that some arrangement had been come to with the Corporation of Warrington with regard to clauses, and it is very important that we should know what that arrangement is —The Chairman: We do not know of any such arrangement.—Mr. Pope: But the Warrington Corpor,ltion has Ivithdrawn from opposition on the strength of it.--Mr. Pernber : I am not aware what those clauses are. I have not seen then-I.—Mr. Pope: But it is no answer to say that you have not get the clauses, for .we are entitled to know at any rate what is the bargain which has been made.—Mr. Pember : I don't know what the beads of the bargain are, but I do know that Warrington has with-

drawn from opposition, and that the heads of an arrange- , merit have been settled between the officials. These, however, have to be sent down to Warrington far the confirmation of the Council, and they have not yet been returned. Even if they were lam not sure that you have a right to see them.—Mr. Pope: I never heard of such a thing in my life as a bargain made with one opponent in the middle of the case and the other opponents not to be allowed to know what the bargain is.—The CHAIRMAN: I suppose we shall know what the bargain is as soon as Mr. Pember has it himself. Mr. PopE: Of course. I believe what my friend Mr. Peru. her says, and perhaps I am more fully informed on the sub- ject than he is, because I do know what the bargain made with Warrington is. It is important that the committee should know what the arrangement is. and that we should have it officially before the committee before we deal with our. own case, because it affects largely the question of the estimate. They have agreed with Warrington on certain works, which will raise the cost of this scheme. The CHAIRMAN: I understand that we are to have it at the ear- liest possible moment, and we cannot have more. On the Committee resuming their inquiry on Tuesday, the Chairman urged on the counsel for the promoters the desirableness of reducing the dimensions of their evidence. He said that if they allowed the 136 witnesses to be ex- amined whose names were on tits list which had been handed to whom the result would be a fiasco. The Com- mittee thought they cught to hear only the evidence .of the principal trades, and that the case of each trade should be represented by ooe witness. The trade case ought to be finished by Thursday night, and it must be finished by Friday. The engineering question and not the trade ques- tion was the crucial part of the case. Mr. Pember (for the promoters) would not bind himself to this arrangement, but promised to do his best to meet the views of the Committee. Mr. C. T. Bradbury, of the firm of Messrs. J. H. Gartside and Co.; cotton spinners, Ashton, , was then called as a witness in support of the bill. He said the cotton trade of Ashton would save at least £29,000 a year if the canal was made. Mr. J. C. Fielden, of Messrs. S. Ogden and Co., cotton manufacturers, Manchester, was next examined on behalf of the promoters, and he was fol- lowed by Mr. Andrews, secretary of the Oldham Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers' Association, who said that, leaving brokerage out, o!dham would save 4s 9d a ton by the canal, and the saving of one brokerage would make a further difference of £B,OOO a year. Mr. ‘lalmsle and Mr. Joseph Leigh, cotton spinners, tf'tocknort, also gave evi- dence, the latter estimating the saving to Stockport spinners at 4s 9d a ton. Mr. Mitchell, chairman of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, and Mr. F. Moss, grain importer, Sal- ford, were afterwards examined, and then the Committee adjourned.

The proceedings were resumed on Wednesday, when Mr. Pember submitted an amended list of witnesses, shorter than the one previously presented. The Chairman remarked that he thought the list of commercial witnesses might be still further reduced. The first witness examined was Mr. G. B. Dewhurst, of the firm of Messrs. Dewhurst and Co., exporters, of Manchester and London, and he stated that the rate of freight of Manchester geods to Calcutta was 225. per ton, of which one-half was for transit from Manchester to Liverpool. He was of opinion that the proposed capital of £6,000,000 for the canal would be raised in Lancashire and the district. Mr. Sam Mendel, for 40 years a shipper in Manchester, who gave evidence as to the advantages of water carriage, was of opinion that the canal scheme would lead to a reduction of charges which must have an important effect upon trade, and would save half per cent. on the value of goods. He had no doubt that the capital would be easily raised Evidence in favour of the bill was also given by Mr. T. Wilson, of the firm of Messrs. Wilson, Latham, and Co., shippers, of Manchester and Bombay, Mr. Gustav Behrens, of the firm of Sir J. Behrens & Co., of Manchester and Bradford, Mr. George Little, managing director of Messrs. Platt Brothers & Co., of Oldham, and others, after which the Chairman intimated that the Committee had heard sufficient evidence from trades and would like to hear what some of the Mayors had to say. Mr. R. Husband, Mayor of Salford, was therefore called, and questioned as to what in his opinion would be the influence of the canal upon his borough. He said he considered that nothing that could happen could be of such advantage to Salford as the opening of this canal. He would not say that the scheme would entirely prevent floods, but it would, by reducing the level of the river, greatly reduce the probability of floods occurring. Mr. John Hopkinson, Mayor of Manchester, said he thought the scheme was mcre than an advantage to Manchester, it was a necessity. The effect of the scheme could not but be favourable upon the floods. The Mayor of Stalybridge gave corroborative evidence. Mr. A. Lupton and Mr. W. Rowley bore testimony to the beneficial effects the scheme would have upon the Yorkshire coal trade. This inquiry was continued on Thursday, when, in ad- dition to some important " trade witnesses," Messrs. Bright and Slagg, two of the Parliamentary representatives of Manchester, and Mr. Armitage, one of the members for Salford, were examined. Mr. Stone, a timber importer at Hull, said the easel would be a very great blessing to the timber trade. Mr. L. J. Crossley (John Crossley and Sons, Limited) gave similar testimony on behalf of the West Riding carpet trade. He said the charges at Liverpool were so heavy that his company had been obliged to import their hemp at Hull, but if the canal was made their import I (trade would be done at Mauchqater, Mr. J. S. Scarborough, president of the Halifax Chamber of Commerce, said that in his district the feeling was unanimous in favour of the scheme. There weuld not be the slightest difficulty in raising the required capital. He believed that when the canal was made the woollen market would be transferred to Manchester. The Mayors of Bury and Heywood were next examined, and ex- pressed their belief that the capital would be raised. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., said he did not suppose there would be. any difficulty in raising the capital, He should prefer, if the bill was passed, that the scheme should be in the hands of a public trust. Questioned as to the propriety of municipal corporations subscribing towards the scheme, the witness said he could not suppose that it was very wrong for them to do so, but they ought to act with great judgment. If the , people of Manchester and Salford believed that the scheme i was a necessary ene,and that it could not be carried out with- out their heip,he should think it wise on the part of the Cot. porations to subscribe. Mr. Slagg thought the people of Manchester were in favour of this scheme in a remarkable ' degree, and he had strong reason to believe that if the pay- ing merits of the scheme were established by the promoters and enginetrs, the public would subscribe very freely. He I agreed with Mr. Bright as to the desirableness of the under- taking being handed over to a public trust. The witness admitted in cross-examination that the certainty of the canal ; being a paying concern had yet to be demonstrated. Mr. Armitage spoke of the enthusiastic feeling prevailing among the working people in favour of the canal, but said the moneyed classes were not fully persuaded yet of the practicability of the scheme. He himself was not prepared to give an opinion upon it, but he had not yet been per- suaded that it would be a financial success. Mr. Alderman Davies, of Warrington, having given evidence in favour of ; the bill, the Committee adjourned, Mr. Pember stating 1 that he hoped to complete his case by the end of next ; week.

div.head: ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE.
div.p: A ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE.

A Drogheda correspondent, writing on Tuesday, says :—A most extraordinary circumstance—a real romance in humble life—has been brought to light within the past few days in this town, giving a forcible illustration of the oft-told aphorism that "truth is stranger that fiction." BY the steamer Colleen Bawn, which left here yesterday for Liver- pool, there went as a deck passenger a man named Edward Finegan, with his wife and eight other relatives, all bound for America. Twenty-eight years ago Edward Finegan, who was then four years married, and was living in Drog- heda, left his young wife, with two little children, and went to America. He proceeded to the gold diggings of Cali- fornia, where, by dint of hard work and industry, he amassed a considerable sum of money. During all his years of wandering he never once wrote to his wife, who in the meantime was, day by day and month by month, anxiously awaiting a letter from him. No letter came, however, Ad as year after year rolled by she was at last induced to believe that her husband was dead. She went to England and worked there as a factory operative. In the course of time she received and accepted an offer of marriage, and became the bride of a worker in tinware, who in a measure consoled her for the loss of "No 1." After a few years of wedded life the seconded husband died, and was gathered to the home of his fathers. Twenty-eight years had now passed since the departure of .‘ No. 1," when, about four weeks ago, a stranger, of American appearance, arrived in Drogheda, and particularly inquired for the Mrs. Finegan of 28 years ago. He was soon told her history by the people of whom he inquired, and then he accused himself, by his neglect and silence, of being the direct cause of all the trouble. He expressed a desire to see her awl make amends, and her friends accordingly, wrote to her in Eng- land apprising her of the safe return of her supposed "dead husband," and of his desire for their reunion. She loqt nc time in responding to the call of love and duty, and rejoined him here in a few days afterwards. They then de- cided to leave for America. and, accordingly, accompanied by all their relatives, the expense of whose passage Mr. Finegan defrayed, they left as before stated, yesteiday.— Dubl i n Express.

div.head: STABBING AT HUYTON
div.p: THE STABBING AT HUYTON
QUARRY.

At Prescot, on Tuesday, William Knox, gardener, Huyton Quarry, was brought up on remand, cliaged with utitayr- fully wounding his son, John Knox, a collier.—Sul_rin- tendent Barker said he had a certificate from Dr. Uorst, stating that prosecutor was not in a tit state to leave his house. The prisoner lived with his sons but for a good while be had spent most ef i his time in drinking, and handed over nothing n support of the house. His sons not liking this, refused to have him with them any longer, and on Saturday night week they tried to put him out of the house. A struggle ensued be i - tween prisoner and prosecutor n the back yard, and the pri- soner stabbed his son.—ln answer to the magistrates, Superintendent Barker added that Dr. Gorst had informed him the wounded man was suffering from pleurisy, which led him to believe that he was afflicted with internal heinorrhage.—lhe prisoner was remanded till Tuesday next when it is hoped the prosecutor will be able to appear in court. The Nirlind inflicted by the prisoner upon his son was 4 very severe one, the blade of the knife entering the yonng man's breast under the left nipple and protruding from hi 3 side in a Slanting direction.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1883.

IT is not at all surprising that the PRig% MINISTER should this week have taken counsel with his followers respecting the state of busi- ness in the House of Commons. We are dis- posed to think that had the conference of Tuesday taken place at an earlier period Of the session it would have been productive of more good, and we should not now be lament- ing the miserably slow pace at which legisla° tion proceeds. Parliament met in the middle of February, we are now entering upon the month of June, yet not a single measure men- tioned in the QUEEN'S Speech has passed the Committee stage. Certainly during the past few days progress in the Grand Committees as well as in the House itself has been more rapid, but if the present session is not to comparatively barren of results, better use wil&. have to be made of the time at the disposal ot Parliament during the next three months that' • has been the case since members were sury moned to Westminster. The present Go- vernment were elected to pass great measures- of reform, and they have honestly endeavoured to carry out the wishes of the electors in this regard; but it must be admitted on all hand that they have been from the very first con' fronted with a combination of circumstances which has prevented the hopes of the electors so far from being realised. It was never, for instance, supposed in 1880 that the Govern- ment would be called upon to deal with a- scarcely veiled rebellion in . Ireland and an open revolt in Egypt-, nor could it have been believed that obstruction open as well as veiled —would have reached the state of perfection it has now attained, yet these difficulties, amongst others which could be mentioned? the Government have had to contend against. We are not without hope, however, that in the end the Government will be found to have been more than equal to any emergency, ana that before another dissolution the legislative anticipations of the most sanguine will have been fully realised. The greatest obstacle to legislation at the present time seems to us to. be, to use Mr. DILLWYN'S words, the struction which has now become a science, and which the recent procedure rules appeafrs, powerless to effectually destroy. is remarkable that notwithstanding the stringency of these rules a' mere handful of Conservative menl" bers and a few Parnellites are able, bY the adroitness of their tactics, to fritter awaY the precious time of Parliament in aimless talk. Adopting Lord R. CHURCHILL'S clic' turn that it is the first duty of the Oppositioo to oppose, they lose no opportunity that pre: sents itself to obstruct the Government at every turn. Recently these obstructionists, , who would fain pose as economists, have shown a very anxious desire to criticise the" estimates, which some of them have done al an inordinate length, and the result,as pointY out by Mr. GLADSTONE on Tuesday, is this The House has sat for twelve nights in Cool' mittee of Supply —a fair proportion up to the present date and it has passed b 4 z 8 votes out of i9O, or only one' seventh of the whole. It is, of course' very desirable that the estimates should be carefully scrutinised, and we are sure it is the wish of the Government to see the varlols items thoroughly sifted but we afe afraid the new-born zeal of certAl members with respect to financia W matters arises more from a wish t° e, waste time than to save money. are all aware that a great deal °: time has been spent by the Grand Committee, on the Bankruptcy Bill and the Crimioa Appeal Bill, these bills must shortly be re e ported to the House, and it is sought by b's obstructionists to undo all the work that h.a been done in the Grand Committees by d's" cussing every clause in detail when the billst reach the House again. We trust that .2to any rate the leaders of the Opposition wl not lend themselves to this course, and should think that the House—after what fallen from Mr. GIADSTONE—wiII not allow, itself to be thus trifled with. The Siandareas, in view of these bills leaving the Committen has spoken out very decidedly against a "organised attempt to impede them, whittle them away, to invalidate the cen!Tl il principle they embody," and it only .requirnt.s a firm attitude on the part of the majorlty.o the House and the leaders of the Opposill on_ to prevent this being done. Tuesday's C.o, _ ference at the Foreign Office has servednt‘u_ demonstrate the unquestionable fact that,.n withstanding recent reverses, there is lute unanimity in the Liberal party as to I"'
