FARNWORTH NATIONAL :CHOOLS• In behalf of these schools, sermons wets preached on Sunday to good congre- gations, by the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Sankey. A good sum was realised. In the list of successfutc ind:dates at the final examina- tion of the Incorporated Law Society, held on the 24th and 25th April, we notice the name of Mr. Alexander Estorest Day, son of the late Mr. Alexander Day, solicitor, for many years clerk to the Runcorn magistrates, and captain of a local volunteer corps. • RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.—The,pnnual sermons on be- half of the Home Missions of the Church of England were preached in the above church on Sunday, in the morning by Vac) Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., and in the evening by the hey. 11. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar of Frodsham. The collections amounted to £l2 14s. ATTEMPT TO AVOID A DISTRAINT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Taomas flashy was charged with having clandestinely removed goods of the value of £2 from 29, Brook-street, in order to avoid a dis- traint for rent due to Mr. Samuel I'laut, of Halton.—The complainant having proved the case, the defendant was ordered to pay £2 18s. Gd. and costs amounting to 9s. GI in two months. RUNCORN STAR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The seventh appropriation meeting of this society was held in Bethesda School ou Wednesday evening under the presi- dency of Mr. J. R. Frith. There was a fair attendance of members. The usual method of drawing by ballot was adopted, and 115 was the lucl:y number. Annie Mary Unsworth, daughter of Mr. Jabez Unsworth, was declared entitled to an advance of .ElOO, free of interest, for 121 years

PRESENTATION TO • RUNCORN ORGANIST.—In conse- quence of tailing health, Mr. J. Clough has been compelled to resign his position as organist of St. John's Presbytetian Chapel, which he has admirably held for several years. Be was not allowed to sever -his connec:iunwithout receiving a gratifying proof of the esteem in which he was held. On saturday he was privately waited ton at his residence by the Rev. E. Williams, the pastor, who, on behalf of the choir, scholars, and congregation, presented hint with a parse of gold. Mr. Clough suitably acknowledged the unexpected gift. A DRUNKEN MAN'S FREAK AT RUNCORN.—OR Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, James Mullen was charged with feloniously stealing a glass of the value of 5d., the property of John -Attwood.—Ttte complainant keeps an ice-cream stall in the market, and on Saturday night the defendant, who was drunk, asked to be supplied with a pennyworth of the cold compound. Having received it, he walked away without returning the glass or offering payment. i`.,:ubse- quently he was apprehended at his lodgings in Mersey-stieet by P.S. Mac Michael, to whom he stated "It was all right." —He was fined 10. and costs.

RUNCORN OPEN-AIR CONCERTS.—The third concert will ba given by the band of the F and G Companies of the lid C.R. Volunteers, in the Market-place, on Thursday nest, commencing at 7-30 p.m. Programme: Selection, "Kyrie and Gloria" (12th Mass) Mozart; cornet sole, ." The Night- ingale," (Reynolds) T. Woods; selection, ." Lift •up your heads" (Handel) ; fantasia, " The Royal Musketeers" (E. Mullot); selection, "Worthy is the Lamb (Handel); slow match, " Valiant " (E. Marie); chorus, " Amen " (Handel). National Anthem.

A DISORDERLY DRUNKARD AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, jun., Darby Mulligan was charged on remand with being drunk in the Cooper's Arms, and also with as- saulting Mrs. Thornton, the landlady. On Wednesday after- noon the prisoner went into the Cooper's Arms in a state of drunkenness. Mrs. Thornton refused to serve him with liquor, and he became very violent and abusive, striking the landlady on the face, and discolouring her eye. She suc- ceeded, however, in eluding him, and locked him up in a room until the arrival of a policeman, who arrested him.— The prisoner was fined 103 and costs in each. In default of payment he went to gaol for 28 days. SALE OF GAS AND WATER SHARES AT RIINCORN.—At Wilson's Hotel, on Monday, Messrs. Marsh and Son offered for sale 75 £5 shares in the Runcorn Gas Company. There was a numerous attendance, and the competition was keen, the shares fetching from £lO 103 to £ll each. Five .£lO shares in the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Co. received numerous bids, and ultimately went at £lO 153. £5O consolidated stock in the Liverpool United Gas Light Company was sold for £97 10s. Mr. Marsh also offered for sale Holly Bank, a handsome villa residence at Halton. We understaEd there was a reserve of £l,lOO on the property, and as only two bids were made, the highest of which was £6OO, it was withdrawn.

STREET ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.—As a horse belonging Mr. Isaac Stubbs, mineral water manufacturer, driven by a youth named James Hesketh, was proceeding down Delph- bridge on Monday afternoon, a pipe at the foundry on the opposite side of the canal emitted a white cloud of steam. Startled at the sound, the horse shied, and rushed down the steep incline, but turning at the foot of the bridge, the cart was dashed against the Egerton Arms, one of the iron bars of the window being bent. Two women and a man who were standing at the corner af the street had a narrow escape. One of the women had her dress torn from the top to the bottom, and it was astonishing how she escaped being crushed to death. The shafts of the cart were broken off, but though the cart was laden with bottles not one Was smashed. Both horse and driver escaped uninjured. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—A boy, named Thomas Dean, 14 years of age, who lives at 4, High-street, Widnes, Was cerionaly injnrwl nn Monday. Dean is plumber's boy at Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works, and he was helping to carry some lead and iron across the gangway leading, from a tower to a chamber, when he slipped and fell a dis- tance of 20 feet, alighting on the roe of the shed beneath. His right arm was fractured, and he was also injured about the face. He was taken to the Accident Hospital, where he was attended by Dr. .Cooper.—On the same afternoon a man, named Charles T. Ralph, 35 years of age, was struck on the head with a bucket whilst working at the Widnes Sewerage Works. His head and back were seriously injured, and he was removed in an insensible condition to the hospi- tal. Dr. McDonnell at once attended to the injured man. A FIDDLBR IN TROUBLE AT RUNCORN.-At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, 'before Mr. John Brundrit and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Thomas Jolley, a grey-haired man, was charged with stealing a fiddle and fiddle bow of the value of 7s 6d, the property of Martin Gillighan.—On the previour morning, whilst the prosecutor was at work at the docks, the prisoner visited his house in Friars-street. He told Mrs. Gillighan that Martin had told him to take the fiddle and be careful not to alter the first string. The instru- ment was lying on the table, and the prisoned picked it up and departed. On her husband coming home at four o'clock Mrs. Gillighan discovered that prisoner's statement was not true, and information was given to the police.—The prose- cutor having stated that he did not give the prisoner authority to take the fiddle, P.C. Finney deposed to appre- hending the prisoner in Higgins' lodging-house in Mersey- street on the previous afternoon. In answer to the charge, prisoner said " It WIS only done in a lark."—The prisoner now said he did not take the fiddle with the intention of stealing it. He took it to a beet house to play during the day. He called Adolph Libohn, a travelling musician, liv- ing in Fryer-street, Runcorn, who, however, only deposed to the prisoner playing the fiddle in various public:houses.— The Bench said they would give the prisoner the benefit of the doubt as to whether he intended to steal the instrument or not, and discharged him. TRAVELLING ON TR-E RAILWAY WITHOUT A TICKET.-071 Monday, at the Liyereool Police Court, Charles Allcatd and William Allcird, 18, Cecil-street, Edge-hill, were summoned for travelling from Beancorn to Edge-hill by the London and North-Western Railway without having procured a ticket. —Mr. Arthur Preston appeared for the London and North- Western Company-; and Mr. Beesley deftrided.—lt appeared from the evidence given by the prosecution that Charles Allcard is a surveyor, and the other defendant it a son of his. He has also a son in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Compady. The defendants on the 10th inst travelled from Runcorn to Edge-hill by the 4.15 p.m. train, and passed through the gate. Charles Allcard walked away, and William Allcard produced a railway pass numbered 5,082,and on being questioned they admitted hav- ing travelled in the train from Runcorn on the pass. The pass it appeared, was-issued for another son of the-defendant's, who has the same name, and is employed in the engineer's department of the company. The pass allowed the youth for whom it was iesned to travel over certain parts of the -company's lines, but not for the distance the defendants had -travelled. They had, kowever, no right to use -it. For the ,defence it was contended that the defendants took the ticket, *which was forgotten by the person for whom it was issued, in order to give it to him, but falling short of money while travelling they used the pass to get through the gates. The -defendants afterwards tessdered the money for their fare. They had no intention of defrauding the company. Mr. Alpass said he thought the defendants' conduct was very bad, and accordingly the bench would impose a -penalty of 40s and costs in each case.

div.head: CHILD BURNED TO DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: CHILD BURNED TO DEATH AT WIDNES.

A sad burning fatality, which shows the danger of leav- ing children alone in any place where there is tire, occurred at Widnes, on Monday. The victim was a girl, named Martha Elizabeth Jonee, aged four years. and seven months, daughter of Squire Jones, labourer, who lives at 36, Kent-street. ;Vhen the girl returned hofne from school at neon on Monday, the mother left her ia charge of the house whilst she went to purchase some provisione. JO a short time the girl was seen to rush into the street en- veloped in a mass ef flaws. and screaming loudly. Mr. Hargreaves, publican. who lives in the neighbenrbood, seized the unfertunate child, and with great presence of mind -cut off her burning clothing with a pair of scissors. Dr. McLennan was sent for, and on arriving he pronounced the case to be a serious one. The child lingered in great agony until Wednesday morning, when she died. The inquest on the body was held at the Prince of Wales Hotel, yesterday, bef../re Mr. Rowbeetom. The tirst witness called was Maria Jonee, the mother of the deceased, who stated that she was only away from home ten minutes. When she returned she found that her girl had been seriously burnt. There were two other little ehil-fren in the house besides the deceased. Thedeceased was burned on the head, body, and legs. Dr. McLennan attended her until death. Ellen Rowe, rife of George Rowe, of 38, Kent-street, said about half-past twelve she heard screams in the street. Looking out she saw the deceased with her hair and cloth- ing on tire, which Mr. J. W. Hargreavea eztinguished. —A verdict of accidental death Witi3 returned.
FRIGHTFUL FATALITY IN A WIDNES

CIIEMIUAL WORKS. On Monday afternoon at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, Me. E. R. Rowbottorn, the deputy coroner, held an inquiry touching the death of Thomas Charlestown. Mr. H.. 6. Richmond, Government Inspector of factories, was present during the proceedings. Mr. Lawrence Kilcross repeesented the thin of Messrs. Matthieson and Co., and ley p.e mission of the coroner, the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, watched the case on behalf of the relatives of the deceased. On the night of the 2nd May, the deceased was working near a pan of hot glvceiine with a man named Hillide, when the latter left him and took away the lamp by whose light they worked. In the dark the deceased, in an attempt to walk away from the place where he was standing, fell inte the scalding liquor, receiving such injuries that after lingering for a month, he died in the Accident Hospital. The folloWing evidence was adduced :—John Charlestown, brother of the deceased living at Birkenherd, said his brother was 38 years of age, and lived at 24 Perry-street Runcorn. He saw him in Widnes Hospital after the accident, and deceased then told him that it occurred through the lid of a well not being down. Richard Hillidge, of 31 Surrey-street Runcorn, employed as a pipefitter at Messrs. Matthieson's works, said the deceased was engaged at the same works and at similar labour. The accident occurred at 10 o'clock pm. on the 2nd of May. He and the deceased were engaged in fixing a steam pipe, and they were standing on a pan 5 feet 6 inches from the ground. His companion fell into another pan of hot glycerine, which was lower than the one on which they were standing. He did not know exactly how the ac- cident happened, as he did not see the deceased fall in. He heard him call out and went to his assistance. He raised him, from the pan and took him into a neighbouring shed, where he stripped him and attempted to ease his pain. They had an oil lamp to light them at their work. It was a naked light. Deceased, when the accident happened, had no light, as he (witnesea had taken it away. Tne deceased was sober. —By Mr. Richmond: No one else was working near at the time. He did not know who had lifted the lid off the pan into which deceased fell.—Mr. Richmond remarked that it was clear the pan had been lifted by someone. In answer to the Coroner, witness said he considered the light given by the lamp was sufficient for his work. Questioned by a juror. Mr. Kilcross siid the deceased had been at the works five years, and was well acquainted with them.—The witness stated it was customary to open the pan lid.—James Butler, of 76, Davies-street, West Bank, deposed that he was a labourer at Messrs. Matthieson's worke, and on the night in question, assisted by three other men, he cleaned out the pan into which the deceased fell. They finished the task about a quarter-past nine. He then saw the deceased and Hillidge at work. His attention was called to a pan in which the liquor was boiling over, and leaving the well which he had been cleaning he did not return until the accident occurred. --By Mr. Richmond: When he came out of the well the liquor was turned on and began to run into the pan. He left the lid open when he went away. He could not give any reason why he left the lid open. He ought to have closed it.—By the Coroner: He was not in the habit of leaving lids open.—ln reply to a juryman, witness said the light the other men'had after he took his away was sufficient to show them that the lid was open. It was not ueccessary for the lid to be open.—By the Coroner: Every man in the works had lanaps.—Mr. Itichmon4: The lamps are suppoaed to be supplied by the firm, are they? Yes.—Miss Downey, matron at Widnes Hospital, said the deceaeed was badly scalded above the knees. He died through a shock to the nervous system consequent upon scalding.—Mr. H. S. Richmond, Government inspector of factories, was then sworn, and stated that he had that day visited the ecene of the accident. There were a row of pans and pipes, to which the witnesses had spoken. Over these, between the pans and the well alluded to, there was a space four or five feet ' in diameter. There was plenty of room to walk on either side of the pans without going across them at all, but being dark the deceased probably could not see where he was going. The only object of the lids was, first that they might be lifted up sometimes to see how full the vessel was, and, secondly, that they might lift it up to have the well cleaned out. He bad seen Mr. Matthieson, who had kindly promised to have the pans fenced, although he was not compelled to do so by Act of Parliament unless women and children worked there. At these works there were no women and children. The danger was that the workmen would not go round the pans, as they could very well do, but they would go across the pans. There was no reason at all why they should go over the pans, He did not think that any blame could be attached to the employer in this case. The employer had provided lids, and he could not be expected to remain at the works all night to see that they were kept on the pans.— i The Coroner remarked that the circumstances of the death had—thanks to the valuable evidence of Mr. Richmond— been clearly placed before the jury. The question was how Came the well to be left open? That had been frankly answered by Butler, who admitted that he had left the lid off, and if there was any negligence it was on the part of that witness. He seemed very sorry that he had forgott'en to close the lid, and it was an act rorgetfulis fol. which he could not be punished. To forget did not make a man culpably negligent. When a man intentionally did not do something which In ought to have done, that amounted to a misdeam.eanoeur, but this was plainly not a case of that kind, but 'empty one of forgetfulness.—A. Juror remarked that Hillidge was to blame for leaving only one light.—The Coroner replied that if it cam , to that, the deceased was to blame for having no light. Hillidge might be to blame for , not seeing where the deceased was.—Mr.Kilcross said it was for such men as the deceased to carry a lamp with him.— After a short deliberation in private the jury returned a 1 v•craict of .coidont:a deatn.

There were 34 boys and 20 girls in attendance at school, and four boys and ten girls receiving industrial training. There were 18 idiots in the house, and 30 lunatics in the asylum. In Runcorn 412 persons were receiving out- door relief at a cost of £37 13s. 9d. per week; Frodsham, 165 persona at a cost of £l6 155.; Budworth. 132 persons at a Cost of £l4 7d. The funeral of the deceased took place on Tuesday, in Runcorn Cemetery, and was taken part in by the members of the Order of the Sons of Temperance. Charlestown was a. member of the Wesleyan Metbodist body, and at one time was the leader of one of the society classes meeting in connection with Halton-road Chapel. The cortege was headed by the E. J. Robinson and George Hack; then followed about 40 members of the Order of the Sons of Temperance, and several members of the Wesleyan denomination, including Messrs. R. Norman, H. Randle, S. Coventry, and John tddock. Considerable number's of people lined the route, and several of the shops were closed. The ceremony at the grave side was conducted by the Revs. E. J. Robinson and George Hack, and Mr. R. Norman offered up prayer. The impressive service of the Sons of Temperance was then read by Bro. Thomas Faulkner.
HEAVY SENTENCE ON A WIDNES MARINE STORE DEALER.
OFFENCES AGAINST THE CONTA- GIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. Holbrook Gasket', jun., Paul Kerley and Owen Kerley, marine store dealers, carrying on business in Cholmondeley-street, were summoned to answer a charge of purchasing a less quantity of brass than is allowed under the Prevention of Crimes Act, 1871.—Paul Kerley did not appear.—Superintendent Barker said under this Act marine store dealers wore not permitted to purchase brass in less quantities than 561bs. Considering the great number of petty larcenies that had been committed in Widnes—thefts of small qaantities of metal, which had no doubt found its way into the marine store dealers hands, he should, if be proved the case, ask their worships to impose the highest penalty allowed.—Jehn R. Holden, who had been liberated ' to give evidence, said he was a labourer, and resided in Pier- street, Widnes. About nine o'clock, on Wednesday, the 16th May, he went to the defendants' marine store, and offered the brass for sale to the de- fendant, Owen. The latter weighed it, and said he "would call it 51bs," and paid witness is 3d for it. He (witness') had been taken in custody by P.S. Robinson on suspicion of having stolen the brass.—P.S. Robinson deposed that about four o'clock on the day in question he visited the marine store in Cholmondeley-street. He found the brass step produced under the writiug desk. Defendant said he had bought it from the last witness with a lot of rags, and lie in consequence took Holden into custody. The name of Sarah Kerley was over the shop door, but he had seen the landlord's book, and the name of Paul Kerley was put down as the tenant.—P.C.'s Laing and Brown, and Mrs. Margaret Dixon, of 11, Cholmondeley-street, deposed to Paul Kerley carrying on business in the shop. Superintendent Barker said he was bringing this evidence because Paul Kerley had attempted to set uo the defence that the shop was not his. Paul, in January, 1881, was convicted at the sessions of re- ceiving stolen lead, and was sentenced to 15 months' impri- sonment. He had also been convicted of various other offences.—The Bench fined Owen ss, and costs 10s. or, in. default, 10 daye' imprisonment, and Paul was fined Dt 10s, and costs 16s, or, in default, two months' imprisonment.

A Ba:mil OF OFFENDERS AT DARESBURY. At the Daresbury Petty Session, on Tuesday, the follow- ing persons wrre summomed for offences against the C3nta- gious Diseases (Animals) Act: John White, farmer, Whitley, for allowing six pigs to he removed from Warring- ton to Whitley without a license, was fined is for each animal, and costs, in all 19s; Ann Simpson, widow, Apple- ton, for similarly allowing three pigs to be removed from Warrington to Appleton, was fined Is for each pig, and costs; William Mortimer, tanuer, Orford, was fined Is and 15s costs for likewise allowing a cow to be removed ; 'Alfred Dawson, farmer, Bakehouse-lane, near Liverpool, for allowing 12 bul- locks to be driven from his reside nce along the highway at Walton Superior, without license, Was fined is each animal and 15s costs; and John Percival, farmer, Antrobus, was ordered to pay 103 6d for allowing two cows to be removed from Warrington to Antrobus without license The drivers in each of the above cases were summoned for driving the animals without a license, but the cases against them were dismissed. _ _

A pig dealer named Joseph Bradbury, Wilderspool-road Latchford, was summoned for having made a declaration in connection with the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act which was false in certain material particular3.—Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, who appeared for defendant, made a technical objection to the charge, which was held by the Magistraw? Clerk (Mr. White) to be a fatal one, both to this and to five other charges of a similar nature which were down for hear- ' ing. Mr. Riley, however, said he would agree to the charge being amended in erne case, hoping that Inspector Williamson when it was heard would withdraw the prosecution in the others.—The ease vas then gone into.—P.S. Booth said that about six o'clock on the 3rd May defendant called at his station, and asked for a license to remove a number of pigs to Little Leigh. Witness asked him If ft was the license that be and Mr. Houghton of Little Leigh, applied for on the previous day, and which was not granted owing to him refusing to sign the declara- tion, and defendant replied it was. On this admission wit- ness refused to grant the license asked for, as he elicited from Mr. Houghton when defendant and Houghton visited him on the previous day that the pigs had been exposed for sale in the Warrington Market. Defendant said You mast not take any notice of him. I say that these pigs have been on my premises 28 days, and that they have not been in the Warrington Market.'" Me filled up the declara- tion form to the above effect, and witness on that granted him a license to remove nine pigs to Mr. Houghton's.—Mr. Houghton was then called, and admitted that he bought nine pigs from defendant in Warrington Market.—ln reply to Mr. Riley, he said he was not prepared to swear that the pigs he got were the same he bought in the Market.—The Bench were of opinion that defendant had made a false declaration, and fined him £5 and costs.
RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' FINANCES.

In our advertising columns we publish a detailed state- ment of the receipts and expenditure of the Runcorn Board of 'Commissioners for the year ended March 25th last. It appears that the general district rate realised £3.6d7 is 7d, wile the income received from the market includint.l- the cottage rents was £243 13s 91. The sum of £996 7s 9d has been received on account of private improvements. The total income was £5,359 us 6d. The expenditure is stated at £5 919 4s Bd, but of this sum £1,254 12s 101 has been expended in private improvements, and will be re- covered. The cost of scavenging and watering has been £1,076 is sd, and the gas supply has cost the ratepayers £672 12a Gd. SLiaries amount to £485 es 2d, establish- ment charges to £149 us 10d, and legal expenses to £lO7 les fid. The election expenses were £lO les 9d. Ile finances of the Free Library Committee are in a very healthy state. Including £4B 7s id, the balance of the penny rate still in the hards of the Commissioners, the committee have a balance of £69 103 sd, but a great propor- tion of-this will be absorbed in new books already ordered. Donations to the library amount to £36, while the income has been further increased by £7 5s 2d paid in fims's. Over £9l has been expended in new books, and £l5 16s 5d in binding old ones. The district auditor has certified the ac- counts as correct.

Leroy the execution creditor.—lt seemed that an execution bad been issued out of the Salford Hundred Court of Record at the instance of George Leroy against the goods of Thomas Walker, who recently kept the Navigation Inn, Runcorn, but who in the meantime had removed to Ellesmere-street to live with his father-in-law, Thomas Royle. The goods at the house in Ellesmere-street were seized by the bailiffs, when Boyle claimed the whole of the furniture as belonging to him, and the amount of the debt and costs £4 17s 8d was paid into court to abide the result of the present inter- pleader summons. Thomas Royle, the claimant, Elizabeth •rnaeph Williamson, Robert Royle, Margaret Con- way, and Mary Green, were all examined by Mr. Burton in suppert of the claim.—Mr. Lake, for the execution creditor, submitted from the claimant's evidence the only conclusion to be drawn was that this furniture belonged to Walker, as he appeared to have peaceable \ possession, and it was upon the strength of this furniture being in his possession that he was enabled to obtain credit to carry on his business.—His Honour, in summing up, said cases of this description were always open to suspicion, but in this instance he thought the claimant had rnadeout a prima facie case, and he should give the claimant a verdict for £3 2s, value of the goods which the claimant had sold in order to pay out the execu- tion, the execution creditor to pay the costs. The business of the court included three adjourned plaints, 53 original plaints, 12 judgment summonses, and the interpleader case.

A LONDON TRAGEDY.

At the Salisbury Hotel, Salisbury-square, London, early yesterday morning, John Michael Routledge (25) was shot by Phomas Kelly k2l), with whom he occupied a double- bedded room. Routledge, who is married, and who is in a sinking condition, states that the affair was accidental, and wAs caused by their examining each other's revolver!. Kelly makes a similar statement. THE FR CH DEFEAT IN TONQUIN. SIXTEEN FRENCHMENiIMPALED. A Paris telegram of yesterday says :—Tbe Gaulois to-da7 publishes some particulsrs of the engagement near Hanoi, in which Comtnandaut Riviera was killed. On leaving the fort be divided his men into two detachments, advancing himself with 150 marines. The second detachment, which numbered 250 men, remained too far in the rear, and the advance guard being surprised by a large body of "Black Flags," was complely annihilated. When the rear guard came up the "Black Flags" fled. carrying off with them Commander Riviera and 15 marines, all of whom were im- paled on the following day. TRAGIC AFFAIR IN LIVERPOOL: A THREE WEEKS' BRIDE KILLED. ,

What is supposed to be a shocking tragedy was enacted in Edgehilll, a suburb of Liverpool, at a late hour on Thursday night. Robert Arthur Holt, rent collector, who resides in Hawthorn Grove, was arrested charged with causing the death of his wife Ellen. The couple have only been married P.l2riut three weeks, and it is aileged that Holt In tho CeAtrso of a game' took up a table knife and de- signedly or by accident stabbed his wife with it behind the left ear, the kßife penetrating the brain and causing instant death. The neighbours sent for the police and Holt was arrested, when he denied having Stabbed the woman, and accounted for her death by saying she was cutting some meet for the dog, when she slipped and fell on the knife, !receiving fatal injuries.

div.head: RUNCORN WORKS ASSESSMENTS.
div.p: RUNCORN WORKS ASSESSMENTS.

At the recent election of Guardians great prominence was given to the question of assessments. The contest was, in fact, as a Guardian once remarked, fought on "assessment lines" It was on thee lines that the candidates nominated by the Ratepayers' Association were run, and that they were not altogether unsuccessful is shown by the fact that three obtained seats at the Board. The action of the Association is likely to bear fruit. A well balanced valuation list is a desiderattecn to the ratepayers in every town, and as the Association drew attention to what they deemed inequalities, in so far are they deserving of the support of the public of Runcorn. In the present year the members of the Assess- ment Committee are likely to have no lack of business to occupy their attention. They are preparing to resist an appeal made on behalf of the proprietors of the Wilderspool Brewery; and on tte 19th inst. Runcorn Gas Company, represented 1w counsel, will appeal against the assessment of their works on the ground that they are unequally assessed compared with other works in the town. div.head: TUE MA.NOHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: TUE MA.NOHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The Saiect Committee on this Bill sat again yesterday, Sir Joseph Bailey presidia,. Mr. Galesworthy, a member of the Manchester City Council, said he had subscribed a thousand pounds tonatds the preliminary expenses in pro- moting the Bill, and if it were passed he was prepared to invest twenty thousand towards completing the scheme. He had in his hand a list of names of gentlemen who had sub- scribed a thousand each towards the preliminary expenses, and ho had no mason to doubt that if the Bill were passed, then these gentlemen would come forward with the neces- sary capital. He did not agree with Mr. Armitage, M P., that the married classes of Lancashire were not enthnsias- ticelly in favour of the scheme. Mr. F. H. WALMSLEY. a surgeon, and a member of the Salford Corporation, said he lived in the neighbourhood of Manchester all his life. In past years they had. been troubled considerably with floods, which did injury to trade and caused a great amount of sickness. If the Ship Canal were constructed, the chances of floods would be lessened,l if not entirely removed. He was of opinion that there would be no lack of capital if the Bill were passed. In commercial centres like Manchester the capital °Huge schemes did not remain in the hands of a few wealthy men , with income; ranging from £5OO to £l,OOO. The list which was in the hands of the last witness represented a large sum of money. Mr. ALFRED HUGHES, of the firm of Messrs. Faulkner and Co., carriers on the Irsvell, gave evidence on behalf of the scheme. He BAid the Irw:Al had been allowed to silt up and become unnavigable by the gentlemen who should have improved it.—By Mr. SAUNDERS : Ho knew that during the lasi three years large sums of money had been spent at Sal- ford arid Wirrington in improving the navigation. . Mr. ALFRED, manager of a Pendlebnry firm of carriers, gave evidence in regard to the neglected condition of the Irwell. At the present time there was only a sufficient depth of water to ailow of boats of fifty tons to pass down, and they could only move freely after heavy rain- falls. _ .

Mr. HENRY W/LEY, superintendent engineer to the health department of the Manchester Corpora- tion, said during laetyear they were only able to send away bv boat 10,000 tons of nightsoil, whereas they would be able to send away 80,000 tons if the Ship Canal were con- structed. The water at Throstle Nest, Manchester, was comparatively clear when the works were idle. About 11.000 closets emptied themselves into the Irwell. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN thought it would be as well not to pursue this question. How did it effect the Ship Canal ? Mr. CHIN'S a lid some of the petitioners raised the sani- tary question of the canal. The CHAIRMAN asked how it could affect the canal unless it was to become a tilthy, stagnant pool. Mr. CRIPPS said that was the paint which was raised. The CHAIRM 1N said there could be no doubt that the river was filthy.lt could not be otherwise, seeing that 11,000 water closets were emptied into it. Dr. CARTER BE,LL, public analyst of Cheshire, gave evi- dence to the etlct that the water of the Irwell was not un- healthy and unsanitary. Dr. Burarmanier gave similar evidence. The CHAIRMAN seppoted the promoters were going to prove that the river would tot be 'worse after the Ship Canal was made. Mr. PE741:12010E STEPHENS hoped they would be able to prove more. They wanted to show that there was a differ- ence between sewer battled up and sewer in an open and flowing river. Mr. Mcf.rrvans said he weald he labia to show that the canal would make the river at Irlam as lAd and filthy as it was before 1845. since which year the nuisance had been re- moved to a great extent. • Dr. TATHAM Said that by the e,anstreetion of the canal and the deepening of the bed of the river, many of the sanitary evils of the water would be removed. For one thing it removed the swamps at Trafford Bridge. It would remove other impurities all along the river. The Committee adjourned until Monday.

CRUELTY TO DONKEYS AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds, and Mr. A. Thomas, Mary Lovely, fish dealer, Brunswick-street, was charged with 'haying on the 11th May cruelly ill-treated a donkey by working it in an unfit state.—Mr. Harper, R.S.P.C.A , Altrincham, stated that on the day in question at the end of Brook-street ha saw a donkey attached to a cart belonging to the defendant. The animal was in fair condition, but on lifting up the saddle he tfound a wound about the size of a crownpiece. It was a very old wound, and was discharging matter. A piece of sacking placed under the saddle over the wound was saturated with matter. It was a very painful wound, and the donkey must have suffered from it for nine days or a fortnight.—The defendant stated that the wound had only been made that morning, but Mr: Harper persisted that it was an old one.—The defendant informed their Worships that the animal was standing at the court door, and the magistrates examined it.—On returning, Mr. Reynolds said the wound appeared to have been a very bad one and the defendant was fined 10s. and costs 10s. 8d.—Isaac Broad- hurst, coal dealer, Blantyre-street, was summoned on a similar charge.—lnspector Harper said on the 11th May he saw the defendant 'h donkey drawing a cart laden with coal and driven by a boy. He perceived that it had a difficulty in walking, and on examining it he found that it was without shoes on its hoofs, which were worn down to the sensitive sole. The animal was it skeleton in condition, and through poverty the skin wee broken out in blisters in three places on its back. Its eyes were neatly closed, and water was running from them, while a " frothy mucous," mixed with blood. tr;ckled down its nostrils. It war, plain to anyone that the donkey was unfit for any kind of work; and that it was dying a lingering death through disease and starvation. He told the boy to take the animal home at once, and he pointed out to the defendant the condition of the animal, telling him that it was dying from hard work and starvation. Defendant said it was well fed and well looked after, and could not account for its condition.—P.S. Mac Michael gave evidence in support of the charge.—The defendant acknowledged that the donkey was an old one, and he had since bought a younger one and turned the animal in question out to grass. The magistrates considered this a worse case than the last, and were surprised that A man in the position of the defen- dant should have worked a donkey in such a state. He ought to have known better.—The defendant was fined 235. and - costa, 10a. ed.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

MISCONDUCT OF IRISH OFFICIALS.—Mr. TREVELYAW, re- plying to questions from Mr. Kenny as to the misconduct of certain officials in Ireland, severely condemned the practice of making calunainous charges against persons on sunny- mous communications and under the shelter of a question in the House of Commons.

FRANCE AND CITINA.—Mr. GLADSTONE said Her Majesty's Government were always on the look out to offer their good offices when a friendly power got into a difficulty. The statn of affairs between France and China did not justifyany in- terference on their part at the present moment. 111 n. EHRINGTOWS MISSION.—Mr. GLADSTONE proposed that the discussion on Mr. Errington and his proceedings at Rome should betaken on Menday evening, when the. Foreign. Office vote was moved. MR. O'KELLY AND His CHALLENGE. The SPEAKER informed Mr. O'Kelly that he had been ordered to attend in his place in consequence of his having sent a challenge to Mr. McCoan. As that hon. gentleman had given a premise not to take part in hostile proceedings, he called on Mr. O'Kelly to give a similar promise. Mr. O'KELLY ollected to the interference of the House in his private affairs. After the course Mr. McCoan had taken there was no necessity for his giving any promise in that House far whose opinion he cared very httle.—Mr. GLADSTONE thought the course taken by Mr. O.:Kelly was not satisfactory, and that he ought to give the promise required.—Mr. O'KELLY said that after the proceeding by Mr. McCoan he considered the matter practically at an end.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he understood that to amount to an intimation that no further hostile pro- ceedings in the matter would take place.—Sir S.NOETECOTI expressed a similar hope, and the orders of the day were proceeded with.

TIFE BOARD ON INLAND REVENUE AND ITS OFFICERS. —On the motion for going into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates' Lend R. CHURCHILL called atten- tion to the orders issued by the Board of Inland Revenue with regard to civil servants communicating with members of that House. He insisted the Board had gone beyond Be power in issuing the order which he contended was at com- plete variance with the law.--Mr. MONK seconded the motion. —Sir S. NORTHCOTE took exception to the statements of Lord Churchill, and said he had scarcely ever heard a speech sd full of mistakes and misstate- ments. He then reviewed the position of the question, and said if there was anything in the order that interfered with civil servants laying their grievances before that House it ought to be removed, but Parliament would take a serious step if they allowed an appeal from superiors to that Hou.e3 with tke view of getting salaries increagea.— Mr. WHITBRED also opposed the resolution.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he was responsible for the order. He thought it an excellent one, and was prepared to stand by it.—Sir D. Worxr supported the resolution.—Mr. GLADSTONE thought the adoption of the resolution would be attended with most serious consequences. He justified the appointments he had made to the Inland Revenue departments, and advised the House to negative the noble lord's proposal.—On a divison the numbers were :—For the resolution, 37; against, 120. RECRUITING FOR THE ARM.—Sir W. BARTELLOT called attention to the present position of recruiting for the army. He regretted the breaks up of the regimental system in favour of the new fangled territorial system, which he thought had nothing to recommend it. Ile comulained of the youth of the soldiers sent abroad, and said if it was persevered in, some day great reverse would come to the English army. —Mr. CAINR thought intemperance the cause of crime in the army.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley, - A DESERTZE.—John Bryan, last from Liverpool, was charged with being a deserter or absentee from the Glamorganshire Militia, Cardiff. during the training, of 1882-3.—The case was remanded till Friday. THE DESERTER.—John Bryan. who was remanded from Wednesday on a charge of beieg a deserter or absentee from the Glamorganshire Militia, Cardiff, during the training of 1882:3, was again brought up.—The Chief Constable said he had received a communication from the military authorities at Car- diff saying that if the pri.oner could give the court a satisfac- tory excuse for his absence they would send a pass and receive him back at Cardiff, but if he could not, then they would ask that the court deal with him.—Prisoner said he went to India before the training, intending to be bask in time for it, but he was taken ill with fever.—The Bench accepted this statement, and orderedthat prisoner be sent on to Cardiff, CHARGE OF ASSIIILY.—James Molyneux, file cutter, 24, Greenall-street, was charged with assaulting Thomas Giblin at George Maguire's, Bink-street, on the 24th May.—There was not sufficient evidence to prove the case, and it was dismissed. QUARREL.—John Edwardson a young man, was summoned on a charge of assaulting a married woman named Ann Bott. Complainant said on Seurday afternoon there was a "little tother " between the defendant and her husband, but after it was settled the defendant went to complainant's door, which he pushed open, and struck Mrs. Bott on the face, giving her a black eye. For the defence it was stated the complainant's' husband threw some lime on the eefendaut, who her struck with a whitewash brush. The Bench dismissed the charge.— Margaret Griffiths was summoned for using defamatory language to Isabella Burgess, on Tuesday, and she was bound over to keep the peace for two months, herself in £lO, and one surety of £5. The defendant now became very uproarious, shouting and gesticulating wildly. She also made a number of vile charges against the complainant. div.head: INQUESTS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: INQUESTS AT WARRINGTON.
SUDDEN DEATH.

An inquest was held on Wednesday, at the White Hurt, Sankey-street, by Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, touching the death of Francis Payne, a tanner, 58 years of age, residing at 2, Mersey-terrace, off Mersey-street, who was found. dead in bed about 10-30 on Monday night.—lt appeared that deceased had been troubled with heart disease for a long time, and a verdict of "Died from natural cauets" VIM returned.

div.head: SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY.
div.p: SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY.

Mr, Barker afterwards held an inquiry at the same place, relative to the death of Margaret Appleton, wife of John Appleton, a labourer at Cartwrisht's glass bottle works, who was burned to death at noon on Monday at her house, 1, Stoney-yard, Bank-street.—John Appleton, husband of de- ceased, said he left home, on Monday, about five minutes to twelve, to take his son's dinner to Whitecrosa works. De- ceased when he left was putting some small sticks into the fire-grate. When he returned home deceased bad been taken to the Infirmary, and he immediately went to that place, but when he arrived she was dead. She was not subject to fits, and when he left her she appeared to be quite well.—By a Juryman: Deceased had some whisky in the morning, and a gill of beer about 10 o'clock, but she was quite sober when he left her. Mr. Joseph Smith, estate and commission agent, said that about five minutes to 12 he saw smoke issuing from unier tke door of the house occupied by the last witness, and he gave an alarm of fire.—Mrs. Bridget Smith, who lives in Bank- street, said she beard the alarm and went to deceased's door. She looked through the key-hole and saw deceased inflames with her arms raised. The door was locked, and she opened it with her own key. She got some water and threw it over deceased.—P.C. Neill said he was in the magistrates' clerk's office when the alarm of fire was raised. He went to de- ceased's house and found persons throwing water on deceased, who was lying on the floor enveloped in tholes. She was taken out of the house as it 19,23 filled witk smoke. The flames were extinguished, and a doctor was sent for, but as he said the case was hopeless deceased was taken to the Inßrmary. She was terribly charred from head to fo9t.— Miss Alice Brandwood, nurse at the Infirmary, deposed to deceased being brought there aboat a quarter to one on Mon- day. She was unconscious, and remained in that state up to the time of her death, which happened at 10 minutes past one.—The Coroner, in addressing the jury, said it was satis- factory to know that death was not caused through driik, as was the case in most accidents.—The reason given for the door being locked .was that deceased when alone in the house was in the habit of locking the door, as she was of a very , retired disposition.—A verdict of "Accidental death " wan I returned.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A SERVANT GIRL.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A SERVANT GIRL.

On the same day Mr. Barker held an inquest at the Ship Inn, Bank Quay, on the body of Maude Mary Cooper. daughter of James Cooper, of 17, Smith-street, who com- mitted suicide by drowning on Thursday evening week.-Jast. Cooper, painter, 17, Smith-street, said deceased was hie: daughter, and was about 16 years of age She was in service- at Mr. Cntchley's, provision dealer, Irlam-street, where she had been about 12 months. He did not think there had. been anything to trouble deceased, who was a very impul- sive girl, and could not bear chiding. In reply to Mr. Buck- ley, a juryman, witness said he had never gone to the girl drunk in his life, and asked her for her wages.— John Critchlev said deceased had been in his service, lie last saw her alive en the previous Thursday night, about 9 , o'clock, when she was at his house. He did not notice- , anything unusaal about her. She went on an errand to Churcli-street, and did not return. He made inquiries, but I could learn nothing of her whereabouts. lie knew of nothing which might have led her to commit the rash act. His daughter found written on a pasteboard ornament (pro- duced) in a drawer the following: "So you think on when I you want me next that you will find Mande in river on , Friday. Amen." He could not say whether the writing I was the deceased's, but be had shown it to the father who I said it was. She was very excitable, and rather eccentric at j times.—By a juryman: She was out rather late on Wednes- ' day night, and his wife told her of it.—Mr. Cooper : Did Critehley give her notice when she had these words ? —Witness: No; she had no words. His wife spoke to her on the Thursday morning about being out late, but they bad no words. Deceased seemed very jolly in the evening before going out on the errand.—Charles Wainwright, a young man, said he walked along the river side on the Thursday night, and saw the de- ceased about a quarter past nine standing against the crane uear the India Rubber Works. She Ivas alone, and close to the water. He knew the girl very well but had never spoken to her, and did not on this occasion. He noticed she had a white apron on.—Frank Kirkham, al ire drawer, said be was on the river in a boat on Tuesday and found the body of deceased floating in the water. It was pulled into the boat and brought to the Ship Inn. When they found the body the dress was not disarranged in any wait. An apron was over the head and tied round the neck. He believed it could have been tied thus by the girl.—Jaue Cooper, stepmother to deceased, said that the girl often visited her, and she was on good terms with her. Sometimes when deceased had been reproved sha would sulk for a long time. So far as witness knew the girl had been comfortable in her employment. A Juryman: Is there any love affair ?—Witnesi said she was not aware that deceased had had a sweetheart. Reply- ing to her. husband, witness said he had never made a pros- lice of going to Mr. Buckley's drunk and asking for the girl's wages.—P.C. Neill said he had known Cooper for many years, and he had always found him to be a sober man; and he was surprised when he heard the remark from Mr. Buckley.—The Coroner: Yes; it is a pity the remark was made.—A verdict to the effect that deceased commit- ted suicide by drowning during temporary insanity, was then returned.

COLLIERY ACCIDENTS AT ST. HELENS On NI.-,nday afternoon a collier named Abbott, while working in a pit belonging to the St. Helens Collieries Company, WaS a!mcst buried beneath a quantity of falling roof. When extricated he was taken to his home in Havelock-et., and attended by Dr. Hay, who found the unfortunate man suffering from severe contusions of the leg and back besides shock to the system generally. Acting on the doctor's advice, he was at once !moved to the Cottage Hospital, at Peasley Cross.—On the' s.me day an accident ef a somewhat different nature occur- red at Ashton Green Colliery. Early in the morning soma. men and boys, to the number of eight, were descending the shaft in a cade, but before they had quite reachel the bot- tom the engine-man stopped the cage, seeming to think that it bad reached the bottom. On discovering his mistake he Ist the cage go again with a jerk, the consequence being that it, went against the bottom of the shaft with great force. Four boys and one man were badly hurt about the feet and ankles by the force of the shock, and will probably be un- able to work for some time. The names of those injured are —James Hughes,i3road Oak ; James T.ckle, Water-lane James Fisher, 109, Chancery-lane; Richardson, Chan- cery-lane and Makin, Williameon-street.

div.head: TERRIBLE STORY OF INHUMANITY.
div.p: A TERRIBLE STORY OF IN- HUMANITY.

A shocking story of "man's inhumanity to man" was unfolded at an inquest held by the West Bromwich coroner, on Tuesday, on the bodies of two young children who had I met with an agonising death by falling into a heap of burn- ing cinders on Saturday last. It seems that a cinder-bank, composed of the live refuse from neighbouring works, had been newly formed in the vicinity of the Union Furnaces, Smethwick, and about this bank the poor children of the neighbourhood were in the habit of clustering, in order to pick up stray pieces of coal and coke for the use of their parents. On the day in question the two deceased, a boy and girl, aged respectively eleven and thirteen, were on this smouldering Black Country volcano, in company with three others, engaged in their filial but perilous task, when the bank suddenly gave way, and precipitated two little girls named Hadley and Evans into the glowing crater beneath. Benjamin Hadley, a child of eleven, and brother of the first-mentioned girl, went valiantly to the assistance of his sister and her companion, but in trying to extricate them he fell in himself, and 'shared their fate. Ultimately an elder brother named Joseph succeeded, at considerable personal risk, in getting all three children out of the furnace, but not until they had sustained such ter- rible injuries as to cause them all three an agonising death. Will it be credited that during the whole of the time this heart-rending tragedy was being enacted, with its ebb and flow of hope and fear, its incidents of disaster and heroism, a strong man, who bad been instrumental in form- ing the fatal mound, stood looking on within a few yards of the spot, and refused not only to stretch a hand to the burning children, but even to render them the slightest as- .sistance when he saw them writhing in agony after their extrication from the cinder heap? According to his view, the children were trespassers; ho had repeatedly ordered them away, ani though he does not say so in many words, he evidently thought when he saw them disappear in the treacherous cinder heap, they were rightly sem-ed.—Bir- mingham Post.

WITAT FRED ARCHER COULDN'T Do.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, a milkman, named Thos. Miller, was charged with driving his cart at a furious pace along Higher Parr-street, on the 17th ult.—P.C.. Radcliffe said the cart seemed to be going at the rate of about 14 or 15 miles an hour, the horse which was drawing it being a very fast one.—Defendant: " That horse couldn't go at seven miles an hour if you were to put Fred Archer on its back." (Laugbier.)—He was fined 103 and costs. Two bicyclists appeared before .the Birkenhead county magistrates, on Thursday, charged with riding on the foot- walk at Eastbam. Both the offenders pleaded that they were only beginners, and did not ;mow that they were doing wrong, one of them remarking that there was no per- son on the road at the time. The magistrates commented on the danger of bicyclists riding on the footpaths, as ly as they did recently on the danger of cyclists riding along the road, but, as the offenders were only beginners, they disaarged them on the payment of Mi. 61 each for _ costs.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST AN ACTOR.—George Elliott, an actor, was charged at the Altrincham Police Court, on Tuesday morning, witla entering tte house of Robert Ives, at Altrincham, with intent to commit a felony. The pri- soner walked into the house, went upstairs, and examined the pocket 6 of a pair of trousers and a coat. On being spoken to by the prosecutor's wife the prisoner rushed out of the house, but was subsequently apprehended. He was fined lOs and costs.

div.head: PPLETON.
div.p: A PPLETON.

PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS ON LICENSED PREMISES.— Joseph Miller, landlord of the Mulberry Tree, Appleton, was charged at Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with having permitted drunkenness on his premises.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for defendant.—P.S. Booth said he was called to the Mulberry Tree by the defendant on the even- ing of the 28th April to quell a disturbance. He went to the house and found Henry Shaw and John Arnold drunk and fighting, and he had great difficulty in getting them out. He went into the house again, and Thomas Brace- girdle began swearing about the disturbance which had just taken place. Witness called the attention of the landlord to the man, and the latter was put out of the house. Wit- ness then spoke to defendant about the men being drunk on his premises, and the latter replied that he kept his house respectable, but admitted he had served the men with drink, and asked witness to let the matter pass.—John Bramhall and William Chapman were called, and the former spoke to the three men being drunk, and the latter to Bracegirdle being in the same state.—Defendant, his wife, Thomas Hamlet, and Thomas Acton were called for the defence.— The Bench said they were of opinion that defendant had permitted drunkenness on his premises, but as this was his first offence they would look leniently upon it, and only fine him 20s and costs.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

WIGAN AND DISTRICT (SUPPORT OF SEWERS) BILL—, On Wednesday, in the House of Commons, this bill, which has passed the House of Lords, came before the unopposed committee, Sir A. Otway (chairman of Ways and Means) presiding. The bill makes provision with respect to the support of public sewers and sewage works in the mining districts in the borough af Wigan and neighbouring places; and it was explained that it would relieve the local authorities of a very serious burden, and teed to the safety of the sewers in a very difficult district to manage. No amendments were suggested and the committee passed it, ordering it to be reported to the House. _ _ _

ALLEGED THEFT OF A PAIR OF TROUSERS-At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, William Dowd, a labourer bailing from Shevington, was charged with steal- ing a pair of trousers at Ashton, the property of Ebenezer Lloyd.—Superintendent Weir, who applied for a remand, said the prosecutor was a Clothes dealer at Lodge-lane, Ashton. Lloyd saw the trousers safe about nine o'clock on Friday night, and at half-past twelve on Saturday at noon he missed them. Information was given to Police-constable MTail, who proceeded in the direction of Golborne, and at a pawnshop belonging to Mrs. Harrison he found the prisoner offering the trousers for sale in pledge. The con- stable charged him with stealing them, and he admitted it, remarking that he was in want. There was, however, a sum of 3P. found in his possession.—Prisoner was remaaded until Friday.

div.head: DITTON.
div.p: DITTON.

Sr. MICHAEL'S.—The procession in honour of Our Lord in the Blessed Sacrament, was held at St. Michael's Church, Ditton Hall, on Sunday, and was a magnificent and edifying spectacle. After an eloquent sermon preached in the after- noon by the Rev. Father A. M. De Ilaza-Radlitz, S.J., the procession started from the church and proceeded through the grounds of Ditton Hall College to the altar erected before the old front of the hall, and then back to the church, where a solemn Te Deum and Benediction brought the imposing ceremony to a close. About 300 persons took part officially in the procession, and these were followed by at least 1,000 others. Between 2,000 and 3,000 people lined the route by which the procession was made, and the greatest decorum prevailed, all evidently being struck at the splendour and solemnity of the ceremony, which was enhanced by the accompaniments of the Ditton brass band. FLIXTON.

FLIXTON, URDISTON, AND SOI7TH BARTON HIGHWAY BOARD.—At the monthly meeting of the Board, held on Tuesday evening, Mr. Thomas Royle-Higginson presiding, the Clerk (Mr. J. W. Whitworth) and the Surveyor (Mr. Edwards) submitted their estimates of the probable expendi- ture of the Board during the coming year, the total being £1,373 7s, as against £1,139 in the previous year. The Clerk showed that the rateable value of the Board's district is £37,000, and a 6d rate produces £937, a 7d rate £1,093, and an 8d rate £1,250. It was decided to issue precepts upon the overseers of the several townships for £l,OOO, and the estimates were referred back far consideration and amendment.

div.head: FRODSHAII.
div.p: FRODSHAII.

TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.— The annual sermons in connection with the Trinity Wes- leyan Sunday School were preached, on Sunday last, in the morning by the Rev. J. M. Bamford, of Frodsham, and in the evening by Richard Johnson, Esq., of Manchester. The musical pertion of the service was very successful, and the cAlections amounted to £2l 9s.

div.head: GO LBORNE.
div.p: GO LBORNE.

GOLBORNE CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL SERMONS.—The anniversary services in connection with the Golborne Con- gregational Sunday Schools were held on Sunday last. In the forenoon an excellent address was given to the scholars, teachers, and friends, by Mr. Samuel King, of Manchester, and in the afternoon and evening sermons were preached by the Rev. W. Kerfoot, of Leigh. Special hymns were sung on each occcasion, and there were large attend- ances, the church being crowded in the evening. The sum of £34 was collected.

A CHILD DROWNED AT GoLBORNE.—On Thursday, forenoon Mr. Rowbottom, the deputy coroner, held an in- quest at the Victoria Hotel, Golberne, on the body of John William Twist, 5 years of age, son of John Twist, over- looker at Messrs. Brewis's mill, and residing in Legh-street. The evidence showed that on Monday afternoon last, the deceased lad left Brewis's school shortly before half-past four, and about half an hour later, his body was observed floating in the brook near School-terrace. It was at once got out by a boy named Murray, and removed to the Vic- toria Hotel. It is supposed that the lad was walking or playing near the brook, and that he accidentally fell in.— The jury returned a verdict of "found drowned."

UI4JIJ-ST WEIGHTS AT GOLBORNH.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Samuel Barfoot, grocer, Golborne, was summoned for having in his possession three light weights.—The defendant said he was not aware that the weights were light.—Supt. Weir stated that he and his assistant visited the defendant's shop on the 16th nit., and examined the weights. Among others they found a 21b. weight 21 drachms light, 14b. weight over 1 drachm light, and a Vb. weight 1 drachm light. Two of the weights were also nnstamped, and had never been stamped by anyone. He found that the last time tha defendant sent his weights to be examined was the 21st June, last year. Since then he (Supt. Weir) had been to Golborne for the purpose of adjusting weights.—The Clerk examined the weights, and observed that one of them appeared to be a curious old weight. It bore the date 1826 and the arms of the City of London, and also one of the Royal George's stamped upon it.—Supt. Weir observed that the weights should show upon them what weight they were. He added that he had summoned the defendant not to get a penalty merely but more for the purpose of letting the public know that they [ must not keep and use weights without having them adjusted —The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.-- Mary Silcock, a grocer, Golborne, was also summoned for having in her possession a 41b. weight 11 drachms light, a 1-lb. weight 1 drachm light, and a 2oz. weight 1 drachm light.—The Bench imposed a penalty of 10s. and costs.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

CAUTION TO CART OWNERS.—Robert Blake was sum- moned at the Newton Petty Ses3ions on Saturday for having no name on his cart. —The defendant stated be had only got the cart on the previous night, and he had his name written on with chalk until he could get it painted.—He promised to pay the cost 9, and the case was dismissed. ScHoor, Arrnrrnesen AT HAYDOCK.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Thomas Burrows, of Hay- dock, was summoned at the instance of William Cawley, School Attendance officer, for neglecting to send his child to school.—Mr. Cawley stated that the defendants child had made 21 out of a possible 115 attendances.—The defendant was fined ss.

TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAME.—John Pimblett, at young man, was charged at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, with trespassing on land at Haydock, belong- ing to Lord Gerrard, in pursuit of game, on the 9th May.— The defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. S. Marsh, of St. Helens, appeared to prosecute, and stated that at this time of the year young hares, partridges, and other game were out and could easily be" nipped up" by a dog. On the night of the date named a gamekeeper in the employ of Sir Robert Gerard saw the defendant with a retriever dog hunt- ing the fences, and subsequently entered a plantation.— John Phill;ps, gamekeeper, was sworn and gave evidence in support of Mr. Marsh's statement.—Tke defendant was tined lOs and costs.

A COT TAGE HOSPITAL AT HAYDOCII. - There has re- cently been opened at New Boston, Haydock, what is known as a cottage hospital for the benefit of those persons who may be accidentally injured and are unable to obtain at their own homes the accommodation, care, and attention which their case requires. A trained nurse has been ap- pointed in charge of the hospital, and provided there is an empty bed anyone seriously injured will be admitted at any time. Patients however, will be required to pay a weekly sum of ss. towards their maintenance while in the hospital. Every requisite, except personal clothing, will be provided, and parties of all denominations can be attended by their respective ministers. The hospital has ly.!en appropriately fitted up, and will no doubt prove a comfortable borne for anyone temporarily disabled, though it is to be hoped that ems of severe injury will be faw and far between.

A HAYDOCK PUBLICAN CHARGED went PERJURY.—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Wednesday, Joseph Rad- cliffe, described as a licensed victualler carrying on busi- ness at the Hare and Hounds Inn, Haydock, was brought up on a charge of committing perjury in an affidavit sworn by him on the 24th May before a commissioner—Mr. Quelch, who prosecuted, stated that in June, 1875, the pri• ,oner entered into an agreement with Mrs. Mary Richards, ving in Bengel-street, to pay her Sc. a week for boarding ,z d lodging his illegitimate child. He continued the pay- ments until the 2nd January last. In April, Mrs. Richards not having received further payments in the meantime, ap- plicd to him for the sum of £l3 12s. then owing. As it was not paid, a writ was issued from the Court of Passage

for its recovery. The writ was served, and in due course application was made for judgment. On the 24th May the prisoner made an affidavit, in which he denied the debt, and stated that he had never paid the prosecutrix any money for the purpose mentioned. The prosecutrix had numerous letters enclosing post-office orders, and telegrams appointing interviews for payments.--Mr. Quelch asked for a remand for the production of the mother of the child.—Mr. Lowe, who appeared for the defence, opposed the application, re- marking that it was an attempt to coerce the prisoner to pay the money instead of allowing the action to take its course in the Court of Passage.—The Bench granted a re- mand until Tuesday. CAPTURE OF A GANG OF GAMBLERS AT HAYDOCK.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, eleven young men were summoned for playing at pitch and toss, at Hay- dock, on the 15th May. The names of the defendants were Edward Forrester, Thos. King, Edward Battersby, Bernard Williams, William Williams, John King, George Marshall, James Smith, John Boardman, John Smith, and Rd. Har- rison.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of the defendants, and pleaded guilty for Thomas King, Battersby, John Smith. and Harrison, and not guilty for the others.— P.C. Hodgkinson stated on Saturday afternoon, the 19th of May, he saw six of the defendatts tossing in Lime•street, Haydock. Those tossing were William Williams, Bernard Williams, Thomas King, John King, John Smith, and John Boardman. He saw them throw money up in the air several times, and the other defendants were there betting sums on the tossing.—ln reply to Mr. Moore, witness said he did not speak to the defendants, and was never nearer to them than 15 yarels.—For the defence Mr. Moore maintained that the summons was bad inasmuch as the defendants were sum- moned for playing at "pitch and toss" and the constable had sworn that they did not "pitch."—The Clerk stated that the defendants could be fined for tossing.—Mr. Moore then maintained that five of the defendants took no part in the tossing, and, therefore, they could not be fined. They had all been summoned for the commission of the same offence, and yet according to the evidence of the officer five of them were not playing at pitch and toss.—Battersby, William Williams, and John Smith were fined lOs and costs each, and the remainder were each fined 5s and costs. HUT TON.

FOWL-STEALING AT HUYTON : CHASE AND CAPTURE OF THE THIEVES.—On Saturday seven hens and a goose were stolen from Rigby's farm, Huyton. Soon after the robbery a carrier going from Prescot to Liverpool was accosted by a man carrying a bundle, who asked him to give him a lift in his cart as far as Liverpool. He complied, and no sooner had the man got into the cart than two other men came up carrying similar bundles, and preferred a like request. The good-natured carrier accommodated all three, but having suspicions of the character and pursuit of the men, quietly looked out for an opportunity of handing them over to the safer keeping of the pnlice. His first idea was to give them into custody at Horn Smithies, but tha situation of the police station there giving them too many chances of escape, especially as he knew the constable would be in bed at the time, he pursued his journey to Old Swan. Here he stopped at the police station, and gave information. Becoming aware of his design, the men bolted, and one or two con- stables followed in bet pursuit. The chase continued almost as far as Prescot, when eventually the men were captured and lodged in the lock-up at Prescot. They gave the names of John Martin, Samuel Edward Taylor, and Thomas Toiney. On Monday they were brought before Mr. W. L. Evans, and remanded for a week. The stolen fowls were found in their bundles.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

B IRGLARIES AT LEIGH.—On Tuesday, at Leigh, Samuel Seddon was brought up on a charge of committing a burglary at Tyldesley, on the 29th of November, 1865.10 n that night the shop and residence of James Owen, tailor, was robbed, and James Kirkman and a man named Winstanley were convicted, Seddon escaping. In the name of Samuel Moat he had since maintAined a good character, having for some years been a publican. Kirkman was now one of the wit- nesses called by the prosecution, and said he served nine months' imprisonment. Seddon entered the premises by the cellar grid, and bundles of clothes were being removed when the alarm was given, and they escaped. A pair of clogs left on the premises were spoken to by a witness as belonging to Seddon. The prisoner was committed for trial. —A man named Adam Turner, who has been several times convicted, was also brought up on a charge of burglary at Bedford, near Leigh. On the night of the 18th instant prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Wilkinson whilst com- mitting a burglary at the residence of Mr. Johnson Mills, High Bailiff of the Bolton County Court. He had ransacked the drawers in the dining-room and laid out silver plate and cutlery ready for removal. The policeman, who was on duty inthe neighbourhood, saw prisoner outside as if look- ing for a way of escape, andat once captured him. Entrance had been effected by breaking the breakfast-room window. This prisoner:was also committed for trial,

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Crank, landlord of the Swan public-house, Over, charged with selling drink during prohibited hours on Sundkay, the 13th ult., was fined and costs; and Elizabeth Capper, to whom the drink was sold, was ordered to pay a penally of £1 and costa.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

PRIMMVEArm, HIGH-STREET.—The anniversary sermons in connection with this chapel were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. J. Rock, of Keighley, York- shire. The trustees were desirous of reducing the debt on the chapel, which amounted to £5OO, and various members of the congregation having promised in subscriptions about £6O, they wished to raise the amount to £l.OO. The collec- tions on Sunday reached upwards of £lB. On Monday, a public tea meeting was held in the schoolroom, followed by a meeting, over which Mr. Lingard, of Alsager, presided. The proceeds were devoted to the above object.

div.head: INCREASED RAILWAY ASSESSMENT.
div.p: INCREASED RAILWAY ASSESSMENT.

The CLERK stated that the county rate committee had given hian notice that they would hear him at their meeting a fortnight that day.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW said it would not be out of place if be brought tinder the notice of the Board the subject of the re-valuation of the railways. Some eighteen months ago he pointed out the necessity of the railways in the union being re-assessed, havinc, found that in his own township, Whiston, in 1845, the London and North-Western Company were paying upon £2,100 per mile, while in 1880, with an increased traffic, they were only paying on £1,630. Since then the Assessment Committee had taken the matter up, and instead of confining them- selves to Whiston had had the whole of the railways in the Union re-valued. He had taken tha figures out, and the re- sults would be gratifying to all who were interested in pay- ing the rates of the U,nion. The figures were as follows : ' Old Valua- New Valua- tion. tion.
