Total For Rainhill alone there had been a reduction amounting to £284. The former rateable value of the London and North- Western lines was £49.597, and now they were assessed by Mr. Marshall at £105,644. At the last meeting of the Assess- ment Committee Mr. Edwards attended on bAalf of the company and agreed to pay on an assessment of £84,515, but the Committee thought they should stand out for the whole £105,644. The Cheshire Lines Committee and the Midland Company had agreed to the increased assessment on their lines in the townships of Bold, Ditton, Halewood, Spoke, 'rarbuck, Widnes, and Little and Much Wooltou.—The Rev. J. BARNACLE said they were very much indebted to Mr. Leatherbarrow for bringing the matter before them.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Leather- barrow for his iaformation, which was very instructive.— The Rev. J. BARNACLE seconded the motion, which was agreed to.

div.head: ST. HELENS MAGISTRATES AND MACHSTRATES.
div.p: ST. HELENS MAGISTRATES AND MACHSTRATES.

The Clerk reported that since last ine,ting the foster parent Anders had been taken before the magistrates and a flee had been inflicted of £2 and costs.—The Rev. T. CRAMBERS remarked that in the newspapers the magistrates were made to say they were sorry the case had come before them That was capable of being interpreted in two wars; He hoped they did not mean that they were sorry the foster parents were prosecuted. He presumed they were sorry there was any necessity for such a case coming before them. —The CHAIRMLN said he had heard from a gentleman who had great exrprience in criminal law that it was a great pity the magistrates let the foster parents off with a fine ; thcy should have sent them to prison. That was his opinion too, and if the case had come before some of the St. Heiens magistrates they would have been sent to prison, but there were magistrates and magistrates in St. Helens.
THE FEVER HOSPITAL,

On the recommendation of the House Committee it was resolved that the chairman of that committee (Mr. Hall), Br. Summers, archi•ect, and the Clerk wait upon the Local Government Board with their plans and proposals for ex- tending the hospital, as it was a matter of urgency. As an instance of the difficulty the Board were in a case was men- tioned where a girl in Widnes bad been attacked by typhus fev, r. The people with whom sht lodged threatened to put her and her father into the stret. She could not he ad• mitted into the workhouse hospital bet:ause it was full, and there was no hospital accommodation in Whines. The House Commit tee. had therefore recommended Widnes Local Board to take an empty house and. the relieving efficer would provide requisites for the girl,--This WaS all the business.

BURGLARY AT WHISTON WORK- HOUSE. On Saturday night the Prescot Union Workhouse, Whiston, was broken into and a large quantity of bread and a few trifling articles were stolen therefrom. The thief was captured on the following day, and proved to be one James Richardson, who seems to have embraced nocturnal depredations in workhouses as one of his objects in life. Both he and his propensity were well known at the house, and therefore as soon as the robbery was discovered suspicion fell upon him, and his known habits facilitatad his capture. About two years ago, after enjoying the hospitality of the same institution for some time and relieving its monotony by a short interval of freedom, he testified his gratitude to his parochial benefactors by returning to it surreptitiously and relieving it of some provisions, which he was afterwards discovered quietly cooking by means of a fire which he had lighted in the middle of a field no great distance from the workhouse. For this escapade he was imprisoned for six months. After his relief from gaol he had a chequered existence cheering himself in cold weather by different workhouse fires, and in the summer time enjoy- ing rural delights in the manner peculiar to Bohemians and gipsies. His last authenticated exploit was a burglarious enterprise at Warrington Workhouse but led to his again enduring six months of prison discipline. This was only , recently, and since then he has kept up his acquaintance ' with Whiston Workhouse by seeking its shelter at intervals,; and, as it would seem, has improved the time thus spent by making himself familiar with its details and the nature of its defences from attacks from without. The weak point of these defences appears to have been the boiler house, and; the custodians of the institution knowing this, had made 1 some special provision in the shape of bolts and bars to strengthen it. However, on Saturday night the guardian of ; the boiler house neglected to put these appliances to their proper use, and thus no impediment being offered to his in- gress, the wily Richardson, in the watches of the night, stole i quietly in. It might have been expected that being thus so much indebted for the success of his enterprise to the care- lessness of the boiler house keeper he would have been im- pelled by feelings of gratitude to spare the property of that functionary, but so far wasi this from being the case that he callously I appropriated it, pocketing a razor, a knife, some forks, and a small supply of tea, sugar, and tobacco, which his friend kept in the boiler house for his use and solace. From this place Richardson had no difficulty in making his way to the bakery, the door of which was secured by a spring lock. It is not clear whether he opened the door with a key or a , vigorous kick, but at all events he did open it, and after half filling a sack with upwards of a hundred small loaves, weighing between 40 and 50 pounds, he quietly closed it behind him and departed as he had come. His freedom was of short duration. When the effects of his visit were dis- covered on Sunday morning, information was immediately given to the police, and a diligent search was made for him. In the course of the day, he was caught under much the same circumstances as those alluded to in reference to his first escapade at Whiston. Among the places searched by the police was a small plantation, in a secluded spot called Duke's Clough. between Rainhill and Cronton, and here he was found comfortably seated at the bottom of an old sand pit, making tea in an old tin can with a fire of sticks, and half-a-dozen loaves by his side, the sack containing the bulk of the stolen bread, serving him as a comfortable support to recline against in an easy attitude. He was removed to Prescot and locked up, and on the following day was brought before Mr. Evans, and after some formal evidence had been given remanded till Tuesday next.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY COURTING ADVENTURE AT BURTONWOOD. HORSEWHIPPING A LOVER.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY COURTING ADVEN- TURE AT BURTONWOOD. HORSEWHIPPING A LOVER.

It has been found in the experience of many that "the course of true love never did run smooth," and a recent occurrence at Burtonwood forcibly reminds one that the time-honoured adage remains as true to-day as ever it did. The event has given rise to an endless amount of gossip and amusement throughout the township, and the principal parties in the transaction, in the exercise of that discretion which is said to be the better part of valour, have found it advisable to make themselves "scarce." It seems that a well-known gentleman, who has far exceeded the three score and ten years allotted to man, has for many years past been the occupant of a farm in a somewhat lovely part of Old Hall-lane, and not far from the celebrated "Fiddle" at Burtonwood. In his service he has had a bouncing damsel of about 20 summers, whose personal charms and attractions appear to have captured the eyes and heart of a " brave " ex-soldier residing in Earlestown. Beyond the old gentle- man and the "fair Juliet "alluded to, the only other occu- pant of the building was supposed to be a man-servant who has attained if not exceeded the period of life known as middle age. But for some considerable time past, a son of the farmer, who occupies the position of a licensed victualler in the same township,has had some suspicion that there were other " visitors" to the house, for whom he did not entertain a particuiar friendliness. On Sunday morning last he was apprised that some other than his father's "household" was to be found inside the building, and he accordingly proceeded thither, arming himself beforehand with a formidable horsewhip. As he entered the house he fonnd everything as usual and his father sitting in the kitchen unconcerned, and unsuspecting that anything was wrong. The table was set for dinner, and that meal was almost ready, but before partaking thereof the son walked upstairs and entered the servant's bedroom. He was considerably surprised when he saw that a "stranger" —the ex-soldier from Earlestown—was fast in the arms of Morpheus with the bedclothes tacked comfortably about him. The latter subsequently turned himself over in a lazy and sleepy fashion, and the "intruder" asked what he was doing there. The voice was not quite as sweet and charm- ing as one he delighted to listen to, and evidently becoming alarmed at the seriousness of the position affairs had taken, the stranger answered "I have not been here long." Reply- ing that he had been there rather too long, the son quietly drew down the bed-sheets and soundly administered to the , ex-soldier a few strokes with the whip.. I He then seized the wearing apparel of the stranger, and marching out of the room with them proceeded to lock them up in the parlour. On returning to the bedroom he asked the 'ex-soldier if he was not going to decamp, and the latter replied that he would, but not without his clothes. He was told, however, that he would have to go without them, and this, coupled with another " dose " of the horse- whip, made him quickly alter his intentions. As he left the house he was attired in nature's own garment, his only covering being one article of underclothing. The "whip" followed him some distance, and the thoroughly novel and unexpected performance created the liveliest interest and amusement to a number of young men who were spectators of the scene. The ejected one pro- ceeded along the fields for some distance escaping the high- way as much as possible, and kept in hiding until someone took pity upon him and he was provided with sufficient clothing to walk home. The young woman who had been the means of bringing the unpleasant predicament upon her unfortunate young man was also turned away from the farm, and has been compelled to seek a livelihood in" fresh fields and pastures new."

div.head: SAD BATHING FATALITY AT NEWTON. INQUES T.
div.p: THE SAD BATHING FATALITY AT NEWTON. INQUES T.

The circumstances attending the death of Henry Platt 15 years of age, son of William Platt, residing at 5., Shef field-row, Vulcan' who was drowned in the bathing pond attached to the Liverpool Reformatory Farm School at Newton, as stated in our last issue, were inquired into on Firday last, by the district coroner, Mr. T. W. Barker, at the Wargrave Inn, Vulcan. Mr. Atty, the governor of the Reformatory School, was in attendance.—The follow- ing evidence was given :—Ann Platt, wife of Wm. Platt, 5, Sheffield-row, Vulcan, deposed that the deceased was her son. He was 15 years of age. He came home from work about 5-30 the previous Wednesday evening, and after having had tea washed himself and went out. lie did net say where he was going. It was about half-past seven when she first heard anything about the occurrence, and the body was brought home the same evening. He was subject to the cramp.—Joseph Hammett, a lad, employed at the Via- duct works, said he was bathing at the pond near the Liver- pool Farm Reformatory School, when the deceased came with two other lads to bathe. Witness had only been once to the pond before, but could swim very well. When the deceased came he undressed and went into the water. He coud swim a little bit, and swam across at the " three foot" end of the bath. He got out and walked to the six-foot end, where he again jumped into the water and aware across. Witness followed him and asked if he could manage across, but the deceased did not reply. Deceased then got out and sat on the bank near the six-foot end,and witness went to the three-foot end. Another lad shouted to him soon after "What's to do with Henry ?" and some one said " He's trying to bottom' it across," but he was seen to be struggling in the water, and another lad called out " He's drowning." Witness there- upon entered the water and tried to catch him, but the body slipped from, his grasp. Another lad named, Mavnes tried to push the deceased to the side, but could not do so. A few minutes afterwards one of the Reformatory lads came and the body was brought to the side. He (witness) thought the deceased had been seized with cramp.—John Chipman, an- ther lad,mnployed at the Vulcan,gave corroborative evidence. In reply/ to the foreman, witness said the deceased did not call out for help.—Joseph Jones, one of the lads at the Re- formatory school said some one came to the school to tell them that a boy was drowning. He (witness) at once dived into the water and to2ched the arm of the deceased. On goieg into the water a second time he succeeded in bringing the body to the sueface. The lad was quite deatl.—ahe C:,,roner said he thought it was perfectly clear that clath was the result of an accident and nothing else. The poor boy had no doutsbt been seized with cramp, and sank before he could be resceled.—The jury then returned a verdict to the effect that the deceaml was accidentally drowned.

WARRTNGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.

GOSPEL TEMPERANCE ADDRESS. ! The popular temperance advocate, the Rev. John Bennett Anderson, of Byrom Hall, Liverpool, delivered a gospel temperance address to a crowded audience In the Workmen's Club, Market-place, Warrington, on Wednesday evening. The Rev. W. Mules presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mrs. Youmans (e-e -president of the Canadian Women's Christian Temperance Association), Mae, Parker, Mies Clarke, the Revs. J. B. Anderson, T. Rippor, and E. Moore. The Blue Ribbon Army choir, under the leadership of the Rev. E. Moore, was present, and sang several tem- perance selections during the evening.—The Rev. Cmitn- max, in hie opening remarks, said that the great object of the later temperance organisations Wi.3 not so much to strengthen the power of resistance in men's souls as to re- move the temptation from them. And this they had tried' to do in various ways, but more notably by leaislation ; and all honour to the men who had devoted their best en- ergies to the accomplishment of this object; all honour, he would say, to Sir Wilfrid Lawson, who had stood so nobly by Local Option. (Applause.) If this object could be ac- complished; if every public-house in the land were to be closed for ever, they would have achieved a great victory; but a still greater victory was achieved when they were successful in winning men to Christ and bringing them to that fountain which would en- able them to resist every temptation that satan mfght bring against them. (Applause.)—The rev. LECTURER, whose subject was " Oh, sir, the drink did it," created frequent roars of laughter by the numerous humorous allusions with which the lecture was interspersed: He related as the foundation for his remarks two thrilling stories of the fatal results of drinking. One was a case which came under the notice of Canon Ellison, and in which a man cut the throat of his own child, and when visited in the prison by Canon Ellison he said it was the drink that did it. It was this touching incident which led the Canon to throw himself heart and soul into the temper- ance work. The other was a case which came under the notice of John B. Gough while visiting a prison in New Hampshire, where a man was incarcerated for life for hav- ing shot dead his own wife. The man was the victim of drink, and had seen his wife's cheeks gradually grow paler and paler through grief at his drunken conduct; but he could not give it up, the result being that one night when he returned home and entered unnoticed,by his wife he saw her image in the glass, her cheeks wetted with tears, and in a moment of remorse he got a gun and shot her dead. " Oh, sir, it was the drink that did it," was the man's answer to Mr. Gough's question. These were true instances. He believed that according to the late Dr. Lancaster's calculation, about 120,000 die annually in Britain through this accursed drink; but thank God there was a stem in the tide, the tide was turning the revenue, and there were not so many deaths through drink as there were formerly. The lecturer related a number of interesting anecdotes, and concluded by urging upon his hearers to exert their energies towards the closing of breweries, and to the attainment of Local Option.—Mrs. YOUMANS then addressed the meeting, and in the course of her remarks said she loved the good, warm-hearted people of the United States, but she was a Briton. They were just enthusiastic enough—fanatical enough if they pleased—to believe that soon the last liquor shop would be closed and the last wife weep for the drunkenness of her husband. They believed that the liquor traffic was going down, and their belief was founded on the Bible. The Saviour came into the world to destroy the work of the devil, and every work that He came to do would be accomplished.— Mrs. PARKER proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer and to Mrs. Youmans; and the Rev. T. RIPPON, in seconding the proposition, said he hoped the electors of Warrington as well as the electors of any other borough or county would have nothing to do with those who courted the publicans' favour. They must fight the battle of temperance both on the plat- form and at the dinner table. As he saw the picture of that grand old man (Mr. Gladstone) on the wall it reminded him that they should see to it that our laws were such as would make it easy to do right and difficult to do wrong, and, as he saw the portrait of Lord Beaconsfield, he was also reminded that if they made temperance their "scientific frontier" they would have "peace with honour." (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Anderson then sang "The bit of blue," the audience joining in the chorus, and the meeting shortly afterwards separated.
CRUELTY TO A PAUPER CHILD AT
ST. HELENS.

On Friday last a case in which the Prescot Board of Guardians were prosecutors, was dealt with by the St. Helens magistrates. The defendant was Ellen Anders, a confectioner, living in Shaw-street, St. Helens, and she was charged with having violently assaulted and beaten Mary Jane Anders, a little pauper child, aged 10 years, who had been placed in the custody of the defendant by the Guardians.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended.—Mr. Swift in his opening state- ment said the girl Anders was a pauper child under tee care of the Guardians. In the year 1879, the Guardians entrusted her to the defendant's husband, Mr. John Shaw, and agreed to pay him 3s. per week on the understanding that he was to bring her up as if she were his own child, he being in fact her foster father. The girl seemed to have practically taken the place of a servant in defendant's house, and seems to have done almost all the work that was done in the house before breakfast time at least. On the morning of the 11th ult. she got up at her usual time, half-past five, got the lodgers their breakfast, lit the fires downstairs, and then went upstairs and scrubbed two rooms. Mrs. Anders afterwards called her downstairs and told her to strip and wash herself. She did so, but whilst she was washing Mrs. Anders began to thrash her with the buckle end of a strap, and continued to belabour her all the time she was washing, and even after the child had put her frock an, Mrs. Anders beat her and then sent her to school without any breakfast. As soon as she got to school the schoolmistress saw something was the matter, and afterwards examined her and found that her back right down from the shoulder was literally covered with marks, some of which seemed to have been newly Inflicted, and the others looked as if they had been caused some time previously. Her ear was also marked, and her elbow was bleeding owing to some skin having been knocked off. He (Mr. Swift) did not know what the defence would be, but it seemed to him that a most aggravated assault had been committed.—Mr. Riley said his client pleaded guilty to having committed an assault but not an aggravated assault.—Mr. Swift said then the only question which the Bench had to decide seemed to be whether the assault had been an aggravated one or not. He would call evidence which he thought would show that a most brutal assault had been committed, for which he thought a pecuniary penalty would not be sufficient, and he therefore asked the bench to send defendant to gaol.—The girl Mary Jane Anders was then called, and corroborated the statement of Mr. Swift, but on cross- examination she admitted having given Mrs. Anders pro- vocation on some occasions, and on a strap being produced to which there was no buckle attached, said that was the one she had been chastised with.—M. A. Baddelv, head- mistress at Cowley Schools, College-street, spoke to having had her attention called to the child on the morning of the 11th ult, and on examining her body, in compiny with Miss Langsdale, the infant school-mistress, finding the marks referred to by Mr. Swift. In consequence of what seemed to have been most cruel treat- ment. She took the child to Superintendent Johnston, and then to Mr. Stuart, relieving officer, and afterwards to the Workhouse at VlThiston where the child had remained since. The child, she said, had not only evidently been very cruelly used, but was also insufficiently clad.—Miss Lange- dale corroborated, and also said that she had on two previ- ous occasions, of which she was sure, and she believed on another, spoken to Mrs. Anders about the cruel treatment to which the child seemed to be subjected, and the defen- dant then promised not to beat her any more when she was in a temper.—Dr. Packer, Huyton, said he had examined the child's body, and found marks which seemed to have been caused by very severe beatings. He thought, however, that the marks might have been caused by a leather strap without a buckle attached.—ln defence. two witnesses were called, one Mary Murray, who had up till recently been a servant with Mrs. Anders, and the other Mary Fair, a charwoman who was often engaged by defen- dant, both of whom said the child Anders, from what they saw of her, seemed to be very stupid, and also inclined to be dishonest. Mr. Riley also said that on the morning in question defendant, who had a very hasty temper, had been angered by the child refusing to wash herself for school.— The Bench decided to impose a penalty. of ,L 2 and 12s e&l costs on the defendant.

A HUYTON HEROINE: PLUCKY ARREST OF A THIEF. An incident occurred at the Blue Bell Inn, Huyton, on Monday, in which a young lady, daughter of Mr-. Thomas Brown, the landlord, manifested no little bravery and reso- lution: About three o'clock in the afternoona,rough-looking man went to the bar of the inn.and asked for a glass of ale. The liquor was headed to him by Margaret Brawn, a younger daughter of the lanilord, who shortly afterwards, hearing, her sister call, left the bar. Asshe was going up- stairs she heard a noise, and on looking round saw the man with his head hanging over the counter and his hand in the till. She at once told her sister what was going on, and the latter. hurried downstaire,just in time to see the man making off. She followed him, and without a moment's hesitation seivd him with one halid by tho collar and with her other hand gripped his wrist, giving it so loving a squeeze that ha was obliged to partially opon his hand and disclose some money, which, after having taken it from the till, he ap- ,parently had not had time to transfer to. his pockets. Half l'cholted by Miss 3rown's grip of his neck he struggled to ; release himself, and pleaded hard to be allowed to restore . the money and go away, but Missitrown declined to let him off so easily, and kept her hold until her sister brought Mr. Crosby, wheelwright, to her assistance. Mr. Crosby took the money fr.em the man and secured him until a policeman. arrived and took him into custody. On Tuesday, the prisoner, who gave, the name of John Johnson, and several other names busides, WAS brought before Messrs. W. Pilkingten, E. Gibbon and T. Pilkington, and remanded for a week, Supt. Barkw statiug that he was a stranger whose antecedents he should like to investigate.

div.head: RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company Vas held at the Gas Works, yesterday.—Mr. W. EIEYES, otaairman of the directors, presided, and moved the adoption of the report, which declared the usual dividend of 10 par oent.—Mr, F. RIGBY seconded the motion, which was unani- acously carried.-1 vote of thanks was passed to the chairman V directors and to the manager (Mr. J. R. Frith).—The OIiAIRIUN, in a graceful tribute to the ability of Mr. Frith, declared tho works one of the best managed in the country. Mr. FEED. RIGBY instituted a comparison between Runcorn works and various others in the country, and expressed the opinion that the company's works occupied the favourable position they did owing to the efficient way in which they were managed by Mr. Frith.

div.head: BOY DROWNED AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BOY DROWNED AT RUNCORN.

A boy, named Thomas Robert Pickstock, son of J. B. l'lckstock, shipwright, living in Mill-street, Runcorn, was drowned in the Weston Canal about half-past four yesterday afternoon. It appeared that the boy, who is 15 years of age, was left in charge of the canal boat 'The Two Brothers," whilst the boatman went to Messrs. Sampson and Davis's office to draw his freight. He was also to return with a horse to draw the boat. Pickstock, however, com- menced to push the boat along by means of a boathook, which, It is surmised, slipped and precipitated him into the water. A man on the opposite side of the canal saw the boy struggling in the water, but was unable to render him any assistance, and he perished before aid arrived. The body was recovered about an hour afterwards by the father, who brought it to the surface by means of a grapnel.

div.head: RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI CO.
div.p: RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI CO.
EX CRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A CAPTAIN.

At Runcorn Police Court, oa Thursday, when the pre- siding magistrate was Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, a sea captain, named William Williams, was brought up, ic custody, charged with stealing a piece of paper, to wit, an authority in writing, of the value of id, the property of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company.—From the statement of Mr. Wigg, it appeared that the ship Barbara, on the 28th May, arrived in Runcorn Docks with a cargo for the Alkali Company, which had to be deliverod free into the com- pany's fiats. The Bridgewater Navigation Company, how- ever, claimed 6d. per ton for dockage and 6d. per ton for discharging ths cargo; and Mr. Wigg telegraphed to the shippers telling them that they must make arrangements to paw these charges before the Alkali Company could receive the cargo. Eventually, to avoid farther delay, the captain (the prisoner) agreed to ply them, and he signed a letter to that effect. That (Thursday) morning he went to the office, accompanied by a shipbroker's clerk, and asked Mr. Wigg to show the latter the letter be had signed. Mr. Wigg consented, and while he was doing so the prisoner rushed forward and seized the letter, which he tore to pieces. In the meantime the firm had acted upon the letter by re- ceiving the cargo. The prisoner was subsequently gives into the custody of a policeman.—Mr. Lake, who appeared for the prisoner, suggested that an apology would amply meet the case ; but Mr. Wigg said he regarded the case as of greater seriousness than a petty larceny.—After some -consideration, the Bench remanded the prisoner until Monday. He was, however, admitted to bail, himself in £2O and two sureties of £lO each.

div.head: BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.
div.p: BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.
MEETING AT WIDNES.

The annual meeting of the Widnes Auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in Lacey-street school-room, on Monday evening. Nine persons composed the aulience, and on the platform were the Revs. R. Harper, who occupied the chair, J. Tesseyman, and D. Ellison (of Manchester, the deputation). Devotional exercises having been engaged in, the Chairman delivered a brief address, observing upon the great work which the society had tic- ooinplished„with which all must be in sympathy. The Bev. Tesseyman gave a few financial facts. The total income of the Widnes branch last year was £l3 12s 2d, and so far as he could see a similar amount would be realised in the present year. Already he had received the foiling sums : Collected by Mrs. Carey .C 4 5s 11d, by Mrs. Robinson £2 is, by Mrs. Tesseyman £1 15s; by sale of scriptures £1 6s 2d, making a total for the present year of £9 8s Id. The annual contribution to the parent society was £lO. Mr. Tesseyman remarked that he was very sorry that the audience was so small, and that so few gentlemen occupied seats on the platform. He had received letters of apology for non- attendance from several gentlemen who expected to be present, viz, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes; Rev.4G. Bond, vicar of Farnworth ; and the Rev. W. H. Duggan. The Rev. D. Ellison was then called upon to give an address. He narrated the simple and affecting incident which was the origin of the Bible Society, and stated a few facts regarding its work. Since it was founded the society had issued a hundred millions of Bibles in about 250 languages or dialects of the world, but these had only sup- plied a small proportion of the vast population of the globe, and there was yet an enormous work to be done. At present in each working day of the year the society issued 5,000 copies of the Bible from its depot in London. Mr. Ellison described the work of the colperteurs of the society, and stated the interesting fact that on Satur- day evenings men went round to publichonses selling the scriptures, and saying a few kind words to the people they found there. ins achievements of the society in foreign countries were narrated at length, and its unsee- tarian character touched upon, Mr. Ellison urging that it should have the hearty support of all those who professed and were called christian. Every man and woman ought to try to ennead the work in every possible way. The Rev. J. Holden proposed a vote of thanks to the deputation for his interesting address. Mr. E. Carey seconded the motion All who had heard Mr. Ellieon's extremely interesting ad- dress would feel as he did very grateful to him for telling them 80 much about a society in which he was sure they all had the deepest interest, though from the smallness of the attendance, perhaps, they in Widnes had not shown it on this occasion. He suggested that in future the meeting should be held in winter, observing that it was not that the public of Widnes were not interested in the Bible that they had not attended the meeting that night,but from some cause which he could not explain. The motion was carried by acclimation, and the meeting separated after singing the Doxology.

div.head: S. JOHN EVANGELIST'S CHURCH, WALTON. ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION.
div.p: S. JOHN EVANGELIST'S CHURCH, WALTON. ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION.

• As this edifice, which owes its existence to the liberality of Sir Gilbert Greenall, is now approaching completion, a description of the building may be read with interest. The architects are Messrs. Paley and Austin, of Lancaster, and they have favoured us with the following details :—The church is cruciform on plan, the four large arches at the crossing supporting a tower 24 feet square outside and 78 feet high to top of parapet. The spire rises 51 feet from top of parapet to the top of vane. The nave, including the tower, is 78 feet long and 21 feet 6 inches wide, and the chancel 37 feet long and 20 wide. The extreme width across transepts is 52 feet. There are also chancel aisles 15 feet long opening by arches into transepts and chancel, that on the south side being arranged as an organ chamber; further eastwards on the south side are the choir and clergy vestries. The entrance is on the south side through a porch of oak, the gable of which is richly carved. The front. which is of Devonshire marble, is placed at the west end of the nave, on a limestone step, and the pulpit, which is of oak, against the north-east crossing pier. The roofs throughout are of oak, the nave and chancel having a "wagon" shaped ceiling, the height from floor to top being, 20 feet. The tower is groined in stone. The floors and pas- sages are laid with ornamental tiles, and polished limestone strips. The stone used for the dressings and walling, and inside face of walls, which is of chiselled ashlar, is the flecked Runcorn. The whole of the wood work of seats and , fittings is of Dantzic oak. The architectural style of the church is decorated, the windows being richly traceried. Most of the windows are filled with painted glass by Messrs. Shriglev and Hunt, of Lancaster and London. The reredos is of oak, the heads of the panels, the cornices, and canopies being richly carved. The sculpture of the panels was ex- ecuted by Mr. Roddis, of Birmingham. The heating is effected by hot water, Mr. Seward, of Lancaster, being the engineer. Mr. R. Fairhurst, of Higher Whitley, Northwich, is the sole contractor. Mr. Perkins is acting as clerk of works.

Messrs. Shrigley and Hunt, of Lancaster and London, have kindly supplied the following additional particulars respecting the subjects treated in the windows of the church :—The subject treated in the lower lights of the east window is the hymn after the Last Supper, with refe- rence to the text "When they had sung an hymn," &e.; the subject extends throughout the five lights, whilst above the transom the heavenly choir join the concert. The prin- cipal pieces of tracery contain figures of angels bearing shields on which are inscribed the sacred monograms. The window has little colour, the effect being of varied silvery whites and golden stains. The treatment of the west win- dow is illustrative of the subject of holy baptism. In the two lower openings of dexter lights is our Lord blessing little children, with the text "Suffer little children to come unto me," citc. In the small centre compartment of base is the representation of a baptism in a church; in the upper openings, above transom, the newly baptised child is re- ceived in charge by the angels—one holds the child in his arms whilst another records its name as being "received into the congregation of Christ's flock." The armed angel bears the banner charged with the red cross, in reference to the words "He shall manfully fight under his banner against sin, the world, and the devil, and continue Christ's faithful soldier and servant unto his life's end." Other

angels and the Holy Innocents rejoice in chorus over the child's redemption. The two lower openings of sinister lights contain the Baptism of our Lord, the text below "Thou didst sanctify water to the mysticil washing away of sin." Above the transom four kneeling angels pour out the four streams of Paradise—Pison, Gihon, Hiddekel, and Euphrates, symbolical of the four streams of the Gospels. Behind the angels are Noah, Moses, Naaman, and Jonah, who hold scrolls on which are texts in reference to their deliver- ance by water, as follows—Noah "The ark wherein few that is eight souls were saved by water;" Moses " The waters , were a wall unto them on their right hand and on their left, thus the Lord saved Israel that day •, " Naaman "Wash me thoroughly from mine iniquity and cleanse me from my sin;" Jonah "The waters compassed me alaout, even to the soul, the depth closed me round about." The small subject in the sinister base is the presentation of our Lard in the Temple. On the scrolls of the small votive figures are written the texts "Open the door to us that knock," "Let us that seek, find," "Give unto us that ask." In the traceries are seven doves, bearing scrolls upon which are written the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit:— Wisdom, strength, understanding, counsel, knowledge, holy fear, true godliness. The westermost window on the north side of the nave is reserved to commemorate the dedication. The central compartment of the tracery con- tains the arms and crest of Sir Gilbert Greenall (Or, on a bend nebuly plain cotised vert three buglehorns , stringed of the first. Crest. Betw. two wings or, a pomme surmounted by a bnglehorn, as in the arms. Motto, "Alta peto"). In the floral ornament of side panels of tracery are entwined scrolls with the motto "Alta pato." The quarries in lower part of window bear, on a small scroll, the motto as above' and the monograms G. G. end 5. G., the initials of Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall. On a band through the three lights is the dedicatory in- scription "To the glory of God and in honour of St. John the Evangelist, this church was erected and endowed by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Baronet, A.D. MDCCCLXXXII." The tracery of the remaining windows of the nave have foliated ornament, in which colour is introduced, the quarries below being painted with conventional patterns. In the heads of the three lights of window on the south side of the south transept, on ruby shields surmounted of crowns, are several sacredmonograms, includingLll.S. The rose foliage surround- ing these shields flow through the tracery. In the quarries below are the Evangelistic and Apostolic symbols of St. John the Divine, the eagle and the dragon rising from the poisoned cup. The window facing this in the north transept is similar in design. In the tracery and beads of lights of window on the west side of the south transept. within wreaths surrounded by foliage, are shields with the symbols of the three Christian graces. On scrolls twined round the wreaths are the texts, "The just live by faith" (emblem, the cross), "We are saved by hope" (emblem, the anchor), "Charity never faileth " (emblem, the heart.) The .window on the east side of north transept is somewhat simi- lar to the one last described, the symbols within the wreaths being those of the persons of the Sacred Trinity. In the centre is the emblem of the Father (the hand reaching from the clouds to help and bless us), on the right the Son is symbolised by the lamb, and on the left is the sacred dove (emblem of the Holy Ghost). The quarries are filled by emblems of the Sacred Trinity, the three fishes in form of a triangle, and the orb enclosed within a trefoil. In the chapel on the east side of north transept the window heads are filled by the emblems of the four Evangelists (the angel, St. Matthew; the lion, St. Mark; the bull, St. Luke; the eagle St. John). The quarries of these windows contain the monograms S.M., S.L., and S.J. In all the above-described , windows colour is introduced in the heads of lights and tra- ceries only. A brilliant silvery effect is maintained, and the light is not obstructed. On the north side of the chan- cel are two two-light windows, in one of which, within a border of scrolls, is a lily plant painted on white quarries. In the upper part of the lights are kneeling angels, who I look up to the Sacred Lamb in tracery above, and bear scrolls with the texts, "Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing." In the ' corresponding window the design varies. The border contains the eagle of St. John, and his name is written on the border scrolls. The foliage is that of the rose. In the tracery is the pelican in her piety, type of Divine love, and the angels below bear the text, "Unto Him that loved us and washed 119 from our , sins in His blood, to Him be glory and dominion fur ever ' and ever. Amen."

div.head: MR. ALDERMAN DA.VIES AND THE
div.p: MR. ALDERMAN DA.VIES AND THE
SHIP CANAL.

Mr. Alderman Davies, of this town, was on Thursday examined before the Parliamentary Committee now inquiring into the merits of the Manchester Ship Canal schetne. On Mr. Alderman Davies being called, Mr. Aspinall asked that the Warrington clauses which had been granted by the pro- moters should be put in.—Mr. Crips said they had twice telegraphed for them that day, but had not vet received them. They would be forthcoming on Friday.—The wit- ness said he could tell the committee what they were. At present they had a free navigation to Bank Qntay, which was the west end of Warrington. At high spring tides barges of 150 tons could sail no to that point—that meent about four-fifths of the year. The quesdon for the Cor- poration was as to how far the ship canal people were pre- pared to allow those vessels to be brought during the neap tides. It had been settled that barges should go to any part of Warrington for 4d a ton all the year round, which was a compromise between 6d at neap tides at the preeent time and free at spring tides. The second matter was :is to the discharge of the sewage. They required the canal company, at their own expense, to extend the sewers to a point half a mile below the present outlet. The third matter related to the swing b idges. The canal would cross two main roads on the southere side of Warrington, and the company would be required to pltice there swing bridges of such a height as to allow bargee of 150 tons or even larger to pass under. The bridges were not to remain open for more than 10 minutes at A time. There was a level crossing too at Warrington of the London and North-Western Railway, and the Canal Company would be required to build a bridge there. Finally, altheuch this was not a matter in whioh the Corporation were imelediately con- cerned, the Canal Company ban agreed to furnish the traders of Warrington with 7,000,000 gallons daily of water suitable for manufacturing put poses in lieu of what might be abstracted from the Mersey. Tne canal would be a great benefit to Warrington, and in addition to other advantages ' would do much to prevent the floods which were often very disastrous. The people of Warrington had subscribed Bor 9 per cent, of the perliemLntery fund, and he thought they would subscribe to the company. The committee subee- quently adjourned for the day.

Yestorday (Friday), the worthy Alderman, in reply to Mr. J. B. Aspiaatt, Q. who apvared for the Corporation of Liverpool, stated that if the Committee pas•-eit the scheme feasihle,Warrington n2ople would solectiln toe.a7ds the necessary capital. He himself had not taken any tree;sh but he had not been asked. He was not waiting until be was satisfied that the scheme was likely to bf.l a paying concern.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 2,188
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 2,188
THE WARRINGTON GAS WORKS.
THE WORKING OF THE UNDERTAKING.

The Gas Committee of the Corporation have had a report on the working of the gas undertaking since the works were acquired by the Corporation in 1677, printed and sub- mitted to the Council, and, as we believe it will be of considerable interest locally, we give the report as follows : Your committee have thought it desirable that in addi- tion to the information contained in the balance sheet and other accounts connected with the gas department, a brief resume of the operations since the works became the pos- session of the Corporation should be laid before the Coun- cil. It will be unnecessary to advert to the terms and agreements involved in the parzbase, which are set forth in a joint bill promoted in Parliament for this and other matters connected with the Town Council, and which re- ceived the Royal assent on the 11th June, 1877, when the works became legally vested in the Corporation. The first members of the committee were—S. M. WEBSTER (mayor), Aldermen llEPairenD (chairman), HoratEs, Davxs, PICKMERE, Councillors FELL, MONKS, WILLIAMS, FAIRCLOUGR, and ARMITAGE. At the period of the transfer' the producing powers of the works left a considerable margin for an increase in consumption, which has since proved to be 25 millions of cubic feet. But at that time a general depression of trade was felt all over the kingdom, and as in other towns, the consumption of gas in Warrington fell below its normal increase, as will be seen by the accompanying diagram. Other causes also operated at the same time in producing the4aame result. It is probably unnecessary to say that the prosperity and suc- cess of any gas-making establishment depend on its keeping well abreast with the requirements of consumers. Hence, the continued increase in the demand, and in several instances in remote parts of the borough the imperfect supply, induced the committee in 1879 to take into con- sideration the best means to be adopted for further increase in the generating and distributing plant. The whole of the available spaca on the works in Mersey-street having been utilised, the question resolved itself into the selection of the best position for the erection of a new station. Ultimately it was found that the most available position was at Longford, and measures were taken for the purchase of sixteen, acres of land in that locality, parallel with the line of the London and North- Western Railway Company, for Corporation purposes. The necessary plans and specifications for the new works were so far completed that tenders for the greater part were taken in March, 1880, of which the following is a brief outline. We may note here, that they are connected with the Lon- don and North-Western Railway system by a high and low level railway, for the bringing in and removal of all materials, and the whole have been erectei from the designs and under the superintendence of Mr. Paterson, the general manager of the works.

div.head: BUILDINGS.
div.p: BUILDINGS.

Retort Rouse. This house is 148 feet long and 60 feet in width, having a working space of 21 feet on each side of the retort-bench, with a view to the introduction of stoking machines, should it be found desirable in the future to adopt them. It contains 12 benches of retorts 18 feet long, seven in each bench, or 168 mouthpieces, capable of manufacturing about 680,000 cubic feet per day. The house contains two chim- neys, octagon shape, 70 feet in height from the floor line. On each side of the house are Coal and cannel stores, each 24 feet wide and 148 feet long. The coal wagons are brought by the railway siding into these stores 14 feet over- head, by the high level railway, and discharged into the space below. Four arched openings on each side communi- cate with the retort-house, and are furnished with weighing machines for the coal barrows. The coke store is also 148 feet long and 36 feet in width, having a low level railway running lengthwise through the shed for the removal of coke, arc. 'This is paved with Yorkshire sets, as are also the coal stores. The retort-house is laid with strong flags. The roofs of these buildings are con- structed of wrought iron, and though light in appearance are possessed of very ample strength. On each aide of the retort-house roof, and longitudinally therecuith, skylights are placed 6-feet deep between the second and third struts of the principals, glazed with j inch rolled plate glass. Adjoining the passage (18 feet) along the side of the coke store, is formed a square having about 80 feet in the clear, bounded on the west side by offices, experimental-room, governor, and station meter-house; on the south side by elevated cisterns for tar, ammoniacal liqaor and water, pump-house, engine-house, smithy, and boiler-house; and on the east side by by the condensers and scrubbers, the centre being occupied by large reservoirs for the storage of tar and liquor. A 6-inch main connects these reservoirs with the Mersey-street works, from which liquor is sent for removal by railway. The tar and liquor are there pumped from the reservoirs into the elevated cisterns, from which tanks are filled by gravity on the high level railway, thus avoiding all expense of haulage. Purifier-house.—The house for the reception of the puri- fiers is 90 feet long, 60 feet in width, and 33 feet in height. The purifiers are placed on the first floor, supported by a series of cast iron columns and girders. Alongside the puri- fier-house is another low level railway for bringing in and removing materials. The contractors for these buildings were Messrs. John Collin and Son, Warrington. The columns for supporting the high level railway in coal stores, also for supporting the roof of the coke store, and the columns and girders for supporting the purifiers are of cast iron, and weigh 79 tons. The girders for supporting the high leyi.l railway in coal stores are of wrought iron, and weigh 35 tons. This portion of the work was carried out by Messrs. Rushforth and Thornton, Bradford.

Gasholder Tank.—On the south of the purifier-house, an:l occupying the southern boundary of the Corporation's lands, is the gasholder tank, which is 122 feet diameter, and 24 feet deep in the clear. It is built throughout with hard and carefully-selected bricks, set in Portland onnent, and finished with a stone curb. The contractors were Messrs. George Smith and Co., Southport.

div.head: APPARATXI9.
div.p: APPARATXI9.

Hydraulic Main.—The main is suspended from wrought iron girders, supported by verticals isolated from the bench, and the level of the main is regulated and maintained by bolts and nuts, thus avoiding the constant variation in level by the heating up, or letting down, the retort beds, with all the evil effects resulting therefrom. There are other im- provements connected with the hydraulic main, which could not be understood without the aid of drawings, but which are effective for their purpose. Condensers.—The condensilg and scrubbing apparatus consists of a double series of vertical 12-inch pipes, 30 feet in height, in which, by mechanical arrangements, the gas is divided into 14 or 28 divisions, corresponding to the number of pipes, in order to produce a slow downward mo ion of the gas, thus securing a more perfect deposition of the liquids held in suspension by the gas. The exhaust is produced by a jet of steam in the Cleland and Korting ex- hauster. Uniform with the condensers in external appear- ance is the steam scrubber, in which, as in the condenser, the gis is subdivided, and the retarded process brought into

operation ; Purifiers.—The purifiers are six in number, twenty feet square and five feet deep. Four of these are charged with oxide of iron for the removal of the sulphur ccmpounds, and two with lime for the removal of carbonic acid. These vessAs are constructed of cast iron, and furnished with wood grids for supporting the purifying material. They are each provided with two shoots, mounted with sealing doers, for the more convenient removal from the purifier of the spent material to the floor below, where it is again oxidized and fitted for further use.. The weight of each of these vessels in cast iron i 18k, and of wrought iron in covers 3,4 tons, together 22 tons, the total weight being 132 tons, and when charged with materials, about 250 tons. These were furnished and fitted up by Messrs. Newton, Chambers and Co., Sheffield.

Hoisting Apparatus —ln combination with the purifiers an arrangement has been adopted for lifting the purifying materials from the lower to the higher level, and discharging them directly into the pu:ifiers, which consist of an 8-h.p. steam engine and endless chain buckets. With the same power the covers of the purifi,rs are lifted, and by a simple and convenient arrangemmt the crab is thrown out of gear when the covers are raised to a certain height, thus provid. ing against the prolphility of accidents when depending on the stoppage of thc engine. This machinery was supplied and fitted up by Messrs. Woodward and Sons, Man- chester.

Station ilfeter.—The station meter is a cnue of 13 feet 3 inches, and ciplble of pissing 70,000 cubic feet of gas per hour, which is jest double the present generating power of the works. The m tkers are Messrs. J. and J. Braddock, Oldham,

GashoWen—The gasholder is 120 feet diameter in the under, and 118 feet in the upper lift, and 46 feet in height, having a capacity of 511,600 cubic feet. It is very efficiently trussed in the roof, and the sides are supported by strong wrought channel iron. Owing to its very exposed situation, Mr. Paterson allowed a considerable increase of strength to the whole fabric beyond that he had usually adopted. The weight of the gasholder is 154 tons, and the wrought iron in the lattice girders and trough guides is 43 tons, together 191 tons of wrought iron. The gas%tolder is supported by fourteen columns of cast iron, each three feet diameter at the base, and 49 feet in height, all of which are bound • to- gether by two rows of lattice girders. The weight of these columns is 191 tons, and the total weight of the structure 558 tons. Notwithstanding the highly satisfactory and sub- stantial eh tracter of the work, it forms he cheapest in con- struction of any with which the engineer his had to do, and is equal t the unusually low figure of a 121 per 1,000 cubic feet capaeity. The contracto:s were Messrs. Clayton, Son, and Co., frunslet, Leeds. Governur.—Tho gas bAralr, discharged from the holder is passed through a governor, the pressure of which is actu- ated by water and the flow of gas regulated with great steadiness and accuracy. From thence it is conveyed through the distributing system of mains in connection therewith.

Distributing Itains.—A 20-inch main leads from the works to a point in Winwick-road opposite the south side of Kerfoot-street. Ti:is main is laid'l;nder the footpoth on the etst side of the rood, and the delis,wing power at it 3 termi- nation under a 2 inch water pressure on the governor i3tqual to 101,000 cultic feet p,!l. hour. An 18-inch main commu- nicates \with the 20 inch, and is continued alontt tie footpath t, the bottom of Ithrsnnarke-street, where it \VAS found nocessory to carry it into the street, and to follow the tr.ck of the old 7-inch main which was removed. The 18-inch terminates at the junction with the lckvsey-street main, and its delivering powers at that paint, under a 2-inch pressure at its juncqon with the 20-inch, ia ((pal to 113,700 cubic

feet per hour. A 16-inch main is laid in Horsernarket-street ,o within 10 yards of the centre of Market-gate, where a junction is made with the old 7-inch there, also with all the principal streets on the lino of the trunk main. The deliver- ing power of the 16-inch is 91,000 cubic feet per hour. In connection with these mains, and laid in the same track, is a 6-inch main from the new works to Market-gate, and from thence to the Mersey-street works, by Bank-street, for the- purpose of sending the ammoniacal liquor to Longford, for removal by railway. A new 10-inch distributing main corn-1 mu nicates with the 20-inch in Winwick-road, and is carried along the suth side of Kerfoot-street to Dallam-lane, and from thence under the footpath on the east side of Dallam-lane to Tanner's-lane, terminating at the cross junction between Tanner's-lane and'Froghall-lane, Bewsey- street and Bewsey-road. The discharging power of the main at this point, under a 2-inch pressure at Winwick-road is 14,350 cubic feet per hour. Another 10-inch main com- municates with the 18-inch in Winwick-road, and is carried under the footpath along Longford-street to Orford-lane, connecting the 3-inch main there, and also the 3-inch main to Orford and the 6-inch in Battereby-lane ; from thence it is carried along Marshhouse-lane by the Barracks, and con- tinued to Manchester-road, where a connection is formed with the 3-inch in that district. The discharging power at this point under a 2-inch pressure at Winwick-road is Equal t ) '2-5,700 cubic feet per hour. From the central junction at Bewsey-street, a 7-inch main is laid under the footpath on the south side of Froghall-lane, and continued along Priestley-street to Sankey-green, past the junction to Lovely-lane The discharging power at this point, under a pressure of 11-inch at Bewsey-street, is equal to 10,200 cubic feet per hour. The 3-inch main thus replaced has been re- laid under the footpath on the opposita side of the street as a subsidiary main, connected at several points with the 7-inch, and is nearly co-extensive therewith. From Sankey- green a 6-inch main is carried down Powvs-street in place of the 3-inch, and a junction made with the 6-inch in Liver- pool-road, which is carried forward to Sankey Bridges, and is there connected with the 3-inch which passes down into the 12-inch lying und,r the canal. Major CARTWRIGIIT moved the resolution of which he had given notice:—" That the business of the Board com- mence at half-past nine a.m , instead of ten o'clock, and that relief cases be proceeded with."—fhis having been seconded, Mr. HAURISON opposed the motion on the ground that the saving of time would be inflilitesimal.—Dr. MACKIE sup- ported the motion, and pointed cut the length of time occu- pied in reading the minutes of the committees, which he urged should be printed, as at the Town Council.—Mr. Jras.Ns also supported the proposed alteration in the time of meeting, stating that he would rather listen to relief cases than to the speeches of the members.—The motion on being put to the vote was lost, and this being the whole of the special business, the members rose, only two Warrington Guardians—the chairman and Mr. Harrison—rejnaining to deal with the applications for relief.

div.head: MR. E. F. BREWTNALL'S PICTURES.
div.p: MR. E. F. BREWTNALL'S PICTURES.

Mr E. F. Brevrinall has contributed 's vary striking pic- tnre to the present exhibition of the Royal Society of Painters in Watercolours, of which body he is an associate. It represents a stretch of common in the evening, with a storm approaching, the heavy, black storm-clouds and the red sunset casting a- lurid glare over the landscape, the eff-ct of which is very telling. In the foreground is a weird- looking fir tree bending in the wind, and just disappearing behind the undergrowth is a horseman hastening home before the storm actually breaks upon. him. The Illustrated Lon- don News, speaking of this picture, says :—" Mr. F. F. Brewtnall takes a higher flight than usual in a drawing (196) highly expressive of the effect of wind ; " while the Sunday Times says :—" Mr. Brewtnall has a peculiarly fine land- scape, entitled 'On the Wings of the Wind ; ' the gale in pro- gress is well depicted, and there is a rosy cloud in the tempes- tuoussky,which gives the charm of colour to the whole draw- ing." Mr. Brewtnal I also has an important picl ure in the Gros- venor Gallery,called "The Fairy Tale," which has been favour- ably noticed by the critics. This picture is amusingly cari- catured in this week's Punch. Coming nearer home, we find Mr. Brewtnall represented in Liverpool by a water-colour drawing of more than usual interest. The Liverpool Daily Post speaks of this picture, the title of which is "Driving Home the Flock," as "a clever work, which will repay care- ful examination, being full of solid painting and poetic feeling." The Courier thus speaks of it: " Mr. E. F. Brewt- nall is represented by only one picture, ' Driving Home the Flock,' a painting of great merit. The colour is admirable, and the entire composition shows fine execution and taste."

In 1878-9, the first year under the Corporation, the increase in the make of gag over the previous year was five millions cubic feet ; in 1879-80, the increase was seven millions ; in 1880.1, four millions; and in 1881-2, when the supple- mentary mains were partly laid, the increase rose to sixteen millions, while during the past year there is another increase of nearly fourteen millions. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Wednesday. Pre- sent—Messrs. J. Greening (chairman), E. C. Cooper, W. Darbyshire, J. Harrison, J. Houghton, Humphries, Hunt, Siddeley, Balharry, W. div.head: A. TAILOR WANTED.
div.p: A. TAILOR WANTED.

Major CaarwrarcinT moved the adoption of the minutes of the House Committee, who recommended that an in- dustrial trainer (a tailor) be appointed for the house.—Mr. WORTHINGTON seconded the motion.—Mr. HARRISOII pre- sumed they really meant to appoint a person to be em- ployed as tailor at the schools. If so, he would like to ask whether it was intended to bring back to the house Green- way, who had been with them for a long time, and who was temporarily employed at the schools.—Mr. BLACKItURS7 asked whether they were going to employ a tailor, for whom they could not obtain a grant from the Local Government Board. It was a matter of grave consideration whether they should appoint a tailor, and he asked whether, if the recommendation were passed, they empowered the commit- tee to appoint a tailor at any salary they liked to give ? Maier CARTWRIGHT, in reply, said it was impossible for them to get on at the house without a tailor. Thera was a great deal of work in arrear, and the committee had been waiting for the appointment of a tailor for the new schools before bringing the matter forward. If the Schools Com- mittee thought proper to appoint someone else besides the the man Greenway, who had been a servant at the house for a great many years, and who was removed to the Barracks temporarily, and on the understanding that he should re- turn to his old place, he hoped tbe Schools Committee would carry out that arrangement. With regard to the statement that there was no necessity for the appointment of a tailor at the house, if gentlemen would only make themselves ac- qnainted with the administration of the house they would not need to ask the chairman of the House Committee any such question. They would know very well that there were 100 cvaildren in the house, and that there were always several boys and girls who required training and who should be put in training as soon as they were admitted into the house. There were now boys who required training in the house whom there was no 709 M for at Pad- gate.—Mr. BLACICIIIIRST : Oh !—Major CARTWRIGHT : Eh? (Cries of Go on.") He repeated that there over 100 boys and girls at the house, and some of them were fit to go to Padgate, but there was no room for them.— Mr. BLACLITURST : We have room for 50.—The Crum- MAN : Mr. Blackhurst, will you allow Major Cartwright to finish ?—Major CARTWRIQFT said the appointment of a tailor was absolutely nev_ssary. It was not a question of what wages they would give, because whatever recommen- dation the committee might make had to be ratified by the Board before the committee coald carry it out. He believed the Local Government Board would not object to the ap- pointment of a tailor for the house because a tailor was absolutely required.—The minutes were adopted.
THE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS: THE NEW OFFICERS-" PERSONS

At a meeting-of the Schools Committee, held on the 29th May, the medical officer's report was read. Three children were ordered by him to the hospital for skin disease, all the other children being in good health. The superintendent was directed to send to Mr. Pierpoint, architect, a list of defects contained in his several reports, and any other he may ascertain. The committee recommended the appoint- : ment of the following industrial teachers :—A tailor and his ' wife without children, at a joint salary of £4O with house and rations a shoemaker and his wife on similar terms; suitable handicraftsman for general work, and wife, on. similar terms; also that the present farm instructor and superintendent of outdoor labour, John Fairhurst, be appeinted to that office, an 4 that his wife be portress9 with other duties as industrial teacher, at a joint salary of 27a. per week, with house, coals, and gas, and ! such vegetables as were growing on the premises. That the ages of the persons to be appointed be from 25 to 40 years of age. That Mr. Mines be re-appointed superintendent and schoolmaster, and Mrs. Mines Matron, at their present salaries (of £lO and £25 as superintendent and matron.)— Mr. DARIaTSHIRE moved the adoption of the minutes. Re- garding the handicraftsman, the committee did not bind themselves to appoint a man of any particular trade. They wanted a " Jack-of-all-trades "—(laughter)—and they would be guided very much in their choice of an applicant by his skill in various directions. The committee wanted a man to attend to the engine, to do coopering, joiner's, and smith's work, dm (Laughter.)-7Mr. HUNT seconded the confirma- tion of the minutes.—Dr. Mamie asked whether the rule laid down about applicants having no children was to be al "perpetual injunction," or was really an injunction that ought to be put in the advertisement at all. He thought it ' was an injunction that Vf;l9 not creditable to them as Guar- dians; it was poeitively putting a stop to procreation. (Laughter.)—Mr. Mower suggested that the archi- tect should supply Napier's trustees with a list of the defects at the schsols, and also with an estimate of the probable cost of putting them in order.—Mr. Danwsuins said the committee might not adhere exactly to the terms of the advertisement in the r:lpeC'. mentioned by Dr. Mackie, but they would prefer c•niples who had no children. To commence with they thought it better to twee peeple without children, and not persons with five or six children. The committee, how- ever, did not wish to throw any reflection upon anyone with children.—Mr. llnnuisate: It would be a great reflec- tion upon them if they had not any. (Laughter.) The minutes were agreed to.—A discussion then eneued respec- ting the proceedings taken against the B,erd by Mr. Napier's trusters, in thecourse of which Major CARTIVRIG2IT Stitt of all work he had seen the cementing at the schools was the hest scamped. There was not the thickness of a sixpence of ce.nent, and he thought if the trustees of Napier's estate saw it they would stop the action; im- mediately.

div.head: DECREASE OF VAGRANCY,
div.p: THE DECREASE OF VAGRANCY,

The CLERK said he had received from Mr. Bsit Cane, a return of the v,u,ra.cy in Lincashire since the new Va4rancy Act came into operation, from which it appeared the vagrancy in the Warrington Union had cleereasid 35 per cent. as against a decrease of 36.8 throughout the county generally.—Mr. COOPER appealed to the public to assist the Guardians in putting a stop to vagrancy by ceasing tkeir indiscriminate almsgiving.

The CLERK read the following letter from the Rey. W. it. Williams (vicar), and Messrs. Win. Royston, and W. H. J. J,nkin9 (wardens) of Padgate Church :.—" We, the utaler- signed, the vicar and churchwardens of Padgate, beg to 'iring to your notice the following facts. For various reason it has I.c,en thought expedient to make- certain repairs, i.nicrove- molts, ttructarat ;,Iteratious,and enlargements o; tie church Padgaie, and embraced wilain thia wink Is the erec7ion of a chancel which previously tho church lid iv.ll possess, and which now approaches .F.-ompletion. This has only been effected afttr every eficrt has beau made ea the part of tbe vicar, hi i Pa11311i011'4F%a.r..,1, W.,:rat)3 to tat4s. stiffiqi,oot tunda

for the purpose; but, as you are probably aware, in carrying out an erection of this kind unforeseen difficulties are met with, and expenses incurred which no foresight can anticipate. That is the case here,as after every exertion has been made we shall have to make a large provision for extra expenses, over and above the amount of the contract, for carrying out the main schema; and one way in which the cost of doing the work has been increased is that it became necessary to take into account the additional accommodation required to seat the officials and children from the new industrial schools built under your auspices. To do this a larger sum than had been contemplated has had to be expended. Under the circumstances we are led to ask you to make a grant to- wards the chancel building fund, and we trust that having regard to the facts we have mentioned this application will receive your favourable consideration."—Major CART- : I am afraid you cannot, grant any- thing, except out of the interest fund. Of course, I don't know whether we have any power to grant anything or any fund to grant anything out of. If we have it is a very proper thing to do, because since our children have gone there it will entail additional expense upon the church people to make room for them; and as I take it for granted that the Protestant portion of the children will go to the church, if it is legal I will pro- pose that a subscription be given.—Mr. HARRISON said he would be glad to support such a proposition. Of course the only fund available would be the fund that had gone by various names—the Nemo fund, or interest fund. He thought out of that fund they might make,a grant, and he thought it would be used for a judicious purpose. It would only be fair to look upon the matter in a favourable light. —Major CARTWRIGHT : It is certainly a very modest re- quest. I would like to know whether it was in consequence of the children going there that this extension was I absolutely necessary P—Mr. J. HOUGHTON said if the chil- dren had not been removed to Padgate the church would have been enlarged, but not to the same extent.—Mr. DARETSHIRE said this was rather dangerous ground to move upon. If they granted the application they might expect a similar application from the Roman Catholics in Woolston who, he thought, would have the greatest number of chil- dren attending their place of worship, and very likely they might have an application from the Wesleyans.—Mr. BLACKHURST : It is not very likely.—Mr. DARHYSHIRE said that already the committee had incurred a small expense for someone of the Roman Catholic denomination to accom- pany the children to and from their place of worship. He did not object to the grant being made, only he wished to intimate that this application would net be the last the Board would have if they granted it.— Mr. HARRISON, in order to put an end to the controversy, moved that the Board offer a suliscription of £lo—Mr. }IL/Cl/HURST seconded.—Mr. J. Hot:Glum : I propose tha t we give more.—Mr. BOND/ELL asked whether it would not be well to postpone the consideration of the application un- til the next Board meeting to see whether any one else was likely to make a call upon them.—Mr. BLACEMIRST : I would deal with the applications as they come before us. —Mr. Husrr proposed as an amendment, that the Board subscribe £so.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Go on, that is an ex- cellent bid.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON : I second ft.—Major CART- WRIGHT asked the clerk whether it would be legal for the Board to give anything. Could they grant a subscription from the common fund of the Union ?—Mr. BROWN : If we cannot I would not grant it at all.—The CHAIRMAN said he should certainly oppose both sums. He should oppose it if was only one sovereign—until he knew that the Board had power legally to give it. (Hear, hear.) He might further say that if the Board con- sent to grant the application he should refuse to sign any cheque for a payment which he believed to be illegal. (Hear, hear.) He thought the proper course to take was to have the matter before the Board, and, if there was any- thing to give, give it. He thought it was possible they might pay a subscription out of the interest fund if they had the assurance of the clerk that they would not be called upon to refund the amount. If, however' the clerk could not give them such an assurance, then before the Board granted money out of public funds he thought they should get the permission of the Local Government Board to give the amount which the Guardians thought they ought to give. - (Hear, hear.)—Dr. MACZIE asked whether there was any arrangement with the vicar and churchwardens to find room for the scholars in that place of worship. If so, he thought the Board were bound to give a quid pro quo in some way or another. The CLERIC said the Board clearly could not in the waY it was proposes!, contribute anything from the Union funds The expenditure mould be an illegal expenditure altogether. —Mr. DARBYMIRE proposed that the discussion be not re- ported at all, and that the Board instruct the Clerk to reply to the letter privately, forwarding a cheque for 20 towards the chancel fund. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HARRISON seconded the proposition.—Major CARTWRIGHT did not think the, Board could call upon the reporters not to report anything that transpired at the Board. He thought this was a very fair application, and that they should meet it upon fair grounds.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE did not mean that there should be any secrecy whatever, but merely that they should obey the scriptural injunction—" Let not thy right hand know what thy left hand doeth."—lt was unanimously decided to subscribe £2O for services to be rendered.

This Company has been formed for the purpose of erecting in Warrington a Conservative Club. with a bowling green and tennis ground attached, for the use of the members of the War- rington Conservative Club and Association, with shops er offices on the ground floor of the building. The premises will be erected by the Company, and toe Club portion shall be let by them to the Warrington Conservative Club Committee, at , such a rent and upon such terms as may be agr.ed on between the Directors and the Club Committee. The shops will be a source of revenue for payment of the ground rent and other ex- penses of the Company Arrangements have been made on favourable terms with the Right Hon. Lord Wiumarleigh for the lease for 999 years of a sit: in Sankey-street, opu_site the Town Hall and the Post Office, for the erection of the buildings. as well as for the bowl- ing green and tennis ground; and Lord Winmarleigh has also offered to take a large number of shares in reduction of the ground rent. The nominal capital of the company has been fixed at £6,000, divided into Li shares, with a view to affording an inducement to the Conservative working men of Warrington and Latchford to take up stares, the desire of the promoters being to fix the amount of tile shares at such a sum as will place them within the reach of working men favourable to the Conservative cause, and so to give them a personal interest in the success of the un- dertaking. Sketch plans and suggested elevations have been prepared by Messrs. Pierpoint and Adams, Architects, Bold-street, War- rington, which may be seen either at their offices, or at the Conservative Club, Academy street. These are, however, subject to final approval by the Committee appolated for that purpose. The buildings proposed to be erected will comprise a hand- some block of two or three storeys, providing ample accommo- dation of every kind for the convenience of the Club, including a large reading room and meeting hall, which will be adapt- able for public meetings, lectures, concerts, &c., and shops or offices on the gri.und floor. The building will be so designed as to permit of the Club portions thereof being easily converti- ble to general uses, if necessary. The promoters believe that the proposed Club will afford most valuable means of bringing Conservatives together, and promoting the general interests of the party in Warrington; and also that the undertaking will prove to be a remunerati ye investment for the shareholders. It is intended that the working of the Club shall be subject to the supervision of the Directors. Applications for shares should be sent in at once, as the Diri.etors wish to proceed with the erection of the buildings with as little delay as possible. Forms of application for shares may be obtained from the Company's Bankers, Solicitors, Architects, or from Mr. JOHN HAMPSON, the Conservative Agent, at the Club, Academy- street, Warrington. Warrington, May. 1883.

LEWIS'S IN LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVIDING OF THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, HOTELS. AN B PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGI- OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known its London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago. and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of precuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints, and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such a change for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make thesale public In Lancashire, where they sell 20.000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. VIRESCOTUNION.--CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS, &c.—Persons desirous of CONTRACTING with the Guar- dians of this Union, for the next six months, for supplying at the Workhouse the several articles hereinafter named, viz. : Flour, oatmeal, salt butter, bacon, lard, cheese, peas, beef, mutton, suet, groceries, wine and spirits, eggs, potatoes, hay, wheat straw, coal, burgy, linen drapery, woollen drapery, smallwares, tinware, hardware, ironmongery, earthenware, leather, boots and shoes, brushes, timber, coffins, and other articles, are requested to deliver sealed Tenders, upon forms to be obtained at my office, at the Board-roots:1 of the said Union, in Whiston, on or before Thursday, the 14th June, before 10 a.m. Such tenders will be opened at the meeting of the Guar- dians on the last-named day. The Guardians will also take tenders for new milk and fregh butter for twelve months. The daily consumption of milk is about 60 gallons. Samples to be seen at the Workhouse. Security will be required for the per- formance of the contrae's. It is competent for any person within the I:Truon to tender for any of the articles separately. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender.—By order of the Board. B. H. HARTLEY, Union Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 31st May, 1883.
